items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists categories of people who can vow valuations (ערכים) or be valued, including priests, Levites, Israelites, women, and slaves. It then notes exceptions: tumtum and androgynos can vow but not be valued, while deaf-mutes, imbeciles, and minors can be valued but cannot vow due to lack of mental capacity.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that everyone can vow valuations (ערכים) and be valued, listing priests, Levites, Israelites, women, and slaves.
The Mishnah adds that a tumtum and androgynos can vow and be vowed, and can vow valuations, but cannot be valued because only definite males and females are valued.
The Mishnah concludes that deaf-mutes, imbeciles, and minors can be vowed and valued, but cannot vow or vow valuations because they lack mental capacity.

items.text: Gemara's first questions on 'הכל מעריכין' and 'נערכין'
items.text_en: Gemara's first questions on 'הכל מעריכין' and 'נערכין'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah's phrase 'הכל מעריכין' comes to include, answering: a minor close to majority (מופלא סמוך לאיש). For 'נערכין', it includes a repulsive person or one with boils, countering a possible exclusion based on the verse 'נדר בערכך' implying only those with market value.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah's phrase 'הכל מעריכין' comes to include, and answers: a minor close to majority (מופלא סמוך לאיש).
The Gemara asks what 'נערכין' comes to include, and answers: a repulsive person or one with boils.
The Gemara raises a possible objection: one might think that only those with market value (דמים) can be subject to valuations (ערכין), based on the verse 'נדר בערכך'.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah teaches us the word 'נפשת' (souls) includes any person, regardless of market value.

items.text: Gemara's questions on 'נודרין' and 'נידרין'
items.text_en: Gemara's questions on 'נודרין' and 'נידרין'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'נודרין' and 'נידרין' come to include, but notes that the Mishnah already explicitly lists tumtum, androgynos, deaf-mute, imbecile, minor, and a child less than a month old. It concludes that 'נידרין' includes a child less than a month old, as the Mishnah first states the general rule and then specifies.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah's term 'נודרין' comes to include, but immediately notes that the real need is for the term 'נידרין'.
The Gemara asks what 'נידרין' comes to include, but notes that the cases of tumtum, androgynos, deaf-mute, imbecile, and minor are already explicitly listed in the Mishnah.

The Gemara considers and rejects that 'נידרין' includes a child less than a month old, since that too is listed explicitly, but concludes that the Mishnah states the general rule first and then specifies the details.

items.text: Parallel to semikhah and temurah: dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis
items.text_en: Parallel to semikhah and temurah: dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis
items.desc_en: The Gemara draws a parallel to the Mishnah in Menachot and Temurah, where 'הכל סומכין' and 'הכל ממירין' come to include an heir, contrary to Rabbi Yehuda's view. The dispute is based on exegesis of the word 'קרבנו' and the analogy between the beginning and end of consecration. Rabbi Yehuda excludes the heir from semikhah and temurah, while the Rabbis include him via the verse 'המר ימיר' and a different analogy.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah's phrase 'הכל סומכין' (everyone lays hands) comes to include, and answers: an heir, contrary to Rabbi Yehuda's view.
The Gemara asks what the Mishnah's phrase 'הכל ממירין' (everyone substitutes) comes to include, and answers: an heir, contrary to Rabbi Yehuda's view.
A baraita is cited: an heir may perform semikhah (laying of hands) and temurah (substitution); Rabbi Yehuda says an heir may not perform semikhah or temurah.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning: the verse 'קרבנו' (his offering) excludes the father's offering, and he derives the beginning of consecration (temurah) from the end (semikhah) via an analogy — just as an heir does not perform semikhah at the end, so he does not perform temurah at the beginning.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the Rabbis' reasoning
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the Rabbis' reasoning
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains the Rabbis' reasoning: the verse 'המר ימיר' (he shall substitute) includes the heir, and they derive the end of consecration (semikhah) from the beginning (temurah) — just as an heir performs temurah at the beginning, so he performs semikhah at the end.
The Gemara asks how the Rabbis interpret the word 'קרבנו' (his offering), and answers: it excludes a gentile's offering, excludes a fellow's offering, and includes all partners in semikhah.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yehuda's alternative
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yehuda's alternative
sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yehuda either does not have the inclusion of all partners in semikhah, or alternatively he does have it.

items.text: Derivation of the gentile and partner from the same verse, and Rabbi Yehuda's use of 'המר ימיר'
items.text_en: Derivation of the gentile and partner from the same verse, and Rabbi Yehuda's use of 'המר ימיר'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the exclusion of a gentile and a partner from the laws of temurah come from the same verse, leaving two extra phrases: one for 'his offering' (not his father's offering) and one to include all partners in semikhah. It then asks what Rabbi Yehuda does with the phrase 'המר ימיר', answering that he uses it to include a woman in the laws of temurah, as a baraita teaches that the entire passage speaks in masculine language, so 'והמר ימיר' comes to include women. The Rabbis derive this from the word 'ואם', while Rabbi Yehuda does not expound 'ואם'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the exclusion of a gentile and a partner from temurah comes from one verse, leaving two extra phrases: one for 'his offering' (not his father's offering) and one to include all partners in semikhah.
The Gemara asks what Rabbi Yehuda does with the phrase 'המר ימיר' (he shall surely exchange).
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yehuda uses it to include a woman in temurah, citing a baraita that the entire passage speaks in masculine language, so 'והמר ימיר' comes to include women.
The Gemara explains that the Rabbis derive the inclusion of women from the word 'ואם', while Rabbi Yehuda does not expound 'ואם'.

items.text: Inclusion for the obligation of Re'iyah: half-slave half-free man, and the dispute between Ravina and the earlier Mishnah
items.text_en: Inclusion for the obligation of Re'iyah: half-slave half-free man, and the dispute between Ravina and the earlier Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'הכל חייבין בראייה' comes to include, initially answering a half-slave half-free man. However, Ravina exempts such a person from Re'iyah, so the Gemara suggests including a person who was lame on the first day and healed on the second. This works for the opinion that all days are make-ups for each other, but for the opinion that all days are make-ups for the first day, the Gemara suggests including a blind person in one eye, contrary to the view of Yochanan ben Dahavai. Alternatively, the Gemara resolves the issue by positing that the Mishnah about the half-slave half-free man is from an earlier Mishnah, while Ravina's ruling is from a later Mishnah, citing the dispute between Beit Hillel and Beit Shammai about forcing the master to free such a slave for the sake of procreation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the phrase 'הכל חייבין בראייה' (all are obligated in the pilgrimage appearance) comes to include, and initially answers: a half-slave half-free man.
Ravina objects that a half-slave half-free man is exempt from Re'iyah, so the Gemara suggests including a person who was lame on the first day and healed on the second.
The Gemara notes that this works only for the opinion that all days are make-ups for each other, but for the opinion that all days are make-ups for the first day, it asks what the phrase includes.
The Gemara suggests including a blind person in one eye, contrary to the view of Yochanan ben Dahavai.

A baraita cites Yochanan ben Dahavai in the name of Rabbi Yehuda that a blind person in one eye is exempt from Re'iyah, based on the verbal analogy of 'יראה' and 'יראה' (he shall see / he shall be seen).
The Gemara alternatively resolves that the Mishnah about the half-slave half-free man is from an earlier Mishnah, while Ravina's ruling is from a later Mishnah.

sub.text: Supporting Mishnah (Beit Hillel and Beit Shammai)
sub.text_en: Supporting Mishnah (Beit Hillel and Beit Shammai)
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah where Beit Hillel initially rules that a half-slave half-free man alternates days serving his master and himself, but Beit Shammai objects that this prevents procreation, and Beit Hillel retracts to rule like Beit Shammai that the master is forced to free him.

items.text: חיוב נשים במקרא מגילה
items.text_en: Inclusion of women in Megillah reading
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what novel case the clause 'הכל חייבין במקרא מגילה' includes, and answers that it includes women, citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's reason that they were part of the miracle.
items.desc: הגמרא מבארת שהביטוי 'הכול' במשנה בא לרבות נשים לחיוב קריאת מגילה, כדברי רבי יהושע בן לוי, משום שאף הן היו באותו הנס.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what novel case the clause 'הכל חייבין במקרא מגילה' includes, and answers that it includes women.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מה בא הביטוי 'הכל' במשנה לרבות, ועונה: לרבות נשים לחיוב קריאת מגילה.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi explains that women are obligated in Megillah reading because they were part of the miracle.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מה בא הביטוי 'הכל' במשנה לרבות, ועונה: לרבות נשים לחיוב קריאת מגילה.

items.text: טומאת זיבה בקטן בן יומו
items.text_en: Inclusion of a day-old infant in zav impurity
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'הכל מטמאין בזיבה' includes, and answers that it includes a day-old infant, citing a dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yishmael about the derivation from 'איש איש'.
items.desc: הגמרא מבארת ש'הכול מיטמאין בזיבה' בא לרבות תינוק בן יומו, כדברי רבי יהודה. רבי ישמעאל חולק וסובר שאין צורך במיעוט זה, שהרי הכתוב כולל כל זכר ונקבה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah's statement 'הכל מטמאין בזיבה' (everyone imparts uncleanness through a zav) comes to include.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מה באה הברייתא 'הכל מיטמאין בזיבה' לרבות.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: the verse 'איש איש' teaches that a day-old infant can become a zav, according to Rabbi Yehuda.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מה באה הברייתא 'הכל מיטמאין בזיבה' לרבות.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael objects that the extra derivation is unnecessary, because 'לזכר' and 'לנקבה' already include minors of any age.
sub.desc: רבי ישמעאל חולק וסובר שאין צורך בריבוי זה, שהרי הכתוב 'לזכר ולנקבה' מרבה כל גיל.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael resolves: 'איש איש' is merely the Torah speaking in human language, not adding a halacha.
sub.desc: רבי ישמעאל חולק וסובר שאין צורך בריבוי זה, שהרי הכתוב 'לזכר ולנקבה' מרבה כל גיל.

items.text: טומאת מת בקטן ומיעוטו מכרת
items.text_en: Inclusion of a minor in corpse impurity and exclusion from karet
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'הכל מטמאין בטמא מת' includes, and answers that it includes a minor, countering a possible exclusion from 'איש'. It then clarifies that 'איש' serves to exclude a minor from karet.
items.desc: הגמרא מבארת ש'הכול מיטמאין בטמא מת' בא לרבות קטן, אף שנאמר 'איש אשר יטמא'. המילה 'איש' באה למעט קטן מכרת, ולא מטומאה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the phrase 'הכל מטמאין בטמא מת' (all become impure through a corpse-impure person) comes to include, and answers that it includes a minor.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מה באה הברייתא 'הכל מיטמאין בטמא מת' לרבות, ועונה: לרבות קטן.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a possible objection: the verse 'איש אשר יטמא' (a man who becomes impure) might exclude a minor, but the phrase 'ועל הנפשות אשר היו שם' (and concerning the souls that were there) teaches otherwise.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מה באה הברייתא 'הכל מיטמאין בטמא מת' לרבות, ועונה: לרבות קטן.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the term 'איש' (a man) in that verse serves to exclude a minor from the punishment of כרת (karet).
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת: אם כן, למה נאמר 'איש' בפסוק? מה הוא בא למעט?

items.text: טומאת נגעים בקטן ופרטי דיני איש ואשה
items.text_en: Inclusion of a minor in negaim and gender distinction
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'הכל מטמאין בנגעים' includes, and answers that it includes a minor, despite the verse 'איש צרוע'. It then explains that 'איש' teaches that a man, but not a woman, must uncover and rend his garments.
items.desc: הגמרא מבארת ש'הכול מיטמאין בנגעים' בא לרבות קטן, שכן הכתוב 'כי יהיה בעור בשרו' כולל כל אדם. המילה 'איש' באה ללמד שאיש פורע ופורם, אבל אשה אינה פורעת ופורמת.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the phrase 'הכל מטמאין בנגעים' (everyone is impure with negaim) comes to include.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מה באה הברייתא 'הכל מיטמאין בנגעים' לרבות, ועונה שהיא באה לרבות קטן.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that it includes a minor, despite the verse 'איש צרוע' (a leprous man) which might exclude him, but the verse 'כי יהיה בעור בשרו' (when there is in the skin of his flesh) includes anyone.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מה באה הברייתא 'הכל מיטמאין בנגעים' לרבות, ועונה שהיא באה לרבות קטן.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: perhaps the inclusion of a minor is indeed from 'כי יהיה בעור בשרו' (when there is in the skin of his flesh), so why is 'איש' (man) needed at all?
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: מדוע לא נאמר שקטן אינו מיטמא בנגעים, שהרי נאמר 'כי יהיה בעור בשרו' לרבות כל אדם?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that 'איש' (man) is needed to teach that a woman is also included in the laws of negaim, as derived from the verse 'והצרוע' (and the leper).
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת: אם כן, לשם מה נכתב 'איש צרוע'? ומשיבה: ללמד שאשה נלמדת מ'והצרוע'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara further resolves that 'איש' (man) teaches a gender distinction: a man must uncover and rend his garments, but a woman does not.
sub.desc: הגמרא מיישבת: 'איש' בא ללמד שהאיש פורע ופורם, אבל האשה אינה פורעת ופורמת.

items.text: כשרות לראות נגעים – מי שאינו בקי
items.text_en: Inclusion of an unskilled examiner in negaim
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'הכל רואין את הנגעים' includes, and answers that it includes one who is not expert in them and their names. It resolves a contradiction by distinguishing between one who can be taught and one who cannot.
items.desc: הגמרא מבארת ש'הכול רואין את הנגעים' בא לרבות מי שאינו בקי בהם ובשמותיהם, בתנאי שמסברי ליה וסבר. רבינא מיישב את הסתירה לכאורה בין הברייתות.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the mishnaic phrase 'הכל רואין את הנגעים' (all may examine negaim) and 'הכל כשרין לראות את הנגעים' (all are fit to examine negaim) come to include.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מה באה לרבות הברייתא 'הכל רואין את הנגעים' ו'הכל כשרין לראות את הנגעים', ועונה: לרבות מי שאינו בקי בנגעים ובשמותיהם.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that it includes one who is not expert in the negaim and their names.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מה באה לרבות הברייתא 'הכל רואין את הנגעים' ו'הכל כשרין לראות את הנגעים', ועונה: לרבות מי שאינו בקי בנגעים ובשמותיהם.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Mar previously stated that one who is not expert in them and their names may not examine negaim.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: והלא אמר מר שמי שאינו בקי בנגעים ובשמותיהם אינו רואה את הנגעים, וסתירה לכאורה לדין הקודם.

sub.desc_en: Ravina resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between one who can be taught and understands, and one who can be taught but does not understand.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: והלא אמר מר שמי שאינו בקי בנגעים ובשמותיהם אינו רואה את הנגעים, וסתירה לכאורה לדין הקודם.

items.text: כשרות לקדש – קטן או אשה
items.text_en: Inclusion in sanctifying the Red Heifer
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'הכל כשרין לקדש' includes, and answers that according to Rabbi Yehuda it includes a minor, and according to the Rabbis it includes a woman, citing the Mishnah.
items.desc: הגמרא מבארת ש'הכול כשרין לקדש' בא לרבות קטן לרבי יהודה, ולאשה לרבנן. המשנה מפרטת את הפסולים: חרש שוטה וקטן, ורבי יהודה מכשיר בקטן ופוסל באשה ובאנדרוגינוס.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah's phrase 'הכל כשרין לקדש' (all are fit to sanctify the Red Heifer) comes to include.
The Gemara answers that according to Rabbi Yehuda it includes a minor, and according to the Rabbis it includes a woman, citing the Mishnah's dispute.

items.text: כשרות להזות – ערל
items.text_en: Inclusion of an uncircumcised man in sprinkling
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'הכל כשרין להזות' includes, and answers that it includes an uncircumcised man, citing Rabbi Elazar that his sprinkling is valid.
items.desc: הגמרא מבארת ש'הכול כשרין להזות' בא לרבות ערל, כדברי רבי אלעזר, שהזאתו כשרה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah's phrase 'הכל כשרין להזות' (all are fit to sprinkle) comes to include.
The Gemara answers that it includes an uncircumcised man (ערל), citing Rabbi Elazar's statement that his sprinkling is valid.

items.text: Inclusion of a Samaritan and an apostate in slaughter
items.text_en: Inclusion of a Samaritan and an apostate in slaughter
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'הכל שוחטין' includes, and answers that one clause includes a Samaritan and another includes an apostate Israelite.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the phrase 'הכל שוחטין' (everyone slaughters) comes to include.
The Gemara answers that one clause includes a Samaritan (כותי) and another includes an apostate Israelite (ישראל משומד).

items.text: Inclusion in ascending to Eretz Yisrael
items.text_en: Inclusion in ascending to Eretz Yisrael
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'הכל מעלין לארץ ישראל' includes, but the daf ends before providing the answer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah's phrase 'הכל מעלין לארץ ישראל' (all may ascend to Eretz Yisrael) comes to include.

items.text: Extension of 'all bring up' and 'all do not take out' to slaves
items.text_en: Extension of 'all bring up' and 'all do not take out' to slaves
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's phrase 'all bring up' includes slaves, and for the one who explicitly teaches slaves, it adds moving from a nice dwelling to a bad one. 'All do not take out' includes a slave who fled from outside the land to the land, and for the explicit teacher, it adds moving from a bad dwelling to a nice one.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: For the one who explicitly teaches slaves in the Mishnah, what additional case does the phrase 'all bring up' include? It answers: moving from a nice dwelling to a bad one.
The Gemara explains that 'all do not take out' includes a slave who fled from outside the land to the land, and for the explicit teacher, it adds moving from a bad dwelling to a nice one.

items.text: All are obligated in sukkah – priests included
items.text_en: All are obligated in sukkah – priests included
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah needs to state that priests are obligated in sukkah, as it is obvious. It explains that one might have thought priests are exempt because sukkah requires dwelling like a home (איש ואשתו), and priests are busy with Temple service. The Gemara teaches that while they are exempt during service, they are obligated when not serving, like travelers who are exempt by day but obligated by night.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah needs to state that priests are obligated in sukkah, as it is obvious.

The Gemara explains that the Mishnah needed to include priests because one might have thought they are exempt, since sukkah requires dwelling like a home (איש ואשתו) and priests are busy with Temple service.
The Gemara resolves that while priests are exempt during service, they are obligated when not serving, like travelers who are exempt by day but obligated by night, as stated by Mar.

items.text: All are obligated in tzitzit – priests included
items.text_en: All are obligated in tzitzit – priests included
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why priests need to be mentioned for tzitzit. It suggests one might think priests are exempt because they are permitted to wear sha'atnez (wool-linen mixture) during service, and tzitzit is linked to the prohibition of sha'atnez. The Gemara teaches that the permission for sha'atnez applies only during service, not at other times.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that all are obligated in tzitzit, including priests, Levites, and Israelites, which seems obvious.

The Gemara explains that the Mishnah needed to mention priests because one might have thought they are exempt from tzitzit due to the permission to wear sha'atnez (wool-linen mixture) during service, since tzitzit is linked to the prohibition of sha'atnez.
The Gemara resolves that the permission for sha'atnez applies only during the time of service, not at other times, so priests are obligated in tzitzit outside of service.

items.text: All are obligated in tefillin – priests included
items.text_en: All are obligated in tefillin – priests included
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why priests are mentioned for tefillin. One might think priests are exempt from head tefillin because they are exempt from hand tefillin (due to the requirement that nothing interpose between the priestly garments and skin), and the two are linked. The Gemara teaches that hand and head tefillin do not impede each other, as per a Mishnah. It then addresses why the hand is singled out for the interposition verse, explaining that the priest's hair was visible between the tzitz and mitznefet, where tefillin are placed.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that all are obligated in tefillin, including priests, Levites, and Israelites, and the Gemara questions why this is not obvious.

The Gemara explains that priests needed to be mentioned, because one might think they are exempt from head tefillin since they are exempt from hand tefillin due to the interposition requirement, and the two are linked.
The Gemara teaches that hand and head tefillin do not impede each other, citing a Mishnah that one does not prevent the other.
The Gemara objects: why is the hand singled out for the interposition verse, when the head also has a verse about the mitznefet (priestly turban) that might interpose?
A Tanna resolves that the priest's hair was visible between the tzitz and the mitznefet, and that is where tefillin are placed, so there is no interposition.

items.text: All are obligated in shofar – priests included
items.text_en: All are obligated in shofar – priests included
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why priests are mentioned for shofar. One might think priests are exempt because they are already obligated in trumpets (חצוצרות) throughout the year, and shofar might be considered redundant. The Gemara rejects this, noting trumpets are different from shofar. Another concern is that since the Jubilee year is compared to Rosh Hashanah for shofar and blessings, and priests are not obligated in Jubilee (as they can redeem their fields at any time), one might think they are exempt from Rosh Hashanah shofar. The Gemara implies this concern is addressed.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that all are obligated in shofar, including priests, Levites, and Israelites, and the Gemara asks why this is not obvious.
The Gemara explains that the Mishnah needed to include priests, because one might think they are exempt since they are already obligated in trumpet blasts throughout the year.
The Gemara rejects the concern, noting that trumpets (חצוצרות) are different from shofar (שופר), so the obligation is not redundant.

The Gemara raises a second concern: since the Jubilee year is compared to Rosh Hashanah for shofar and blessings, and priests are not obligated in Jubilee (as they can redeem their fields at any time), one might think they are exempt from Rosh Hashanah shofar.

items.text: Completion of the previous Mishnah's discussion on release years
items.text_en: Completion of the previous Mishnah's discussion on release years
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the previous sugya: although women are not subject to land-release (השמטת קרקע), they are subject to money-release (השמטת כספים) and slave-release (שילוח עבדים), so the Mishnah's 'everyone' is needed to include them for the latter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the previous sugya: although women are exempt from land-release (השמטת קרקע), they are subject to money-release (השמטת כספים) and slave-release (שילוח עבדים), so the Mishnah's 'everyone' includes them for the latter.

items.text: Everyone is obligated in Megillah reading
items.text_en: Everyone is obligated in Megillah reading
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah needs to state that everyone is obligated in Megillah reading, and answers that it teaches that even priests, Levites, and Israelites who are engaged in Temple service must interrupt their work to hear the Megillah, as per Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah needs to state that 'everyone is obligated in reading the Megillah', since it is obvious.

sub.text: Gemara's answer citing Rav Yehuda said Shmuel
sub.text_en: Gemara's answer citing Rav Yehuda said Shmuel
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah is needed to teach that even priests, Levites, and Israelites who are engaged in Temple service must interrupt their work to hear the Megillah, as per Rav Yehuda's statement in the name of Shmuel.

items.text: Everyone is obligated in Zimmun (Grace after meals)
items.text_en: Everyone is obligated in Zimmun (Grace after meals)
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's 'everyone is obligated in Zimmun' is needed to include priests who eat sacred foods (קדשים). One might think that since the verse says 'they shall eat those things wherewith atonement was made', and atonement is involved, they might be exempt from Zimmun. The Gemara teaches that the verse 'and you shall eat and be satisfied' applies to them as well, obligating them in Zimmun.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah needs to state that 'everyone is obligated in זימון (invitation to bless after a meal)', since it is obvious.

The Gemara explains that the Mishnah is needed because priests who eat קדשים (sacred offerings) might be thought exempt due to the verse 'וְאָכְלוּ אוֹתָם אֲשֶׁר כֻּפַּר בָּהֶם' (they shall eat them, for atonement was made with them), implying their eating is for atonement, not for satisfaction; but the Mishnah teaches that the verse 'וְאָכַלְתָּ וְשָׂבָעְתָּ' (you shall eat and be satisfied) applies to them as well, obligating them in זימון.

The Gemara explains that the Mishnah is needed for priests who eat sacred foods (קדשים), as one might think that since the verse says 'they shall eat those things wherewith atonement was made' and atonement is involved, they might be exempt from Zimmun.
The Gemara resolves that the verse 'וְאָכַלְתָּ וְשָׂבָעְתָּ' (and you shall eat and be satisfied) applies to them as well, obligating them in Zimmun.

items.text: Everyone joins for Zimmun
items.text_en: Everyone joins for Zimmun
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that everyone joins together for Zimmun. The Gemara explains this is needed for a case where priests eat terumah or sacred foods and a non-priest eats non-sacred food. One might think that since the non-priest cannot eat with the priest, they should not join. The Gemara teaches that since the priest can eat with the non-priest (by eating non-sacred food), they can join.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah needs to state that 'everyone joins together for זימון', since it is obvious.

The Gemara explains that the Mishnah is needed because a priest eating תרומה (priestly portion) or קדשים and a non-priest eating חולין (non-sacred food) might be thought unable to join together, since the non-priest cannot eat the priest's food; but the Mishnah teaches that since the priest can eat the non-priest's food, they can join.
The Gemara explains that the Mishnah is needed for a case where priests eat תרומה (priestly portion) or sacred foods, while a non-priest eats non-sacred food.
One might think that since the non-priest cannot eat with the priest (due to the priest's sacred food), they should not join for Zimmun.
The Mishnah teaches that although the non-priest cannot eat with the priest, the priest can eat with the non-priest (by eating non-sacred food), so they can join.

items.text: Everyone can make valuations (ערכין) – including priests
items.text_en: Everyone can make valuations (ערכין) – including priests
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that everyone can make valuations. The Gemara questions why this is necessary, and Rava explains it is needed for the case of Ben Bukhri, who testified that a priest who contributes the half-shekel does not sin. The Gemara discusses the dispute between Ben Bukhri and Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, and then explains that one might think that since priests are exempt from the half-shekel, they might also be exempt from valuations, but the Mishnah teaches otherwise.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah needs to state that 'everyone makes valuations (ערכים)', since it is obvious.

Rava explains that the Mishnah is needed to include a priest like בן בוכרי (Ben Bukhri), who argued that priests who donate the half-shekel are sinning, but the Gemara clarifies that since priests are not obligated לכתחילה (a priori) to bring the shekel, if they do bring it they sin by bringing חולין (non-sacred items) into the Temple courtyard, unless they give it to the community.

The Gemara resolves that one might have thought that since valuations are linked to shekels, and priests are exempt from shekels, they would be exempt from valuations; but the Mishnah teaches that they are obligated.
Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai objects that a priest who does not give the half-shekel sins, and cites a verse about the priest's meal-offering being entirely burnt.
The Gemara asks how the priestly offerings (omer, two loaves, showbread) can be eaten if they belong to the priests.

The Gemara resolves that for Ben Bukhri, since priests are not obligated to give the half-shekel לכתחילה (a-priori), if they do give it they sin by bringing חולין (non-sacred items) into the Temple courtyard, unless they give it to the community.
The Gemara concludes that one might have thought that since priests are exempt from the half-shekel, they are also exempt from valuations, but the Mishnah teaches otherwise.

items.text: Abaye's objection to the first derivation
items.text_en: Abaye's objection to the first derivation
items.desc_en: Abaye objects to the previous derivation linking valuations to the half-shekel, arguing that the verse 'and all your valuations shall be according to the shekel of the sanctuary' teaches that valuations must be at least a shekel, not that one must be subject to the half-shekel to be subject to valuations.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects that the verse 'וְכׇל עֶרְכְּךָ' (and all your valuation) comes to teach that valuations should not be less than a סלע (sela coin), not to link valuations to shekels.

items.text: Abaye's alternative derivation from redemption of the firstborn
items.text_en: Abaye's alternative derivation from redemption of the firstborn
items.desc_en: Abaye offers a different reason: one might think that since priests are exempt from redemption of the firstborn (פדיון הבן), they might also be exempt from valuations, but the Mishnah teaches that they are not exempt.

sub.desc_en: Abaye offers an alternative explanation: the Mishnah is needed because one might think that since valuations are linked to פדיון הבן (redemption of the firstborn), and priests are exempt from פדיון הבן, they would be exempt from valuations; but the Mishnah teaches they are obligated.

items.text: Rava's objection to Abaye's derivation
items.text_en: Rava's objection to Abaye's derivation
items.desc_en: Rava objects to Abaye's derivation by pointing out that if the logic were applied to the ram of the guilt-offering (איל אשם), it would absurdly exclude tumtum and androgynos from bringing it, which is not the case.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects that if the link were to פדיון הבן, then by the same logic, a טומטום (androgynous) or אנדרוגינוס (hermaphrodite), who are exempt from valuations, would be exempt from bringing an איל אשם (ram for a guilt-offering), which is absurd.

items.text: Rava's (or Rav Ashi's) final derivation
items.text_en: Rava's (or Rav Ashi's) final derivation
items.desc_en: Rava (or Rav Ashi) explains that the Mishnah is needed because one might think that since the verse says 'and he shall present him before the priest', a priest cannot present another priest for valuation, but the Mishnah teaches that a priest can indeed be valued.

sub.desc_en: Rava (or Rav Ashi) explains that the Mishnah is needed because one might think that since the verse says 'וְהֶעֱמִידוֹ לִפְנֵי הַכֹּהֵן' (and he shall stand him before the priest), a priest cannot be the subject of valuation before another priest; but the Mishnah teaches that priests are indeed obligated in valuations.

items.text: Derivation of who can be valued: including the disfigured and excluding the dying
items.text_en: Derivation of who can be valued: including the disfigured and excluding the dying
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the source for including a person with a blemish or boils (מנוול ומוכה שחין) in valuations, and for excluding a dead person and a goses (dying person). It cites a baraita that derives these from the verses 'by your valuation', 'souls', and 'he shall present... and he shall value'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that the word 'נערכין' (are valued) comes to include a disfigured person and one afflicted with boils in the category of those who can be valued.
The Gemara asks: From where are these matters (the inclusion of the disfigured and the exclusion of the dying) derived?
The baraita teaches that the verse 'בערכך' (by your valuation) includes a standard valuation (ערך סתום) and excludes valuation of individual limbs.
The baraita continues: One might think to exclude a case where the soul is dependent (a dying person), but the verse 'נפשות' (souls) teaches that only a dead person is excluded, not a living one.
The baraita further derives that a גוסס (dying person) is also excluded, based on the verse 'והעריך... והעמיד' — only one capable of standing (העמדה) is subject to valuation.
The baraita concludes with another derivation: the plural 'נפשות' teaches that one who values a hundred people is liable for each one, not just one.

items.text: Expanding the obligation of valuations through "nefashot" and "ve-hayah erkekha"
items.text_en: Expanding the obligation of valuations through "nefashot" and "ve-hayah erkekha"
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the plural "nefashot" that a woman who makes a valuation is obligated, and that a repulsive person or one afflicted with boils is included. It also uses "ve-hayah erkekha" to include a tumtum and androginos in the laws of valuations for monetary worth, while excluding them from the specific categories of male and female valuations.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the plural 'נפשות' (souls) that a woman who makes a valuation is obligated, expanding beyond the explicit case of a man.
The Gemara offers an alternative interpretation that 'נפשות' includes a repulsive person or one afflicted with boils, countering a possible exclusion based on monetary worth.
The Gemara uses the phrase 'והיה ערכך' to include a tumtum and androginos in the laws of valuations for monetary worth, countering a possible exclusion from the general rule.
The Gemara concludes that the term 'הזכר' excludes a tumtum and androginos from the specific categories of male and female valuations, as they are neither a definite male nor a definite female.

items.text: The meaning of "be-erkekha" for a vague vow
items.text_en: The meaning of "be-erkekha" for a vague vow
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that "be-erkekha" includes a vague vow (erekh satum), where one says "a vague valuation upon me" and pays the minimum valuation of three shekels. It discusses why the minimum is three shekels and not fifty or one, and concludes that the verse teaches that such a vow is not subject to the assessment of means (hasagat yad), or alternatively, that it is subject to it.

sub.desc_en: Mar states that 'be-erkekha' includes a vague valuation (ערך סתום), and the Gemara asks what this vague valuation is.
A baraita is cited: one who says 'a vague valuation upon me' pays the minimum of valuations, which is three shekels.
The Gemara objects: why not say the minimum is fifty shekels? It answers with the principle that when in doubt, one takes the smaller amount.
The Gemara objects: why not say the minimum is one shekel, based on the verse 'all valuations shall be in the sacred shekel'? It answers that verse refers to the assessment of means (השג יד).

The Gemara asks: if so, what purpose does the verse serve? Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha answers that it teaches that a vague vow is not subject to the assessment of means (השג יד), since it is considered as if specified.

An alternative version states that Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha says the vague vow IS subject to the assessment of means, and the verse teaches this lest one think it is considered as specified.

items.text: Excluding a corpse and a goses from valuations
items.text_en: Excluding a corpse and a goses from valuations
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from "be-erkekha" that one pays the full valuation, not the value of limbs. It then uses "nefashot" to exclude a corpse, and "ve-he'emid ve-he'erikh" to exclude a goses (a dying person). It questions why the verse "nefashot" is needed if the exclusion of a corpse is already derived, and explains that it is needed for the earlier derivations.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative interpretation of 'בְּעֶרְכְּךָ' (in your valuation) to teach that one pays the full valuation, not the value of limbs.
The Gemara questions how this interpretation can stand, since the word 'בְּעֶרְכְּךָ' was already used earlier to teach about a standard valuation (עֵרֶךְ סָתוּם).
The Gemara answers that the word 'בְּעֶרְכְּךָ' can be read as two separate terms — 'עֵרֶךְ' (valuation) and 'בְּעֶרְכְּךָ' (in your valuation) — allowing both derivations.
The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from the plural 'נְפָשֹׁת' (souls) that a corpse is excluded from valuations.
The Gemara objects that the word 'נְפָשֹׁת' was already used earlier for other derivations.
The Gemara answers that the word 'נְפָשֹׁת' can be read as both the singular 'נֶפֶשׁ' (soul) and the plural 'נְפָשֹׁת' (souls), allowing multiple derivations.
The Gemara asks whether a גּוֹסֵס (a dying person) should also be excluded from valuations, just as a corpse is.
The Gemara answers that the verse 'וְהָעֲמִיד וְהֶעֱרִיךְ' (and he shall stand and value) excludes a גּוֹסֵס, since such a person cannot stand.
The Gemara questions why a separate verse is needed to exclude a corpse, since the same verse 'וְהָעֲמִיד וְהֶעֱרִיךְ' should also exclude a corpse.
The Gemara concedes that indeed, the exclusion of a corpse could also be derived from 'וְהָעֲמִיד וְהֶעֱרִיךְ'.
The Gemara asks why the word 'נְפָשֹׁת' is needed at all, if the exclusion of a corpse is already derived from 'וְהָעֲמִיד וְהֶעֱרִיךְ'.
The Gemara answers that the word 'נְפָשֹׁת' is needed for the earlier derivations (such as including a repulsive person or one afflicted with boils).

items.text: Further expansions from "nefashot"
items.text_en: Further expansions from "nefashot"
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from "nefashot" that one who vows the valuation of multiple people is obligated, and that a woman who makes a valuation is obligated. It also includes a repulsive person or one afflicted with boils, and explains that these derivations are necessary because the earlier ones were not needed for these cases.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara derives from "nefashot" (souls) that one who vows the valuation of a hundred people is obligated, not just one.
The Gemara derives from "nefashot" that a woman who makes a valuation is obligated, not only a man.

The Gemara derives from "nefashot" that a repulsive person or one afflicted with boils is included in valuations, and explains that this derivation was necessary because the earlier ones were not needed for these cases.

items.text: The inclusion of tumtum and androginos for monetary worth and the principle of being judged by their value
items.text_en: The inclusion of tumtum and androginos for monetary worth and the principle of being judged by their value
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a verse is needed to include a tumtum and androginos for monetary worth, since even a palm tree would be valued. Rava explains that it teaches they are judged by their value (nikhnas bi-khevodo). Abaye challenges this with a baraita about a slave and an ox, and the Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between sacrifices for the altar and consecrated property for the Temple upkeep.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a verse is needed to include a tumtum and androginos for monetary worth, since even a palm tree would be valued if one said 'the value of a palm tree.'
Rava answers that the verse teaches that a tumtum and androginos are judged by their value (nikhnas bi-khevodo).
The Gemara explains the reasoning: one might have thought that only those subject to valuations (ערכין) are judged by their value, but not those who are not.
Abaye objects by citing a baraita about a slave and an ox, showing that even items not subject to valuations (ערכין) are judged by their value.
The Gemara challenges: but a donkey and a cow are not subject to valuations, yet they are judged by their value, contradicting Rava's reasoning.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between sacrifices for the altar (קדשי מזבח) and consecrated property for the Temple upkeep (קדשי בדק הבית).
The Gemara questions the resolution by examining the continuation of the baraita, which seems to contradict the distinction regarding consecrated property.

items.text: Dispute on dedicating a limb as an olah
items.text_en: Dispute on dedicating a limb as an olah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah's case of saying 'her foot is an olah' is analyzed. Rabbi Meir derives from the verse that only the limb is consecrated, not the whole animal, and the animal is sold for olah purposes with proceeds being non-sacred except for the limb's value. Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yosei, and Rabbi Shimon argue that the entire animal becomes an olah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether dedicating a limb makes the whole animal an olah, and answers from the verse that only the limb is consecrated.
The Gemara resolves that the animal is sold for olah purposes, with proceeds being non-sacred except for the limb's value, according to Rabbi Meir.

sub.text: Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yosei, and Rabbi Shimon's position
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yosei, and Rabbi Shimon's position
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yosei, and Rabbi Shimon argue that the entire animal becomes an olah, citing the same verse.

items.text: Distinction between life-dependent and non-life-dependent limbs
items.text_en: Distinction between life-dependent and non-life-dependent limbs
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that even according to Rabbi Meir, the dispute only applies to a limb that does not sustain life. For a limb that sustains life, the entire animal is consecrated. Alternatively, the distinction is between consecration of the body and consecration for monetary value.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that even according to Rabbi Meir, the dispute only applies to a limb that does not sustain life, but for a life-dependent limb the entire animal is consecrated.
The Gemara offers an alternative resolution: the distinction is between consecration of the body (קדושת הגוף) and consecration for monetary value (קדושת דמים).

items.text: Contradiction resolved: whole animal vs. single limb
items.text_en: Contradiction resolved: whole animal vs. single limb
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction from the earlier statement that consecrating a male animal for its monetary value consecrates the body. It resolves that this applies when consecrating the whole animal, but not when consecrating a single limb.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: the earlier statement that consecrating a male animal for its monetary value consecrates the body seems to conflict with the resolution just given.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: the rule that consecration for monetary value consecrates the body applies when consecrating the whole animal, but not when consecrating a single limb.

items.text: Rabbah's query on consecrating a limb for its monetary value
items.text_en: Rabbah's query on consecrating a limb for its monetary value
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that Rabbah's query about consecrating a limb for its monetary value was asked regarding a blemished animal, similar to a donkey. It then notes that Rabbah's query about 'the value of my head for the altar' was resolved after hearing the Mishnah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that Rabbah's query about consecrating a limb for its monetary value was asked regarding a blemished animal, similar to a donkey.
Rabbah asks whether one who says 'the value of my head for the altar' must pay its value or is exempt.
The Gemara resolves that the query was only relevant before hearing the Mishnah; after hearing it, the answer is clear.

items.text: Rabbah's query: 'the value of my head for the altar'
items.text_en: Rabbah's query: 'the value of my head for the altar'
items.desc_en: Rabbah asks whether one who says 'the value of my head for the altar' is judged by his dignity (i.e., the value is assessed based on his worth as a person) or not. The Gemara leaves the question unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: Rabba asks whether 'the value of my head for the altar' is assessed by its worth or not, and the question remains unresolved (תיקו).
The Gemara leaves the question unresolved (תיקו), considering whether no precedent exists for a valuation not based on dignity, or no precedent exists for such a valuation toward the altar.

items.text: Rava's query: 'my valuation upon me for the altar'
items.text_en: Rava's query: 'my valuation upon me for the altar'
items.desc_en: Rava asks whether one who says 'my valuation upon me for the altar' is judged with the ability to pay (heseg yad) or not. The Gemara leaves the question unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: Rava asks whether 'my valuation upon me for the altar' is subject to financial assessment or not, and the question remains unresolved (תיקו).
The Gemara leaves the question unresolved (תיקו), unable to determine whether the rule of השג יד applies to valuations for the altar.

items.text: Rav Ashi's query: consecrating an ancestral field for the altar
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's query: consecrating an ancestral field for the altar
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi asks whether one who consecrates an ancestral field for the altar is redeemed at the fixed rate (50 shekels per homer) or at its actual value. The Gemara leaves the question unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi asks whether dedicating an ancestral field for the altar is redeemed by its fixed value or by its market value, and the question remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on an infant under one month
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on an infant under one month
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that an infant under one month can be vowed (for its monetary value) but not evaluated (for its fixed erekh value). The Gemara presents a dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages: Rabbi Meir holds that one who says 'erekh' for such an infant must pay its monetary value, as one does not utter words in vain, while the Sages say he pays nothing. Rav Giddel's ruling that one who says 'erekh of a vessel' pays its monetary value is aligned with Rabbi Meir, and the Gemara explains why this is not obvious.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that an infant under one month can be vowed (for its monetary value) but not evaluated (for its fixed erekh value).
A baraita records a dispute: Rabbi Meir says one who evaluates an infant under one month pays its monetary value, while the Sages say he pays nothing.

The Gemara asks what underlies the dispute and explains: Rabbi Meir holds that one does not utter words in vain, so the speaker intended monetary value; the Sages hold that one may utter words in vain.
The Gemara notes that Rav Giddel's ruling that one who says 'erekh of a vessel' pays its monetary value aligns with Rabbi Meir, and questions why this is not obvious.

The Gemara explains that without the ruling, one might think even the Sages would agree here, since there is no room for error about vessels, but Rav Giddel teaches that the Sages still hold one may utter words in vain.

items.text: Clarifying Rabbi Meir's reasoning
items.text_en: Clarifying Rabbi Meir's reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Meir's statement was necessary, and explains that without it one might think his decree applies only where there is a concern for confusion, but here there is no such concern. The Gemara teaches that Rabbi Meir's principle is that a person does not utter words in vain, applying equally in both cases.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Meir's statement was necessary, given his general principle.

The Gemara explains that without Rabbi Meir's statement one might think his decree applies only where there is a concern for confusion, but here there is no such concern; the teaching shows that Rabbi Meir's principle is that a person does not utter words in vain, applying equally in both cases.

items.text: Rav's statement about consecrating another's animal
items.text_en: Rav's statement about consecrating another's animal
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whose opinion Rav's statement follows, concluding it is Rabbi Meir's. It then notes that Rav already said a similar statement about a vessel, and explains the novelty: one might think that with an animal, the person intends to have it consecrated immediately, not to give its value, so the teaching is necessary.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whose opinion Rav's statement about consecrating another's animal follows, and answers that it follows Rabbi Meir.
The Gemara objects that Rav already stated a similar ruling regarding a vessel, so why repeat it for an animal?
The Gemara explains the novelty: one might think that with an animal, the person intends immediate consecration rather than giving its value, so the teaching is necessary.

items.text: Rav Ashi's qualification
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's qualification
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi qualifies that Rav's statement applies only when one says 'upon me' (עָלַי), but if one says 'this is' (הֲרֵי זוֹ), it does not apply.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi qualifies that Rav's statement applies only when one says 'עָלַי' (upon me), but if one says 'הֲרֵי זוֹ' (this is), it does not apply.

items.text: Mishnah: Non-Jew and valuations
items.text_en: Mishnah: Non-Jew and valuations
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Rabbi Meir says a non-Jew can be evaluated but cannot evaluate others; Rabbi Judah says he can evaluate but cannot be evaluated. Both agree that non-Jews can make and be subject to vows of dedication.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the dispute: Rabbi Meir says a non-Jew can be evaluated but cannot evaluate others; Rabbi Judah says the opposite; both agree on vows of dedication.

items.text: Gemara: Scriptural basis for the dispute
items.text_en: Gemara: Scriptural basis for the dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: Rabbi Meir derives from the verse that Israelites evaluate but non-Jews do not, yet non-Jews can be evaluated from the word 'אִישׁ'. Rabbi Meir explains his reasoning: the verse includes more in the category of those evaluated (e.g., deaf-mute, imbecile, minor) than those who evaluate. Rabbi Judah derives that Israelites are evaluated but non-Jews are not, yet non-Jews can evaluate from 'אִישׁ'. He explains his reasoning: the verse includes more in the category of those who evaluate (e.g., tumtum and androgyne) than those evaluated.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with the general rule that Israelites evaluate but non-Jews do not, and then cites Rabbi Meir's position that a non-Jew can be evaluated, derived from the word 'אִישׁ'.
Rabbi Meir explains that his ruling is based on the verse including more in the category of those evaluated (deaf-mute, imbecile, minor) than those who evaluate.
Rabbi Judah explains that his ruling is based on the verse including more in the category of those who evaluate (tumtum and androgyne) than those evaluated.

items.text: Rava's analysis of the opinions
items.text_en: Rava's analysis of the opinions
items.desc_en: Rava states that Rabbi Meir's halakhic conclusion is reasonable but his reasoning is not, while Rabbi Judah's reasoning is reasonable but his halakhic conclusion is not. He explains: Rabbi Meir's conclusion is supported by a verse about non-Jews not building the Temple, but his analogy to deaf-mute etc. is flawed because they lack intelligence. Rabbi Judah's analogy to tumtum and androgyne is good because they have intelligence yet are excluded, but his conclusion is contradicted by the same verse.

sub.desc_en: Rava opens by stating that Rabbi Meir's halakhic conclusion is reasonable but his reasoning is not, while Rabbi Judah's reasoning is reasonable but his halakhic conclusion is not.

Rava explains that Rabbi Meir's conclusion is supported by the verse 'לֹא לָכֶם וָלָנוּ לִבְנוֹת אֶת בֵּית אֱלֹהֵינוּ' (You have nothing to do with us to build a house to our God), but his reasoning from deaf-mute, imbecile, and minor is flawed because they lack intelligence.

Rava explains that Rabbi Judah's reasoning is reasonable because he adduces proof from tumtum and androgyne, who have intelligence yet are excluded from being valuated, but his conclusion is contradicted by the same verse about non-Jews not building the Temple.

items.text: Addressing the verse and a challenge
items.text_en: Addressing the verse and a challenge
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Judah interprets the verse 'לֹא לָכֶם וָלָנוּ', and Rav Chisda answers that the valuation money is hidden away. A challenge is raised from a mishna about non-Jewish consecrated items, but Rava resolves it by explaining the verse refers to weakening of hands (רִפְיוֹן יָדַיִם) in building the Temple.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Judah interprets the verse 'לֹא לָכֶם וָלָנוּ'.
Rav Chisda answers that the valuation money of a gentile is hidden away.
The Gemara objects that if the money is hidden away, one who uses it should not be liable for misuse, citing a baraita about sin offerings and money cast into the Dead Sea.
A baraita is cited that for gentiles' consecrations for Temple maintenance, one is liable for misuse, contradicting the idea that the money is hidden away.
Rava resolves the difficulty by explaining that the verse refers to weakening of hands (רִפְיוֹן יָדַיִם) in building the Temple, not a halakhic exclusion.

items.text: Contradiction about gentile donations and its resolution
items.text_en: Contradiction about gentile donations and its resolution
items.desc_en: Two baraitot conflict: one says we accept a gentile's donation for the Temple, the other says we do not. Rabbi Ila in the name of Rabbi Yochanan resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between the early period (when even water and salt are not accepted) and the late period (when a fixed item is not accepted but an unfixed one is). Rav Yosef defines a fixed item as a 'cubit of the raven's nest' and raises an objection from a verse about a letter to Asaph, but Abaye deflects by noting that the Persian monarchy never retracts its word.

sub.desc_en: Two baraitot are cited: one says we accept a gentile's donation for the Temple treasury, the other says we do not.

sub.text: Rabbi Ila in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Ila in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ila citing Rabbi Yochanan resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between the early period (בתחילה) and the late period (בסוף).

sub.text: Rabbi Asi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Asi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Asi citing Rabbi Yochanan elaborates: in the early period even water and salt are not accepted; in the late period a fixed item (דבר המסוים) is not accepted but an unfixed one is.
Rav Yosef defines a fixed item as a 'cubit of the raven's nest' and then objects by citing a verse about a letter to Asaph, implying that even a fixed item was accepted from a gentile.

Abaye deflects the objection by noting that the Persian monarchy never retracts its word, citing Shmuel's principle that if the monarchy says 'I will uproot mountains,' it does so and does not retract.

items.text: Gentile's terumah and the case of a donated beam
items.text_en: Gentile's terumah and the case of a donated beam
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav rules that if a gentile separates terumah from his granary, we examine him: if he intended it as an Israelite, it is given to the priest; otherwise, it is stored away, suspecting he intended it for Heaven. A baraita about a gentile who donated a beam with a divine name written on it is cited: if he says he intended it as an Israelite, the beam is cut and the remainder used; otherwise, it is stored away. The Gemara infers that only when the name is written does it require storage, but the Gemara explains that the baraita teaches that even with the name, the remainder is usable because a name in a non-sacred place is not holy, as per a mishnah.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav rules that if a gentile separates תרומה (priestly portion) from his granary, we examine him: if he intended it as an Israelite, it is given to the priest; otherwise, it is stored away, suspecting he intended it for Heaven.

A baraita is cited about a gentile who donated a beam with a divine name written on it: if he says he intended it as an Israelite, the beam is cut and the remainder used; otherwise, it is stored away.
The Gemara infers from the baraita that only when the divine name is written on the beam does it require storage, implying that without the name, no storage is needed.
The Gemara explains that the baraita teaches that even with the divine name, the remainder is usable because a name in a non-sacred place is not holy.
A mishnah is cited that if a divine name is written on handles of vessels or legs of a bed, it is cut and stored away, supporting the principle that a name in a non-sacred place is not holy.

items.text: Changing a designated charity coin
items.text_en: Changing a designated charity coin
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Rabba bar Avahu states that one who says 'this sela for charity' may change it. The Gemara initially assumes this applies only to oneself but not to another. Rav Ammi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan rules that it applies both to oneself and another. Rabbi Zeira distinguishes between saying 'upon me' (which requires giving the coin itself) and 'this is' (which allows change). Rava objects, arguing the opposite, and concludes there is no difference.

sub.text: Rav Nachman citing Rabba bar Avahu
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman citing Rabba bar Avahu
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Rabba bar Avahu rules that one who says 'this sela for charity' may change it.
The Gemara initially assumes the leniency applies only to oneself but not to another.
Rav Ammi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan rules that the leniency applies both to oneself and to another.
Rabbi Zeira distinguishes between saying 'עלי' (upon me), which allows change, and 'הרי זו' (this is), which requires giving the coin itself.
Rava objects, arguing the opposite: saying 'זו' (this) allows change because the donor retains responsibility, while 'עלי' (upon me) does not.
Rava concludes that there is no difference between the two formulations.

items.text: Baraita supporting Rava's view
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Rava's view
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that seems to say 'a vow of charity, and not a consecration of charity'. The Gemara explains it means that charity is subject to the prohibition of delaying (bal t'acher) but is not like consecration, which prohibits use; charity may be used.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited that appears to support Rava's position, stating 'a vow of charity, and not a consecration of charity', which the Gemara initially reads as a self-contradictory phrase.
The Gemara asks what the baraita means, noting that the literal reading 'neither a vow nor a consecration of charity' is nonsensical.
The Gemara resolves the baraita: charity is subject to the prohibition of delaying (בל תאחר) but is not like consecration, which prohibits use; charity may be used.

items.text: Alternative version and final ruling
items.text_en: Alternative version and final ruling
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana reports that Rav Zevid from Nehardea taught the tradition differently: Rav Nachman in the name of Rabba bar Avahu in the name of Rav rules that one who says 'this sela for charity' may change it, whether for himself or another, whether he said 'upon me' or 'this is'. A baraita adds that before the coin reaches the charity collector, it may be changed; after it reaches him, it is forbidden.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana reports that Rav Zevid from Nehardea taught the tradition differently from the earlier version.

sub.text: Rav Nachman citing Rabba bar Avahu citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman citing Rabba bar Avahu citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Rabba bar Avahu in the name of Rav rules that one who says 'this sela for charity' may change it, whether for himself or another, and whether he said 'upon me' or 'this is'.
A baraita adds that before the coin reaches the charity collector, it may be changed; after it reaches him, it is forbidden.

items.text: Gemara's question about Rabbi Yannai's practice
items.text_en: Gemara's question about Rabbi Yannai's practice
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions a previous ruling by citing Rabbi Yannai who borrowed and repaid charity funds, and explains that the poor prefer the delay because it allows them to accumulate more produce.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges a previous ruling by citing Rabbi Yannai's practice of borrowing and repaying charity funds.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yannai's case is different because the poor prefer the delay, as it allows them to accumulate more produce.

items.text: Baraita on changing a donated item for a mitzvah
items.text_en: Baraita on changing a donated item for a mitzvah
items.desc_en: A baraita states that an Israelite who donates a menorah or lamp to a synagogue cannot change its use. Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba thought this applies even for a mitzvah, but Rabbi Ammi reports Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that it is only prohibited for a secular purpose, but permitted for a mitzvah.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that an Israelite who donates a menorah or lamp to a synagogue may not change its use.
Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba thought the prohibition applies equally to a secular purpose and a mitzvah.
Rabbi Ammi reports Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that the prohibition applies only to a secular purpose, but for a mitzvah it is permitted to change the item's use.

items.text: Gentile's donation and the distinction from an Israelite
items.text_en: Gentile's donation and the distinction from an Israelite
items.desc_en: Rabbi Asi quotes Rabbi Yochanan that a gentile's donation to a synagogue can be changed only after the donor's name is forgotten. The Gemara clarifies that this applies specifically to a mitzvah purpose, because a gentile's intent is for a mitzvah (since he has no personal benefit), whereas an Israelite might have personal motives, so changing it is permissible even before the name is forgotten.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Asi quotes Rabbi Yochanan that a gentile who donated a lamp or candelabrum to a synagogue may change its use only after the donor's name is forgotten.
The Gemara asks: For what purpose does this distinction apply? If for a non-mitzvah purpose, why mention a gentile — even an Israelite would be forbidden to change it.

The Gemara answers: It applies specifically to a mitzvah purpose; the gentile's intent is purely for the mitzvah (since he has no personal benefit), whereas an Israelite might have personal motives, so changing it is permissible even before the name is forgotten.

items.text: Story of Shazrak the Tayyaea and the lamp
items.text_en: Story of Shazrak the Tayyaea and the lamp
items.desc_en: A story is told about a gentile named Shazrak who donated a lamp to the synagogue of Rav Yehuda. Rachaba changed its use, and Rava was upset. Alternative versions attribute the change to Rava or the synagogue attendants. The dispute hinges on whether the donor might return and see the change.

sub.desc_en: A story is told about Shazrak the Tayyaea who donated a lamp to Rav Yehuda's synagogue; Rachaba changed its use and Rava was upset.
Alternative versions are given: some say Rava changed it and Rachaba was upset; others say the synagogue attendants of Pumbedita changed it, and both Rachaba and Rabbah were upset.
The Gemara explains the dispute: the one who changed it holds the donor is unlikely to return, while the one who was upset holds that sometimes the donor might happen to come and see the change.

items.text: Mishnah: The dying and the condemned
items.text_en: Mishnah: The dying and the condemned
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a dying person (goses) and one being led to execution cannot make vows or valuations. Rabbi Chanina ben Akavya says he can be valued because his blood is fixed. Rabbi Yose says he can vow, value, and consecrate, and if he damages, he is liable.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that a dying person (goses) and one being led to execution cannot make vows or valuations.
Rabbi Chanina ben Akavya states that the condemned can be valued because his blood is fixed (his value is predetermined).
Rabbi Yose says the condemned can vow, value, and consecrate, and if he damages, he is liable.

items.text: Gemara's explanation for the Mishnah and the source for the condemned
items.text_en: Gemara's explanation for the Mishnah and the source for the condemned
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that a goses cannot vow because he has no monetary value, and cannot be valued because he cannot stand for evaluation. For the condemned, the Gemara asks why he cannot be valued, and cites a baraita deriving from the verse "כׇּל חֵרֶם לֹא יִפָּדֶה" that a condemned person's vow is void, but excludes one before the verdict is finalized.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains why a goses cannot vow or be valued, then questions why a condemned person cannot be valued.
A baraita is cited, deriving from the verse 'כׇּל חֵרֶם לֹא יִפָּדֶה' that a condemned person's vow is void, but excluding one before the verdict is finalized.

items.text: Rabbi Chanina ben Akavya's use of the verse and Rabbi Yishmael's derivation
items.text_en: Rabbi Chanina ben Akavya's use of the verse and Rabbi Yishmael's derivation
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Chanina ben Akavya, who allows valuation for the condemned, interprets the verse "כׇּל חֵרֶם". It answers that he uses it for Rabbi Yishmael's teaching: that those executed by heaven can be ransomed, but not those executed by human court. The verse also includes all capital punishments, even lighter ones where an accidental violation is atoned for.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Chanina ben Akavya, who allows valuation for the condemned, interprets the verse "כׇּל חֵרֶם" (anything dedicated).
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Chanina ben Akavya uses the verse for Rabbi Yishmael's teaching: those executed by heaven can be ransomed, but not those executed by human court.
The Gemara adds that the verse also includes all capital punishments, even lighter ones where an accidental violation is atoned for.

items.text: Dispute between Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yose about liability for damages
items.text_en: Dispute between Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yose about liability for damages
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that all agree a condemned person can vow, value, and consecrate; the dispute is whether he is liable for damages. Rav Yosef says they argue about whether an oral loan is collected from heirs. Rava says all agree it is not, but they argue about whether a loan written in the Torah is like a written document.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the first tanna actually disputes Rabbi Yosei's statement that a condemned person can vow, value, and consecrate.
The Gemara clarifies that all agree a condemned person can vow, value, and consecrate; the dispute is only about liability for damages.
Rav Yosef explains that the dispute is about whether an oral loan is collected from heirs.
Rava rejects Rav Yosef's explanation, stating that all agree an oral loan is not collected from heirs; the dispute is about whether a loan written in the Torah is like a written document.

items.text: Alternative version: dispute about damages by the condemned
items.text_en: Alternative version: dispute about damages by the condemned
items.desc_en: An alternative version applies the dispute to a baraita about a condemned person who injures others: the first opinion holds him liable, but Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says he is exempt because he cannot be brought back for a court hearing.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents an alternative version of the dispute, applied to a baraita about a condemned person who injures others: the first opinion holds him liable, but Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar exempts him because he cannot be brought back for a court hearing.

items.text: Dispute over oral loan collection from heirs
items.text_en: Dispute over oral loan collection from heirs
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the underlying dispute between the Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar. Rav Yosef explains they argue about whether an oral loan is collectible from heirs; Rabbah says they agree it is not, but argue whether a loan written in the Torah is like a written loan.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Tanna Kamma holds that an oral loan is collectible from heirs, based on the Mishnah's implication.
Rav Yosef explains that the dispute is about whether an oral loan is collectible from heirs: the Tanna Kamma holds it is, Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar holds it is not.
Rabbah argues that all agree an oral loan is not collectible from heirs, but they dispute whether a loan written in the Torah is like a written loan.

items.text: Challenge from the case of a pit digger
items.text_en: Challenge from the case of a pit digger
items.desc_en: A baraita about a pit digger in the public domain whose ox dies is brought as a challenge. Rabbi Ila and Rav Adda bar Ahavah resolve it by explaining the ox was made a treifah or the case was adjudicated. Rav Nachman cites a tradition that judges sit at the mouth of the well.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about a pit digger in the public domain whose ox dies, challenging the previous discussion by showing that heirs are liable for damages.
Rabbi Ila in the name of Rav answers that the case is when the ox stood in court (עמד בדין) before dying, but the Gemara objects that the baraita says 'killed him' (הרגו).
Rav Adda bar Ahavah resolves the objection by explaining that the ox was made a טריפה (a dying animal) so it was considered dead at the time of the incident.
Rav Nachman cites a tradition from Chaggai that the case involved the ox dying and being buried, and the halacha is that judges sit at the mouth of the well (to adjudicate immediately).

items.text: Sprinkling blood on a condemned person
items.text_en: Sprinkling blood on a condemned person
items.desc_en: A baraita states that one going to be executed may have his hatat and asham blood sprinkled on him, but if he sins at that hour, they do not attend to him. Rav Yosef explains the reason is not to delay his judgment. Abaye questions this, and the Gemara clarifies that the case is when his offering was already slaughtered.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that one going to be executed may have his hatat and asham blood sprinkled on him, but if he sins at that hour, they do not attend to him.
The Gemara asks for the reason why they do not attend to him.
Rav Yosef explains that the reason is not to delay his judgment.
Abaye objects that if the reason is not to delay judgment, then even the initial sprinkling should be forbidden.

The Gemara clarifies that the case is when his offering was already slaughtered, so the sprinkling does not delay judgment, but if not, it is considered as if he sinned at that hour and they do not attend to him.

items.text: Mishnah: Woman executed while pregnant
items.text_en: Mishnah: Woman executed while pregnant
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a woman going to be executed is not waited for to give birth, but one in labor is waited for. The Gemara explains that the fetus is considered part of her body, but a verse teaches that the fetus is also killed. Rabbi Yoshiyah's view that both must be equal is addressed by the word 'gam'.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a woman going to be executed is not waited for to give birth, but one in labor is waited for; the executed woman's hair is permitted for benefit, but an executed animal's is forbidden.

The Gemara questions why the Mishnah's first ruling is necessary, since the fetus is part of the mother's body, and suggests a concern that the fetus is the husband's property, which the Mishnah rejects.

The Gemara objects that perhaps the fetus is indeed the husband's property, and Rabbi Avahu in the name of Rabbi Yochanan cites the verse 'וּמֵתוּ גַּם שְׁנֵיהֶם' to include the fetus in the death penalty.
The Gemara objects that the verse is needed for Rabbi Yoshiyah's requirement that both parties be equal, and responds that the word 'גַּם' provides the extra inclusion.

items.text: Timing of death: mother vs. fetus
items.text_en: Timing of death: mother vs. fetus
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses why a woman in labor is waited for: the fetus is a separate body once it begins to emerge. Rav Yehuda quotes Shmuel that they strike the woman to kill the fetus first to avoid disgrace. The Gemara questions this, citing that a fetus dies first naturally, but in execution the mother dies first. A counterexample of a fetus moving after death is dismissed as mere reflex.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah waits for a woman in labor, and answers that once the fetus begins to emerge, it is considered a separate body.
Rav Yehuda quotes Shmuel that when a woman is executed, they strike her womb to kill the fetus first, to prevent her disgrace.
The Gemara objects: does this imply the mother dies first? But we know that the fetus dies first naturally.
The Gemara cites a baraita that a one-day-old inherits, but a fetus does not because it dies first, and Rav Sheishet explains the inheritance rule.
The Gemara resolves: in natural death the fetus dies first because the angel of death cuts its organs, but in execution the mother dies first.
The Gemara objects: there was an incident where a fetus moved after the mother's execution.
The Gemara dismisses the objection: that movement was merely a reflex, like the twitching tail of a lizard.

items.text: Cutting open a dead pregnant woman on Shabbat
items.text_en: Cutting open a dead pregnant woman on Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman quotes Shmuel that if a woman dies in labor on Shabbat, they bring a knife and cut open her belly to save the fetus. The Gemara asks why this is necessary, implying it is obvious.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman reports Shmuel's ruling that if a woman dies in labor on Shabbat, they bring a knife and cut open her belly to save the fetus.
The Gemara asks why this ruling is necessary, implying it is obvious that one must save the fetus.

items.text: Gemara's question about cutting flesh on Shabbat
items.text_en: Gemara's question about cutting flesh on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why cutting hair is permitted on Shabbat, as it seems like cutting flesh. Rabba explains that the case involves bringing a knife through a public domain, and the Gemara clarifies that the ruling is based on doubt, citing a mishnah about clearing a collapsed building.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that cutting hair on Shabbat is like cutting flesh, which is forbidden.
Rabba explains that the ruling applies to bringing a knife through a public domain on Shabbat, not to cutting flesh.
The Gemara questions whether the ruling teaches that we violate Shabbat due to doubt.
The Gemara cites a mishnah about clearing a collapsed building on Shabbat due to doubt of life, showing that doubt permits Shabbat violation.
The Gemara resolves that the ruling teaches that even without a prior presumption of life, doubt permits Shabbat violation.

items.text: Question on the Mishnah's ruling about the executed woman
items.text_en: Question on the Mishnah's ruling about the executed woman
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the hair of an executed woman is permitted, since it is an item of forbidden benefit. Rav answers that the case is where she said 'give my hair to my daughter,' implying that without her statement, it would be forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the hair of an executed woman is permitted, since it is an item of forbidden benefit.
Rav answers that the case is where she said 'give my hair to my daughter,' implying that without her statement, it would be forbidden.

items.text: Rav's explanation about foreign hair
items.text_en: Rav's explanation about foreign hair
items.desc_en: Rav clarifies that the case involves a foreign hairpiece, and only because she said 'give' is it permitted; otherwise, it is considered part of her body and forbidden.

sub.desc_en: Rav explains that the case involves a foreign hairpiece, and only because she said 'give' is it permitted; otherwise it is considered part of her body and forbidden.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's question and Rava's distinction
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's question and Rava's distinction
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that this ruling is needed for Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's question about the hair of righteous women. Rava explains that the question is about hair that is attached to a comb, not a hairpiece.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that this ruling is needed for Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's question about the hair of righteous women.
Rava explains that the question is about hair that is attached to a comb, not a hairpiece.

items.text: Reiteration of Rav's principle for attached hair
items.text_en: Reiteration of Rav's principle for attached hair
items.desc_en: The Gemara restates that when hair is attached to the body, only if she said 'give' is it permitted; otherwise, it is part of her body and forbidden.
