sub.desc_en: The Gemara reiterates that when hair is attached to the body, only if she said 'give' is it permitted; otherwise, it is part of her body and forbidden.

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's objection and alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's objection and alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak objects that the Mishnah compares the woman to an animal, implying her body is forbidden. He explains that the difference is that the animal's death prohibits it, while the woman's final judgment prohibits her.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak objects that the Mishnah's comparison of the woman to an animal implies that her body itself is forbidden, just as the animal's body is forbidden.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's alternative explanation
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's alternative explanation
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves the objection by explaining that the animal's death prohibits it, while the woman's final judgment (her execution) prohibits her, not her body itself.

items.text: Levi's tannaitic support for Rav
items.text_en: Levi's tannaitic support for Rav
items.desc_en: A baraita taught by Levi supports Rav's view: a woman going to be executed may give her hair, but after death it is forbidden because a corpse is forbidden for benefit. The Gemara clarifies that the prohibition is on the adornment of the dead.

sub.desc_en: Levi teaches a baraita supporting Rav: a woman going to execution may give her hair, but after death it is not given because a corpse is forbidden for benefit.
The Gemara objects that the baraita's conclusion is obvious.
The Gemara clarifies that the baraita teaches that the adornment of the dead (נויי המת) is forbidden for benefit, not the corpse itself.

items.text: Baraita supporting Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak
items.desc_en: A baraita supports Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: a dead woman's hair is permitted, but a slaughtered animal is forbidden, because the animal's death prohibits it, while the woman's final judgment prohibits her.

sub.desc_en: A baraita supports Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's distinction: a dead woman's hair is permitted because her death alone prohibits her, while a slaughtered animal is forbidden because its final judgment (the court's verdict) prohibits it.

items.text: Mishnah on arakhin valuations
items.text_en: Mishnah on arakhin valuations
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that valuations cannot be less than a sela or more than fifty sela, with examples. It also discusses a case where one has five selas, with Rabbi Meir saying he gives only one and the Sages saying he gives all.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara marks the conclusion of the previous chapter with the formula 'הדרן עלך' (we return to you).
The Mishnah opens with the rule that valuations cannot be less than a sela or more than fifty sela, and gives examples of how this applies when one becomes wealthy.
The Mishnah presents the case of one who has five selas, and records the opinion of רבי מאיר (Rabbi Meir) that he gives only one sela.
The Mishnah records the opposing opinion of the חכמים (Sages) that he gives all five selas, and then repeats the general rule about the minimum and maximum.

items.text: Gemara's derivation of the minimum and maximum
items.text_en: Gemara's derivation of the minimum and maximum
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives the minimum from the verse 'by the shekel of the sanctuary' and the maximum from 'fifty.' It then explains the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages regarding the five selas case, with scriptural interpretations.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source of the rule that valuations cannot be less than a sela.
The Gemara answers that the verse 'and all your valuations shall be by the shekel of the sanctuary' teaches that no valuation may be less than a shekel.
The Gemara derives the maximum of fifty selas from the verse that specifies fifty shekels for the valuation of a male between twenty and sixty.
The Gemara asks for the reason behind Rabbi Meir's opinion that one with five selas gives only one sela.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Meir derives from the verses 'fifty' and 'shekel' that the obligation is either fifty or a shekel, so if he has five selas he gives only one shekel.
The Gemara asks for the reasoning of the Rabbis who require giving all five selas.

The Gemara explains that the Rabbis interpret the verse about the shekel to teach the minimum, but when he has means, the verse 'according to the means of him that vowed' requires him to give all he can afford.
The Gemara asks for Rabbi Meir's response to the Rabbis' interpretation.

The Gemara explains that Rabbi Meir interprets that verse to teach that the valuation is according to the means of the one who vowed, not the one about whom the vow was made, and the Rabbis respond that it implies that when he has means you take from him.

items.text: Rav Adda bar Ahava's case of multiple valuations
items.text_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava's case of multiple valuations
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava discusses a case where one has five selas and makes two valuations, giving four to the second and one to the first, which fulfills both obligations because a later creditor who collected first keeps what he collected.

sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava presents a case: one had five selas, made two valuations, gave four to the second and one to the first, and fulfilled both obligations.
The Gemara explains the reason: a later creditor who collected first keeps what he collected.
The Gemara clarifies the timing: when he gave to the second, the first was already encumbered; when he gave to the first, he had nothing left.

items.text: Mishnah: Partial payment for two valuations
items.text_en: Mishnah: Partial payment for two valuations
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one gave four sela'im to the first valuation and one to the second, the second is fulfilled but the first is not, as all funds are subject to the first.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if one gave four sela'im to the first valuation and one to the second, the second is fulfilled but the first is not, because all funds are subject to the first.

items.text: Gemara's question: Simultaneous pledges with limited funds
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Simultaneous pledges with limited funds
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava asks: if one had five sela'im and said 'two valuations upon me' in one utterance, do they take effect simultaneously, requiring two and a half for each, or is each fully subject to all five? The question remains unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava asks whether two simultaneous pledges of valuation (ערכין) with only five sela'im in hand take effect proportionally or each claims the full amount, and the question remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Gemara: Clarifying the Mishnah's rule on minimum and maximum
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarifying the Mishnah's rule on minimum and maximum
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah states 'no less than a sela and no more than fifty'—it teaches that less than a sela is invalid but more is valid, and more than fifty is invalid but less is valid, aligning with the Rabbis.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah adds the clause 'no less than a sela and no more than fifty' — what additional information does it provide beyond the earlier ruling?

The Gemara explains that the clause teaches that less than a sela is invalid but more than a sela is valid, and more than fifty is invalid but less than fifty is valid, and the anonymous Mishnah follows the Rabbis' opinion.

items.text: Mishnah: Opening for a woman who saw a discharge
items.text_en: Mishnah: Opening for a woman who saw a discharge
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the opening period for a woman who saw a discharge (zavah) is no less than seven days and no more than seventeen.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the opening period (פתח) for a woman who experienced a flow (טועה) is no less than seven days and no more than seventeen days.

items.text: Gemara: Baraita detailing the opening period for each claim
items.text_en: Gemara: Baraita detailing the opening period for each claim
items.desc_en: The Rabbis taught: if a woman says she saw one, two, or three days of impurity, her opening is seventeen days; for four days, sixteen; for five, fifteen; for six, fourteen; for seven, thirteen; for eight, twelve; for nine, eleven; for ten, ten; for eleven, nine.

sub.desc_en: A baraita details the opening period (פתח) for a woman who says she saw one to eleven days of impurity, with the opening decreasing from seventeen to nine days as the reported days increase.
The baraita continues: if she says she saw two days of impurity, her opening is also seventeen days.
The baraita continues: if she says she saw three days of impurity, her opening is still seventeen days.
The baraita continues: if she says she saw four days of impurity, her opening is sixteen days.
The baraita continues: if she says she saw five days of impurity, her opening is fifteen days; for six days, fourteen.
The baraita continues: if she says she saw seven days of impurity, her opening is thirteen days.
The baraita continues: if she says she saw eight days of impurity, her opening is twelve days.
The baraita continues: if she says she saw nine days of impurity, her opening is eleven days.
The baraita concludes: if she says she saw ten days of impurity, her opening is ten days; for eleven days, nine.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Minimum and maximum openings for a woman with irregular bleeding
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Minimum and maximum openings for a woman with irregular bleeding
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a woman who experiences a fixed pattern of irregular bleeding (a 'zavah') has a minimum opening of seven days and a maximum of seventeen days. The specific numbers are given: for a twelve-day pattern, the opening is eight days; for a thirteen-day pattern, the opening is seven days.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the minimum and maximum opening periods for a woman with irregular bleeding (zavah), giving specific numbers for twelve- and thirteen-day patterns.

items.text: Gemara's question and answer about the opening calculation
items.text_en: Gemara's question and answer about the opening calculation
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahavah asks Rabbah why the Mishnah needs to specify all these numbers; why not simply say the opening is seven days? Rabbah answers that the Mishnah is speaking about the opening for a woman who is a 'zavah' (with a fixed pattern) and her opening (the number of days she must count before bringing a sacrifice).

sub.text: Rav Adda bar Ahavah's question to Rabbah
sub.text_en: Rav Adda bar Ahavah's question to Rabbah
sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahavah asks Rabbah why the Mishnah needs to specify all these numbers; why not simply say the opening is seven days?
Rabbah answers that the Mishnah is speaking about the opening for a woman who is a זבה (with a fixed pattern) and her opening (the number of days she must count before bringing a sacrifice).

items.text: Baraita about women who bring a sacrifice that is eaten
items.text_en: Baraita about women who bring a sacrifice that is eaten
items.desc_en: A Baraita is cited: All women who experience irregular bleeding (zavot) bring a sacrifice that is not eaten, except for those with an opening of seven or eight days, whose sacrifice is eaten. The Gemara corrects the wording: it should say 'all zavot who have irregular bleeding' bring a sacrifice that is not eaten, except for those with an opening of seven or eight days.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that all women who are uncertain about their status (טועות זבות) bring a sacrifice that is not eaten, except for those with an opening of seven or eight days, whose sacrifice is eaten.
The Gemara objects: Are all uncertain women actually zavot? And furthermore, can a woman who saw blood for only one or two days bring a sacrifice?
The Gemara corrects the baraita: it should read 'all zavot who are uncertain' bring a sacrifice that is not eaten, except for those with an opening of seven or eight days, whose sacrifice is eaten.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on plagues: minimum and maximum weeks
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on plagues: minimum and maximum weeks
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that for plagues (negaim), there is no less than one week and no more than three weeks. The Gemara explains: the minimum of one week refers to plagues on a person, and the maximum of three weeks refers to plagues on houses.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule that for plagues (negaim), the quarantine period is no less than one week and no more than three weeks.
The Gemara explains that the minimum of one week applies to plagues on a person, and the maximum of three weeks applies to plagues on houses.

items.text: Rav Pappa's homily and the dispute between Rabbah and Rav Yehuda
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's homily and the dispute between Rabbah and Rav Yehuda
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa interprets a verse: 'Your righteousness is like the mountains of God' refers to plagues on a person, and 'Your judgments are like the great deep' refers to plagues on houses. Rav Yehuda and Rabbah dispute the meaning of the verse: Rav Yehuda says that without the righteousness (plagues on a person), no one could withstand the judgments (plagues on houses); Rabbah says the righteousness is because of the judgments. This dispute is linked to a dispute between Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina about whether God 'overpowers' or 'carries' the world's sins.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa interprets the verse 'Your righteousness is like the mountains of God' as referring to plagues on a person, and 'Your judgments are like the great deep' as referring to plagues on houses.
The Gemara asks: what is the plain meaning of the verse?
Rav Yehuda explains: were it not for the righteousness (plagues on a person), no one could withstand the judgments (plagues on houses).
Rabbah explains: the righteousness (plagues on a person) is because of the judgments (plagues on houses).
The Gemara asks: what is the basis of their dispute?
The Gemara explains that the dispute parallels a dispute between Rabbi Elazar (who says God 'overpowers' sins) and Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina (who says God 'carries' sins).
The Gemara resolves: Rabbah aligns with Rabbi Elazar (God overpowers), and Rav Yehuda aligns with Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina (God carries).

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on various minima and maxima
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on various minima and maxima
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists several halachic minima and maxima: no fewer than four intercalated months in a year and no more than eight; the two loaves are not eaten in less than two days nor more than three; the showbread is not eaten in less than nine nor more than eleven; a minor is not circumcised before eight days nor after twelve. The Gemara asks about the phrase 'no more than eight' regarding intercalated months: Rav Huna explains that the Sages did not see fit to intercalate more than eight months. The Gemara then asks why not nine?

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists halachic minima and maxima for intercalated months, the two loaves, the showbread, and circumcision of a minor.
The Gemara asks about the meaning of the Mishnah's phrase 'no more than eight' regarding intercalated months.
Rav Huna explains that the Sages did not see fit to intercalate more than eight months.
The Gemara asks why specifically nine intercalated months are excluded.

items.text: Objection to eight deficient months
items.text_en: Objection to eight deficient months
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if eight months are deficient, the moon would appear two days early, but earlier it was said that three days early is the threshold. The answer is given via Rav Mesharshiya's principle of a leap year, where the extra month compensates, and the remaining one-day discrepancy is dismissed as imperceptible.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if eight months are deficient, the moon would appear only two days early, contradicting the earlier threshold of three days.
Rav Mesharshiya explains that the case involves a leap year where the extra month compensates, and the remaining one-day discrepancy is imperceptible to people.

items.text: Ulla's statement on the reason for eight months
items.text_en: Ulla's statement on the reason for eight months
items.desc_en: Ulla explains that the reason the Sages do not allow more than eight deficient months is that they did not see fit to reduce more than eight, providing the rationale for the Mishnah's rule.

sub.desc_en: Ulla states that the sages did not see fit to have more than eight deficient months in a year, explaining the Mishnah's limit.

items.text: Objection to nine deficient months and resolution
items.text_en: Objection to nine deficient months and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why nine is not allowed, since it would cause the moon to appear three days early, but eight also causes two days early. The answer again uses Rav Mesharshiya's principle of a preceding leap year, and the remaining one-day discrepancy is attributed to human imperceptibility.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if nine deficient months are forbidden, the moon would appear only two days late, not three.
Rav Mesharshiya again invokes the leap year principle, where a full month compensates for the deficient ones.
The Gemara resolves that the remaining one-day discrepancy is due to the moon having appeared but people not noticing it.

items.text: Dispute over the length of the intercalated month
items.text_en: Dispute over the length of the intercalated month
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: What is the dispute between the Tanna Kamma and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel? It is about the intercalated month, as taught: How long is the intercalated month? Thirty days. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says: One month.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the dispute between the Tanna Kamma and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel is about, and answers that it concerns the intercalated month.
The Gemara cites a baraita that states the Tanna Kamma holds the intercalated month is thirty days, while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds it is one month.

items.text: Challenge from a baraita about Rosh Hashanah
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraita about Rosh Hashanah
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: Shavuot only occurs on the day of waving, and Rosh Hashanah only occurs either on the day of waving or on the day after the intercalated month. This challenges Ulla's view that we make eight deficient months but not full ones, and Rav Huna's view that we make full months.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita stating that Shavuot only falls on the day of the waving of the omer, and Rosh Hashanah only falls either on that day or on the day after the intercalated month, and shows that this works for Ulla's view of making eight deficient months.

The Gemara objects that according to Rav Huna, who allows making full months, one would sometimes find Rosh Hashanah occurring on the day after the day after the intercalated month, contradicting the baraita.

items.text: Rav Huna's response to the challenge
items.text_en: Rav Huna's response to the challenge
items.desc_en: Rav Huna retorts: Does Ulla's view work? We don't make eight deficient months, but we do make seven. Sometimes we make seven in winter and not in summer, and then Rosh Hashanah would occur on the day after the intercalated month!

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna retorts that Ulla's position also fails, because even if we make seven deficient months instead of eight, sometimes we make them in winter and not in summer, causing Rosh Hashanah to fall on the day after the intercalated month.

items.text: Resolution: The baraita follows Acheirim
items.text_en: Resolution: The baraita follows Acheirim
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves: The baraita follows Acheirim, who say there are only four days between one Shavuot and the next, or five in a leap year. Rav Mesharshiya explains: In a leap year with a thirty-day intercalated month, Rosh Hashanah can occur on the day of waving.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the baraita follows Acheirim, who hold a different calendar calculation.
The Gemara objects that even according to Acheirim, Rosh Hashanah cannot fall on the day of waving (יוֹם הָנֵף).
Rav Mesharshiya explains that in a leap year with a thirty-day intercalated month, Rosh Hashanah can indeed fall on the day of waving.

items.text: Rav Adda bar Ahava's question and Ravina's objection
items.text_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava's question and Ravina's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava asks Rava: Does Acheirim come to teach us a number? Rather, he teaches that we do not need to sanctify based on sighting. Ravina objects: There is also the day of the hour and the day of thirty years, but since they don't occur every year, they are not counted.

sub.text: Rav Adda bar Ahava's question to Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava's question to Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava asks Rava whether Acheirim's statement merely teaches a number, and suggests it actually teaches that we do not need to sanctify the new month based on sighting.
Ravina objects that there are also the day of the hour and the day of thirty years, but since they do not occur every year, they are not counted.

items.text: Shmuel's view supporting Rav Huna
items.text_en: Shmuel's view supporting Rav Huna
items.desc_en: Shmuel holds like Rav Huna, saying a lunar year is never less than 352 days nor more than 356 days. The Gemara explains: If both months are full, the difference is six days; if both deficient, two; if one full and one deficient, four.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that Shmuel also holds like Rav Huna, citing Shmuel's ruling that a lunar year is never less than 352 days nor more than 356 days.
The Gemara explains the calculation: if both months are full the difference is six days, if both deficient two, and if one full and one deficient four.

items.text: Challenge from a nazirite vow and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge from a nazirite vow and resolution
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited: If one says 'I am a nazirite like the days of the moon,' he counts 354 days. But if the year can be 356, sometimes it would be six days more! The Gemara resolves: In vows, follow common language, and most years are 354 days.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: one who vows to be a nazirite 'like the days of the moon' counts 354 days, implying a fixed lunar year.
The Gemara objects: if the lunar year can be 356 days, sometimes the nazirite would be six days short.
The Gemara resolves: in vows, follow common language, and most years are 354 days.

items.text: Rabbi's practice supporting Rav Huna
items.text_en: Rabbi's practice supporting Rav Huna
items.desc_en: A baraita recounts: Rabbi made nine deficient months, and the new moon appeared on time. Rabbi was surprised, and Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi suggested that perhaps it was a leap year.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a baraita showing that Rabbi (Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi) also holds like Rav Huna regarding making deficient months.
The baraita recounts that Rabbi made nine deficient months, yet the new moon appeared on time, surprising him.
Rabbi expresses surprise: 'We made nine deficient months, yet the new moon appeared on time?'
Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi suggests that perhaps it was a leap year, which would explain the discrepancy.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Shofar blast counts and instruments
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Shofar blast counts and instruments
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that on Rosh Hashanah there must be at least 21 shofar blasts and at most 48, and specifies the types of instruments used (silver trumpets, reed pipes). It also lists the days when the pipe plays before the altar.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating the minimum and maximum number of shofar blasts sounded in the Temple: no fewer than twenty-one and no more than forty-eight.

The Mishnah continues, specifying the minimum and maximum numbers of lyres and flutes used by the Levites, listing the twelve days in the year when the flute plays before the altar, and describing the material and style of the flute.

items.text: Gemara's first question: Who are the priestly families for the pipe?
items.text_en: Gemara's first question: Who are the priestly families for the pipe?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks which families supplied the priests for the pipe service, citing opinions from Rabbi Meir (servants of priests), Rabbi Yosi (families Pegarim and Tzippora from Emmaus), and Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus (Levites).

sub.desc_en: The Mishna states that the pipe players were servants of the priests, according to Rabbi Meir.
Rabbi Yosi says they were from the families of Pegarim and Tzippora from Emmaus, who were fit to marry into the priesthood.
Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonos says they were Levites.

items.text: Gemara's second question: Rabbi Yehuda vs. Sages on blast count
items.text_en: Gemara's second question: Rabbi Yehuda vs. Sages on blast count
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a dispute: Rabbi Yehuda says shofar blasts must be at least 7 and at most 16, while the Sages say 21-48. The argument is whether tekiah-teruah-tekiah is one combined blast (Rabbi Yehuda) or three separate ones (Sages).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the mishna's ruling is not in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda permits only 7 to 16 blasts.
The Gemara explains the dispute: Rabbi Yehuda counts tekiah-teruah-tekiah as one unit, while the Sages count each as separate.

items.text: Gemara's third question: Rabbi Yehuda's proof from verses
items.text_en: Gemara's third question: Rabbi Yehuda's proof from verses
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda cites verses 'And you shall sound a teruah' and 'they shall sound a teruah' to argue that tekiah-teruah-tekiah is one unit. The Sages counter that the verses refer to the simple teruah before and after the tekiah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning, and he cites verses to prove that tekiah-teruah-tekiah is one unit.
Rabbi Yehuda proves from the verses that tekiah-teruah-tekiah is one unit.
The Sages explain that the verses refer to the simple teruah before and after the tekiah.

items.text: Gemara's fourth question: Sages' reason from another verse
items.text_en: Gemara's fourth question: Sages' reason from another verse
items.desc_en: The Sages argue from 'When you assemble the congregation, you shall sound but not raise an alarm' that tekiah and teruah are distinct, since if they were one, God would command half a mitzvah. Rabbi Yehuda says it's just a symbolic sign.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the reasoning of the Rabbis, citing the verse about assembling the congregation.
The Gemara explains that if tekiah, teruah, and tekiah were one unit, God would command half a mitzvah, which is impossible.
Rabbi Yehuda responds that the single tekiah in that verse is merely a symbolic sign, not a mitzvah unit.

items.text: Gemara's fifth question: Rav Kahana's statement aligns with whom?
items.text_en: Gemara's fifth question: Rav Kahana's statement aligns with whom?
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana said 'There is nothing between tekiah and teruah' — this matches Rabbi Yehuda's view that they are one unit. The Gemara asks if it could also align with the Sages, but concludes it must be Rabbi Yehuda.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks in accordance with whose opinion Rav Kahana's statement that there is nothing between tekiah and teruah goes, and answers that it is in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda, noting that this is obvious.

items.text: Gemara's sixth question: Could it be like the Sages?
items.text_en: Gemara's sixth question: Could it be like the Sages?
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers if Rav Kahana's statement could also mean 'nothing between them' in the Sages' sense (they are separate but adjacent). It asks: if so, why did he say 'not anything'? It concludes it must be Rabbi Yehuda's view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara considers whether Rav Kahana's statement could also align with the Sages, excluding only Rabbi Yochanan's lenient view, and concludes it must be according to Rabbi Yehuda.

items.text: Gemara's seventh question: What does 'not anything' mean?
items.text_en: Gemara's seventh question: What does 'not anything' mean?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if Rav Kahana meant the Sages' view, why say 'not anything'? It would be obvious that there is nothing between them. The phrase must emphasize that they are truly one unit, as per Rabbi Yehuda.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the previous answer: if Rav Kahana's statement aligns with the Rabbis, why emphasize 'not anything'? The phrase implies a complete unity, supporting Rabbi Yehuda's view.

items.text: Gemara's eighth question: Twelve days of pipe and Hallel
items.text_en: Gemara's eighth question: Twelve days of pipe and Hallel
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists twelve days when the pipe plays: first Passover, second Passover, first Shavuot, and eight days of Sukkot. The Gemara asks why these days differ from others regarding Hallel (individual vs. communal recitation).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the flute plays specifically on these twelve days, and answers that it is because the individual completes the full Hallel on them.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan cites the list of eighteen days in the Land of Israel and twenty-one in the Diaspora when the individual completes the full Hallel, supporting the answer.

items.text: Gemara's ninth question: Why Sukkot vs. Passover on Hallel?
items.text_en: Gemara's ninth question: Why Sukkot vs. Passover on Hallel?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: why on Sukkot we say Hallel every day, but on Passover only the first day (and in diaspora two days)? It explains that Sukkot has eight days, each a full holiday, while Passover's intermediate days are chol hamoed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Hallel is recited every day of Sukkot but not on the intermediate days of Passover.

items.text: Initial distinction between Sukkot and Passover
items.text_en: Initial distinction between Sukkot and Passover
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Sukkot has different offerings each day, while Passover does not, which explains why song is said on Sukkot but not on Passover.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the days of Sukkot are distinct in their offerings, unlike Passover, so song is said on each day of Sukkot but only on the first day of Passover.

items.text: Shabbat and Rosh Chodesh excluded
items.text_en: Shabbat and Rosh Chodesh excluded
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers Shabbat and Rosh Chodesh: Shabbat is excluded because it is not called a 'moed', and Rosh Chodesh is excluded because it is not sanctified for work, as derived from a verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why hallel is not recited on Shabbat, which is distinct in its offerings, and answers that Shabbat is not called a 'moed'.
The Gemara asks why hallel is not recited on Rosh Chodesh, which is called a 'moed', and answers that it is not sanctified for work.
The Gemara cites a verse to prove that only a night sanctified as a festival requires song, excluding Rosh Chodesh.

items.text: Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur excluded due to judgment
items.text_en: Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur excluded due to judgment
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur do not have song, and answers with Rabbi Avahu's teaching that the ministering angels questioned why Israel does not sing, and God replied that it is inappropriate when the King sits in judgment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why hallel is not recited on Rosh HaShana and Yom Kippur, which are called appointed days and are sanctified with regard to labor.

The Gemara answers that hallel is not recited due to Rabbi Abbahu's teaching, in which the ministering angels ask why Israel does not sing on these days, and God replies that it is inappropriate while the King sits in judgment.

items.text: Chanukah and Purim: miracles and diaspora
items.text_en: Chanukah and Purim: miracles and diaspora
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Chanukah has song due to the miracle, but Purim does not because song is not said for a miracle that occurred outside the Land of Israel, as stated by Rabbi Yitzchak.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Chanukah, which has neither a special offering nor a prohibition of labor, still warrants hallel due to the miracle, so Purim, which also has a miracle, should likewise warrant hallel.
Rabbi Yitzchak answers that hallel is not recited on Purim because one does not recite a song of praise for a miracle that occurred outside of Eretz Yisrael.

items.text: Objection and resolution regarding diaspora miracles
items.text_en: Objection and resolution regarding diaspora miracles
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak objects that the Exodus was a diaspora miracle yet we say Hallel. The Gemara resolves with a baraita that before entering the Land, all lands were fit for song; after entering, they were not, but after exile, the original permission returned. Rav Nachman and Rava debate whether reading the Megillah itself is Hallel.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak objects that the exodus from Egypt, a miracle outside Eretz Yisrael, is commemorated with Hallel, contradicting the claim that no Hallel is said for diaspora miracles.
The Gemara cites a baraita that before entering Eretz Yisrael all lands were fit for song, but after entry only Eretz Yisrael was fit, resolving the objection.
Rav Nachman offers an alternative answer: the reading of the Megillah itself is equivalent to reciting Hallel.
Rava gives a third reason: after the exodus one can say 'servants of the Lord', but after Purim the Jews remain servants of Ahasuerus, so Hallel is inappropriate.
The Gemara resolves the difficulty with Rav Nachman's view by citing the baraita that after the exile, the original permission for all lands to recite song was restored.

items.text: Definition of chalil and abuv
items.text_en: Definition of chalil and abuv
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa explains that the chalil and abuv are the same instrument, called chalil because its sound is sweet (chalei kaleih).

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa explains that the chalil and abuv are the same instrument, called chalil because its sound is sweet.

items.text: Temple instruments: abuv, tziltzol, makhteshet, and their repairs
items.text_en: Temple instruments: abuv, tziltzol, makhteshet, and their repairs
items.desc_en: A baraita describes the abuv (a smooth, thin reed pipe from Moses' time), the tziltzol (a copper cymbal that was repaired by Alexandrian craftsmen), and the makhteshet (a copper mortar for spices). These two vessels from the First Temple were damaged and never fully restored. Rav and Shmuel debate their value relative to gold, and Rabbi Nathan interprets a verse to mean they were secondary.

sub.desc_en: The baraita describes the abuv (a smooth, thin reed pipe from Moses' time) and the tziltzol (a copper cymbal), noting that attempts to plate or repair them with gold or Alexandrian craftsmanship spoiled their sound, and removing the additions restored it.

The baraita continues with the makhteshet (a copper mortar from Moses' time) used for compounding incense spices; after damage and repair by Alexandrian artisans it did not work as well, and removing the repair restored its function.

The baraita concludes that these two vessels (the cymbal and the mortar) were remnants of the First Temple, were damaged and never fully repaired, and cites verses from David and Ezra referring to them.

Rav and Shmuel debate the value of these two vessels relative to gold: one says each is worth two gold vessels, the other says both together are worth one gold vessel; Rav Yosef's baraita supports the latter.
Rabbi Natan interprets the verse's 'two' (שניים) as 'pairs' (שניים), meaning there were two cymbals and two mortars.

items.text: Shiloach spring and other Temple instruments
items.text_en: Shiloach spring and other Temple instruments
items.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel teaches about the Shiloach spring, which was widened but then reduced to restore its flow, illustrating a verse. He also states that the hirdavlim (identified by Abaye as a type of cymbal) were not in the Temple because they disturb the melody. Finally, Rava bar Sheila quotes Shmuel about the magrefa in the Temple.

sub.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel teaches that the Shiloach spring originally spurted water through an opening the size of an issar coin; the king widened it to increase the flow, but the water decreased.
The spring's flow decreased after widening, so they narrowed it again and it resumed its original flow, demonstrating that human intervention cannot improve on nature.
This episode fulfills the verse 'Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might' (Jeremiah 9:22).
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel further states that the hirdavlim was not used in the Temple; the Gemara asks what hirdavlim is.
Abaye explains that hirdavlim is a hydraulic organ (טבלא גורגדנא), which was not used because its pleasant sound disrupts the melody.
Rava bar Sheila quotes Rav Matna quoting Shmuel that there was a magrefa (a type of instrument) in the Temple.

items.text: Baraita on the organ's dimensions and capacity
items.text_en: Baraita on the organ's dimensions and capacity
items.desc_en: A baraita describes the organ in the Temple as one cubit wide and tall, with ten pipes each producing one hundred types of song, totaling a thousand. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak notes this is an exaggeration.

sub.desc_en: The baraita describes the organ's dimensions and its ten pipes, each producing one hundred types of song, totaling a thousand.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak notes that the baraita's numbers are exaggerated, providing a mnemonic to distinguish it from the earlier mishnah.

items.text: Dispute over the identity of the Temple singers
items.text_en: Dispute over the identity of the Temple singers
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes a dispute about whether the singers were slaves or Levites, linking it to the fundamental question of whether song is primarily vocal or instrumental. It then reinterprets the dispute as being about whether one can elevate from the platform (duchan) to lineage and tithes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Ḥanina ben Antigonus hinges on whether the primary component of song is vocal (allowing slaves) or instrumental (requiring Levites).
The Gemara objects that this explanation fails to account for Rabbi Yosei's position, since neither option (vocal or instrumental) would justify requiring Israelites of pure lineage.
The Gemara resolves that all agree the primary component is vocal, and the actual dispute concerns whether one may elevate from the platform (דוכן) to lineage and tithes.
The Gemara details the three positions: slaves hold no elevation, Levites hold elevation for both lineage and tithes, and Israelites hold elevation for lineage but not tithes.

items.text: Whether song is indispensable for the sacrifice
items.text_en: Whether song is indispensable for the sacrifice
items.desc_en: A Tannaitic dispute is presented: Rabbi Meir holds that song is indispensable for the sacrifice, deriving it from a verse linking song to atonement. The Sages disagree, using the same verse to teach that song must be performed during the day.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with the dispute: Rabbi Meir holds that the song is indispensable for the sacrifice, while the Sages hold it is not.
The Gemara explains Rabbi Meir's reasoning: the verse compares the Levites' service to atonement, so just as atonement is indispensable, so is the song.
The Gemara explains that the Sages use the same verse to teach, per Rabbi Elazar, that just as atonement is performed during the day, so too the song must be during the day.

items.text: Scriptural sources for the principle of song
items.text_en: Scriptural sources for the principle of song
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel derives the principle of song from the verse 'and to serve in the name of the Lord'. The Gemara rejects an alternative interpretation (raising hands) and then brings Rav Mattana's derivation from the verse about serving with joy, distinguishing it from Torah study and first fruits.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel derives the principle of song from the verse 'and to serve in the name of the Lord', identifying this service as song.
The Gemara objects that the verse might refer to the lifting of hands for the Priestly Benediction, but rejects this because the verse distinguishes between service and blessing.
Rav Mattana derives the requirement for song from the verse about serving with joy and goodness of heart, and rejects the alternative of Torah study because it is not called 'goodness'.
The Gemara objects that the verse might refer to first fruits, but rejects this because first fruits are called 'goodness' but not 'goodness of heart'.

items.text: Song for first fruits and the requirement of wine
items.text_en: Song for first fruits and the requirement of wine
items.desc_en: Rav Mattana derives that first fruits require song through a verbal analogy. The Gemara then cites Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani that song is only said over wine, and resolves the apparent contradiction by noting that one brings grapes and then presses them into wine.

sub.desc_en: Rav Mattana derives that first fruits require song via a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) between the word 'goodness' in the verse about serving God with joy and the verse about rejoicing in all the goodness.

The Gemara objects by citing Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan, who derives from the verse about the vine that song is only recited over wine, which would seemingly exclude first fruits that are not accompanied by a wine libation.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by citing Rabbi Yosei's teaching that if one brings grapes and presses them into wine, the verse 'you shall bring in' includes wine as a valid form of first fruits, thus allowing song over the wine.

items.text: Additional scriptural derivations for song
items.text_en: Additional scriptural derivations for song
items.desc_en: Various Amoraim bring additional verses to prove that song is a Temple service: Chizkiya from the verse about Kenaniah, Rabbi Yochanan from 'work of work', Rabbi Yitzchak from 'lift up a song', Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak from 'they shall lift up their voice', and a Tanna from the verse about the sons of Kehat. Chananya ben Achi Rabbi Yehoshua adds another verse.

sub.desc_en: Chizkiya derives the requirement for song from the verse about Chenaniah, reading 'yasor' as 'yashir'.
Rabbi Yochanan derives song from the phrase 'work of work', identifying it as the service that requires another service.
Rabbi Yitzchak cites the verse 'Se'u zimrah' as the source for song.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak cites the verse 'Hem yis'u kolam' as the source for song.
A Tanna derives song from the verse about the sons of Kehat, interpreting 'yisa'u' as an expression of song.
Chananya ben Achi Rabbi Yehoshua cites the verse 'Moshe yedaber' as another source for song.

items.text: Sources for the prohibition of switching Temple service
items.text_en: Sources for the prohibition of switching Temple service
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi and Rabbi Yonatan each derive from a verse that a Levite who performs a service not assigned to him is liable to death. A baraita supports Rabbi Yonatan's interpretation, distinguishing between death for switching with another Levite and a mere warning for performing a service not his own.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi derives the obligation for Levites to sing from the verse about the trumpeters and singers being as one.
Rabbi Yonatan derives the obligation from the verse equating priests and Levites, indicating Levites perform a service on the altar.
A baraita supports Rabbi Yonatan's interpretation, distinguishing between death for switching with another Levite and a mere warning for performing a service not his own.

items.text: Abaye's inference that a singer who timed for a gatekeeper is liable to death
items.text_en: Abaye's inference that a singer who timed for a gatekeeper is liable to death
items.desc_en: Abaye states a tradition: a singer who timed (played an instrument) for his fellow gatekeeper is liable to death, citing a verse about the stranger who approaches. He clarifies that 'stranger' here means a stranger to that specific service.

sub.desc_en: Abaye states a tradition that a singer who timed for his fellow gatekeeper is liable to death, citing a verse.
Abaye clarifies that 'stranger' in the verse refers to a Levite who is a stranger to that specific service, not a non-Levite.

items.text: Objection and resolution regarding the punishment
items.text_en: Objection and resolution regarding the punishment
items.desc_en: An objection is raised from a baraita stating that a singer who timed or a timer who sang is only liable to a warning, not death. The Gemara resolves this as a dispute between Tanna'im: one holds it is a capital offense (with a rabbinic decree), the other holds it is only a warning (without a decree).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita stating that a singer who served as a gatekeeper and a gatekeeper who sang are not liable to death but only to a warning.
The Gemara resolves the objection by presenting a baraita about Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya and Rabbi Yochanan ben Gudgada, indicating a dispute between tanna'im.
The Gemara suggests that the dispute is about whether the punishment is death (with a rabbinic decree) or merely a warning (without a decree).
The Gemara rejects the previous analysis, stating that everyone agrees the punishment is only a warning, and the dispute is whether the Sages decreed a prohibition on assisting.

items.text: Rabbi Avin's inquiry about song for a communal freewill burnt-offering
items.text_en: Rabbi Avin's inquiry about song for a communal freewill burnt-offering
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avin asks whether a communal freewill burnt-offering requires song, based on the verse 'your burnt-offerings'—does it include both obligatory and freewill offerings, or only the obligatory ones of all Israel?

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avin raises a dilemma whether a communal freewill burnt-offering requires song, questioning whether the verse 'your burnt-offerings' includes both obligatory and freewill offerings or only the obligatory ones of all Israel.

items.text: Attempts to prove from Hezekiah's offering
items.text_en: Attempts to prove from Hezekiah's offering
items.desc_en: The Gemara tries to prove from Hezekiah's offering that a freewill burnt-offering requires song, but Rav Yosef, Abaye, Rami bar Rav Yeiva, and Rav Aviya each offer alternative explanations. Rav Ashi concludes that the consultation was about the agent of the community, not the type of offering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove from Hezekiah's offering that a voluntary burnt-offering requires song, arguing that if it were obligatory, no consultation would have been needed.
Rav Yosef rejects the proof, explaining that the offering was the obligatory New Moon burnt-offering, and the consultation was about whether the New Moon had been established in time.
Abaye objects to Rav Yosef's explanation, citing the verse that explicitly states the offering was on the sixteenth of the first month, not the New Moon.
Rami bar Rav Yeiva suggests that the consultation was about the lamb that comes with the omer offering, questioning whether the New Moon had been established in time.
Rav Aviya objects that the date could be determined from the performance of the Paschal offering and matzah, so there was no need to consult.

Rav Ashi resolves the issue by explaining that the consultation was merely a formal gesture of respect, as with a prayer leader asking permission from the congregation, and not about the type of offering.

items.text: Proof from the destruction of the Temple
items.text_en: Proof from the destruction of the Temple
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a tradition about the First Temple's destruction: the Levites sang a psalm not associated with any offering. The Gemara questions whether this was a freewill offering, but Rava and Rav Ashi explain it was an impromptu song, not a regular service. The discussion concludes that the song was not for a freewill offering.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei states the principle that merit is brought about on an auspicious day and liability on an inauspicious day.
The Sages relate that on the day the First Temple was destroyed, the Levites were standing on their platform and singing a psalm, but they were interrupted by the enemy.
The Gemara asks what offering this song accompanied, ruling out an obligatory burnt offering since the daily offering had ceased, and suggesting it was a voluntary burnt offering.
The Gemara objects that if no animals were available for obligatory offerings, none would be available for voluntary ones either, but answers that a young bull happened to come into their possession.
Rava (or Rav Ashi) rejects the proof by noting that the psalm sung was not the song of that day, but merely an impromptu lamentation.
The Gemara explains that the Levites were on the platform because Reish Lakish permits reciting songs not for an offering, but they do not sing for voluntary burnt offerings to avoid mishap.

items.text: Final resolution from a baraita
items.text_en: Final resolution from a baraita
items.desc_en: Rav Mari bar Rav Kahana teaches a baraita that equates the freewill burnt-offering with the peace-offering in terms of sanctity and fixed time, implying that a communal freewill burnt-offering does require song, as it has a fixed time like the peace-offering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the resolution is and introduces a baraita taught by Rav Mari bar Rav Kahana.

Rav Mari bar Rav Kahana's baraita juxtaposes burnt-offerings and peace-offerings, deriving that just as the peace-offering has a fixed time, so too the burnt-offering that requires song must have a fixed time, thereby excluding voluntary burnt-offerings.

items.text: The inquiry about song for independent libations
items.text_en: The inquiry about song for independent libations
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether libations brought on their own require song, given Shmuel bar Nachmani's statement that song is only said over wine. The question is whether song requires both eating and drinking, or just drinking alone.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises the dilemma whether libations brought alone require song, citing Shmuel bar Nachmani's statement that song is said only over wine, and questions whether song requires both eating and drinking or just drinking.

items.text: Attempted proof from Rabbi Yosei's baraita
items.text_en: Attempted proof from Rabbi Yosei's baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yosei says merit is rolled to a worthy day, and the song mentioned must be for libations, since the daily offering ceased on the 17th of Tammuz and a free-will burnt offering would not need song according to Rav Mari.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Yosei's baraita about rolling merit to a worthy day, which includes the detail of the Levites singing on the platform.
The Gemara asks what offering the song accompanied, ruling out an obligatory burnt offering since the daily offering ceased on the 17th of Tammuz.
The Gemara rejects the possibility of a voluntary burnt offering, citing Rav Mari's teaching that such an offering does not require song, and concludes the song must have accompanied libations.

items.text: Rava and Rav Ashi's rejection of the proof
items.text_en: Rava and Rav Ashi's rejection of the proof
items.desc_en: Rava or Rav Ashi object that the song in the baraita is the daily psalm, not for libations, and the mention of standing on the platform is explained by Reish Lakish's principle that song can be said without a sacrifice. The Gemara concludes that the case of libations cannot be proven due to the destruction.

sub.desc_en: Rava or Rav Ashi objects that the song in the baraita is not the daily psalm for that day, so it was merely a lamentation, not a song for an offering.

The Gemara explains that the Levites were standing on the platform per Reish Lakish's principle that song may be recited without an offering, but they do not sing for libations alone to avoid a mishap.

items.text: Return to the baraita's text
items.text_en: Return to the baraita's text
items.desc_en: The Gemara restates Rabbi Yosei's statement about rolling merit to a worthy day, setting up the chronological discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara restates Rabbi Yosei's principle that merit is rolled to an auspicious day, setting up the subsequent chronological discussion.

items.text: Chronological difficulty with the Jubilee year
items.text_en: Chronological difficulty with the Jubilee year
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the baraita's 'first' Yom Kippur after the Jubilee can occur in the 25th year of exile, given the verse in Ezekiel. It calculates that if the city was destroyed at the beginning of a Sabbatical cycle, the years do not align.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the baraita's 'first' Yom Kippur after the Jubilee can occur in the 25th year of exile, citing the verse in Ezekiel that identifies the year as a Jubilee.

The Gemara objects that if the destruction occurred at the beginning of a Sabbatical cycle, the Jubilee would fall in the fifteenth year after the destruction, not the fourteenth as implied by the verse.

items.text: Ravina's resolution and the counting of exile years
items.text_en: Ravina's resolution and the counting of exile years
items.desc_en: Ravina explains that the verse refers to the 14th year after the year the city was struck, but the Gemara objects that this would make the total 26 years. Ravina responds by excluding the year of the exile itself, similar to the objector's own calculation.

sub.desc_en: Ravina answers that the verse refers to the fourteenth year after the year the city was struck, i.e., counting from the following year.

The Gemara objects that if the destruction year is not counted, the total from the first exile to Ezekiel's prophecy would be twenty-six years, not twenty-five, citing the baraita of Mar about the exiles.
Ravina rejects the objection by pointing out that the objector's own calculation also yields twenty-six years unless one excludes the year of the exile, and the same applies to his own counting.

items.text: Final resolution: only two exiles
items.text_en: Final resolution: only two exiles
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the remaining difficulty by explaining that there were only two exiles, not three, and provides the precise years relative to Jehoiakim's conquest and Nebuchadnezzar's reign.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Ravina's explanation still leaves the count of nineteen years difficult.
The Gemara resolves the difficulty by explaining that there were only two exiles, not three, and specifies the years relative to Jehoiakim's subjugation and Nebuchadnezzar's reign.
The Gemara cites the statement of Mar that in the first year of his reign Nebuchadnezzar conquered Nineveh, supporting the interpretation of the years.

items.text: Opening statement: Second Temple destroyed in a post-sabbatical year
items.text_en: Opening statement: Second Temple destroyed in a post-sabbatical year
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that the Second Temple was destroyed in a post-sabbatical year, and similarly the first Temple was destroyed in a post-sabbatical year.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that the Second Temple was destroyed in a post-sabbatical year, and similarly the first Temple was destroyed in a post-sabbatical year.

items.text: Question and answer: How can the Second Temple be in a post-sabbatical year?
items.text_en: Question and answer: How can the Second Temple be in a post-sabbatical year?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the Second Temple could be destroyed in a post-sabbatical year, given its 420-year duration. It calculates that 420 years equals 8 Jubilee cycles (400 years) plus 14 years, leaving 6 years, meaning it was destroyed in the sixth year of a shemittah cycle. It identifies this as Rabbi Yehuda's view, who holds that the Jubilee year counts for both the previous and next cycle, making the total 14 years and placing the destruction in a post-sabbatical year.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the Second Temple could be destroyed in a post-sabbatical year, and calculates that 420 years equals 8 Jubilee cycles plus 14 years, leaving 6 years, meaning it was destroyed in the sixth year of a shemittah cycle.

The Gemara identifies this as Rabbi Yehuda's view, who holds that the Jubilee year counts for both the previous and next cycle, making the total 14 years and placing the destruction in a post-sabbatical year.

items.text: Objection: Rabbi Yehuda's view fails for the First Temple
items.text_en: Objection: Rabbi Yehuda's view fails for the First Temple
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the view is Rabbi Yehuda, then the First Temple's destruction cannot be in a post-sabbatical year. A baraita states that Israel counted 17 Jubilees from entering the land to the exile, but not from the entry, as that would place the destruction at the start of a Jubilee, contradicting the verse about the fourteenth year after the city was struck. Instead, subtract 7 years of conquest and 7 of division, and the verse is fulfilled.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if Rabbi Yehuda's counting method is used for the First Temple, the calculation would place its destruction at the beginning of a jubilee, contradicting the verse that says it was destroyed in the fourteenth year after the city was struck.

A baraita is cited stating that Israel counted 17 Jubilees from entering the land to the exile, but not from the entry, as that would place the destruction at the start of a Jubilee, contradicting the verse about the fourteenth year after the city was struck.
The baraita resolves the contradiction by subtracting 7 years of conquest and 7 of division, so the verse about the fourteenth year is fulfilled.

items.text: Further objection: Rabbi Yehuda's calculation yields a different year
items.text_en: Further objection: Rabbi Yehuda's calculation yields a different year
items.desc_en: The Gemara continues: if it is Rabbi Yehuda, applying the 17 Jubilees to the Second Temple would place its destruction in the third year of the shemittah cycle, not the sixth. The Gemara answers that the years of the exile under Sennacherib until Jeremiah returned them are not counted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the Tanna is Rabbi Yehuda, applying the 17 Jubilees from the First Temple period to the Second Temple would place its destruction in the third year of the shemittah cycle, not the sixth.
The Gemara answers that the years of the exile under Sennacherib until Jeremiah returned them are not counted in the Jubilee tally.

items.text: Alternative answer: The Rabbis' view and the priestly watches
items.text_en: Alternative answer: The Rabbis' view and the priestly watches
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative: the view is actually the Rabbis, and the statement 'and similarly in the second' refers to the remainder (the last years). This is supported by the fact that the watch of Yehoyariv existed in the Second Temple, as a baraita describes the return of four priestly watches from exile and their division into 24 watches.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative answer: the view is actually the Rabbis, and the statement 'and similarly in the second' refers to the remainder (the last years).
The Gemara argues that this interpretation is logically compelling, because otherwise the watch of Yehoyariv would not have existed in the Second Temple.
A baraita is cited describing the return of four priestly watches from exile and their division into 24 watches, confirming that Yehoyariv's watch existed in the Second Temple.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: The arrangement of priestly watches
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: The arrangement of priestly watches
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes how the priestly watch of Jedaiah was established as primary and Jehoiarib as secondary, and that even if Jehoiarib (the first watch) ascends, Jedaiah is not displaced.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah establishes the arrangement of priestly watches, stating that Jedaiah is primary and Jehoiarib secondary, and that even if Jehoiarib ascends, Jedaiah is not displaced.

items.text: Rav Ashi's explanation of the six-year gap
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's explanation of the six-year gap
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that the six years mentioned in the Mishnah do not count the years until Ezra ascended and sanctified the Temple, citing verses from Daniel and Ezra that show the Temple was completed in the sixth year of Darius and Ezra came the following year.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that the six years until Ezra ascended and sanctified are not counted, citing verses about the cessation and completion of the Temple work.
A baraita supports Rav Ashi by stating that Ezra ascended with his exile in the following year, as per the verse.
A Tanna teaches that in the following year Ezra ascended with his exile, citing a verse from Ezra that he came in the seventh year of the king.

items.text: The seventeen jubilees from entry to exile
items.text_en: The seventeen jubilees from entry to exile
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that Israel counted seventeen jubilees from entering the land until leaving, and notes that if they counted from entry, the Temple would have been destroyed at the beginning of a jubilee, contradicting the verse about fourteen years after the city was smitten.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that Israel counted seventeen jubilees from entering the land until leaving, and that counting from entry would place the Temple's destruction at the start of a jubilee, contradicting the verse about fourteen years after the city was struck.

items.text: Proof of seven years of conquest from Caleb
items.text_en: Proof of seven years of conquest from Caleb
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives the seven years of conquest from Caleb's statement that he was 40 when sent as a spy and 85 at the division of the land, and from the tradition that the first year was the Tabernacle, the second year the spies were sent, showing that seven years were spent conquering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where do we derive the seven years of conquest? It cites Caleb's statement about his age.
The Gemara calculates that Caleb was 78 when crossing the Jordan and 85 when dividing inheritances, thus establishing seven years of conquest.

items.text: Proof of seven years of division
items.text_en: Proof of seven years of division
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers two alternative proofs for the seven years of division: either from the parallel with the seven years of conquest, or from the impossibility of finding the verse about fourteen years after the city was smitten if the division took a different amount of time.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where do we derive the seven years of division? It offers one answer: just as there were seven of conquest, so too seven of division.
Alternatively, the Gemara derives the seven years of division from the fact that the verse about fourteen years after the city was struck is not found otherwise.
The Gemara offers a second answer: From the fact that you cannot find the verse about 'fourteen years after the city was smitten' unless the division took seven years.

items.text: Mishnah: Minimum number of lambs and musical instruments
items.text_en: Mishnah: Minimum number of lambs and musical instruments
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that no fewer than six inspected lambs are kept in the Lamb Chamber for Shabbat and Rosh Hashanah, and no fewer than two trumpets, nine harps, and one cymbal, with no upper limit.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that no fewer than six inspected lambs are kept in the Lamb Chamber for Shabbat and Rosh Hashanah, and no fewer than two trumpets, nine lyres, and one cymbal.

items.text: Gemara's clarification: The Mishnah refers only to tamid offerings
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification: The Mishnah refers only to tamid offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah mentions only six lambs when there are many daily and additional offerings, and answers that the Tanna is referring only to the tamid offerings, and the mention of Shabbat and festivals is merely a mnemonic.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: there are many daily and additional offerings, so why only six lambs?

The Gemara explains that the Tanna is only discussing the daily offerings (תמידין), and the mention of Shabbat and festivals is merely a mnemonic, so the rule is that no fewer than six lambs are kept.

items.text: The requirement for a four-day inspection of the daily offering
items.text_en: The requirement for a four-day inspection of the daily offering
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the mishnah's ruling that the daily offering requires inspection four days before slaughter as the opinion of Ben Bag Bag, who derives this from a verbal analogy between 'guard' in the context of the daily offering and 'guard' regarding the Passover lamb. The Gemara then notes that the mishnah's phrasing 'enough for the Sabbath' supports this interpretation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the mishnah's ruling that the daily offering requires inspection four days before slaughter as the opinion of Ben Bag Bag.

sub.text: Supporting baraita of Ben Bag Bag
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita of Ben Bag Bag
sub.desc_en: Ben Bag Bag derives the requirement for a four-day inspection of the daily offering from a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) between 'guard' in the verse regarding the daily offering and 'guard' regarding the Passover lamb.
The Gemara notes that the mishnah's phrasing 'enough for the Sabbath' (כְּדֵי לַשַּׁבָּת) rather than 'for the Sabbath' (לַשַּׁבָּת) supports the identification with Ben Bag Bag.

items.text: The number of trumpets and cymbals
items.text_en: The number of trumpets and cymbals
items.desc_en: Rav Huna states that up to 120 trumpets may be added, based on a verse. Rav Asi explains that the single cymbal mentioned in the mishnah is derived from the verse 'Asaph with cymbals,' and even though the verse says 'cymbals' (plural), since one person plays both, they are considered one.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Up to how many trumpets may be added?
Rav Huna (or some say Rav Zavdi in Rav Huna's name) answers: Up to 120, citing the verse about 120 priests blowing trumpets.
The verse 'and with them 120 priests blowing trumpets' is cited as the source for the maximum of 120 trumpets.
The Gemara asks: From where are these matters (that only one cymbal is used) derived?
Rav Asi answers, citing the verse 'and Asaph with cymbals to sound aloud' as the source.
The Gemara objects: The word 'מצלתים' (cymbals) is in the dual form, implying two cymbals, not one.
The Gemara resolves: Since the two cymbals perform one function and one person plays them, the verse calls them one.

items.text: The minimum number of Levites and the rule for minors
items.text_en: The minimum number of Levites and the rule for minors
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that no fewer than twelve Levites stand on the platform, and minors may enter the courtyard only when the Levites sing, and only with vocal song. Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov adds that minors do not ascend for the count or to the platform but stand on the ground with their heads between the Levites' feet, and are called 'young Levites.'

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states the minimum of twelve Levites on the platform, that minors enter only during song and sing only vocally.
Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov adds that minors do not ascend for the count or to the platform but stand on the ground with their heads between the Levites' feet, and are called 'young Levites.'

items.text: The twelve Levites correspond to the musical instruments
items.text_en: The twelve Levites correspond to the musical instruments
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa explains that the twelve Levites correspond to the nine harps, two lyres, and one cymbal, as derived from the verse about the sons of Heman.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the twelve Levites correspond to.
Rav Pappa answers that the twelve Levites correspond to the nine harps, two lyres, and one cymbal, as derived from the verse about the sons of Heman.

items.text: Source for minors entering only during song
items.text_en: Source for minors entering only during song
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan derives from a verse that minors enter the courtyard only when the Levites sing, as the verse mentions 'to oversee the work' alongside the singers.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source of the Mishnah's rule that minors enter the courtyard only when the Levites sing.

Rabbi Yochanan cites the verse 'וַיַּעֲמֹד יֵשׁוּעַ בָּנָיו וְאֶחָיו... לְנַצֵּחַ עַל עֹשֵׂה הַמְּלָאכָה בְּבֵית הָאֱלֹהִים' to prove that minors enter only when the Levites sing, as the verse links overseeing the work with the singers.

items.text: The distinction between nevel and kinnor and Rabbi Yehuda's opinion
items.text_en: The distinction between nevel and kinnor and Rabbi Yehuda's opinion
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the mishnah's statement that they did not play nevel or kinnor implies that these are distinct instruments, suggesting it contradicts Rabbi Yehuda, who says the Temple kinnor had seven strings and is called nevel in the future due to its many strings. The Gemara resolves that even according to Rabbi Yehuda, in the future world, the kinnor with many strings is called nevel because its sound is like a nevel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the mishnah's distinction between nevel and kinnor implies they are separate instruments, suggesting it contradicts Rabbi Yehuda.
Rabbi Yehuda states that the Temple kinnor had seven strings, citing the verse 'שׂבַע שְׂמָחוֹת' (seven joys).
Rabbi Yehuda adds that the kinnor of the Messianic era will have eight strings, derived from 'עַל הַשְּׁמִינִית' (upon the eighth).
Rabbi Yehuda states that the kinnor of the World to Come will have ten strings, citing 'עֲלֵי עָשׂוֹר וַעֲלֵי נָבֶל' (upon the ten and upon the nevel).
The Gemara resolves that even according to Rabbi Yehuda, in the World to Come, the kinnor with many strings is called nevel because its sound resembles a nevel.

items.text: The term 'young Levites'
items.text_en: The term 'young Levites'
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that they were called 'supporters of the Levites,' but the mishnah calls them 'young Levites' because their voices are thin while the others' voices are deep, so they support and the others do not.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah cites Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's statement that minors do not ascend to the platform and are called 'young Levites'.
A baraita teaches that the minors were called 'supporters of the Levites'.
The Gemara asks why the tanna of our mishnah calls them 'young Levites' rather than 'supporters'.

The Gemara answers that since the minors have thin voices and the adults have deep voices, the minors sing in a high pitch and the adults cannot, so they are called 'young Levites' because they cause the adults anguish.
The Gemara concludes the chapter with the standard formula 'We have returned to you, [the chapter] 'No valuations.'

items.text: Introduction to the chapter on valuations
items.text_en: Introduction to the chapter on valuations
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that valuations have leniencies and stringencies: one who vows the valuation of any Israelite gives fifty shekels, but if he vows his monetary worth, he pays his actual value.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah opens by stating that valuations, ancestral fields, a forewarned ox that killed a slave, a rapist, a seducer, and a defamer all have lenient and stringent aspects.

The mishnah explains the leniency and stringency in valuations: one who vows the valuation of any Israelite, whether handsome or ugly, pays fifty shekels, but if he vows his monetary worth, he pays the actual value.

items.text: Whether a gentile can be valued
items.text_en: Whether a gentile can be valued
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the mishnah's mention of 'Israelite' that a gentile cannot be valued, which seems to contradict Rabbi Meir who says a gentile can be valued but cannot vow a valuation. The Gemara resolves that even Rabbi Meir would agree, but the mishnah chose to mention Israelite for clarity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the mishnah's mention of 'Israelite' that a gentile cannot be valued.
The Gemara objects that the mishnah seems to contradict Rabbi Meir, who holds that a gentile can be valued but cannot vow a valuation.
The Gemara resolves that even Rabbi Meir would agree, but the mishnah chose to mention 'Israelite' for clarity.

items.text: דיון על אי-הזכרת גויים במשנה
items.text_en: Gemara's digression on praising a gentile
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah incidentally teaches that one should not say 'How beautiful is this gentile,' as per Rav Yehudah citing Rav. It then addresses why the Mishnah specifies 'the fairest among Israelites and the ugliest among gentiles' rather than just 'the fairest among Israelites,' explaining that the Mishnah deals with one nation, not two. An objection is raised from another Mishnah that contrasts the greatest in priesthood and the smallest in Israel, but that is resolved by noting that it is one nation, with priests being more sanctified. An alternative answer is given: the Mishnah needed to teach the case of an ancestral field, which only applies to Israelites.
items.desc: הגמרא דנה מדוע המשנה לא מזכירה גויים, ומסיקה שזה משום שאסור לומר 'כמה נאה גוי זה', או משום שהמשנה עוסקת רק באומה אחת, או משום שדיני שדה אחוזה לא שייכים בגויים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah incidentally teaches, per Rav Yehudah citing Rav, that one may not say 'How beautiful is this gentile.'
sub.desc: הגמרא מסבירה שהמשנה נקטה 'ישראל' כדי ללמד אגב אורחא שאסור לומר על גוי 'כמה נאה'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah does not simply say 'the fairest among Israelites and the ugliest among gentiles,' and answers that it deals with one nation, not two.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: אם הטעם הוא לאסור שבח גוי, היה ראוי לשנות גם 'את הכעור שבגויים'? ותירצה שהמשנה אינה עוסקת בשתי אומות.

sub.desc_en: An objection is raised from another Mishnah that contrasts the greatest in priesthood and the smallest in Israel, but it is resolved by noting that it is one nation, with priests being more sanctified.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה מהמשנה שמזכירה כהונה וישראל, ומתרצת ששניהם אומה אחת, אלא שכהנים מקודשים יותר.

sub.desc_en: An alternative answer is given: the Mishnah needed to teach the case of an ancestral field (שדה אחוזה), which only applies to Israelites, so it specifies Israelites.
sub.desc: תירוץ חלופי: המשנה נקטה ישראל בלבד משום שהסיפא עוסקת בשדה אחוזה שאינה שייכת לגויים.

items.text: משנת שדה אחוזה ושדה מקנה
items.text_en: Mishnah: Redemption of ancestral field vs. purchased field
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that for an ancestral field, whether consecrated from sandy land or orchards, one redeems it at the fixed rate of a homer of barley seed for fifty shekels of silver. For a purchased field, one redeems it at its market value. Rabbi Eliezer says that both ancestral and purchased fields are redeemed at market value, the only difference being that an ancestral field requires an additional fifth.
items.desc: המשנה מבארת את ההבדלים בין שדה אחוזה לשדה מקנה: בשדה אחוזה נותן חמישים שקל כסף לכל בית זרע חומר שעורים, ובשדה מקנה נותן את שוויו. רבי אליעזר מוסיף שבשדה אחוזה מוסיף חומש.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating the rule for redeeming an ancestral field at a fixed rate, and for a purchased field at market value.
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת בהבחנה בין שדה אחוזה לשדה מקנה לעניין פדיון, ומפרטת את דין שדה אחוזה.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer states that both types of field are redeemed at market value, differing only in the additional fifth for an ancestral field.
sub.desc: רבי אליעזר חולק וקובע כי גם בשדה מקנה נותן חמישים שקל, וההבדל היחיד הוא חומש בשדה אחוזה.

items.text: Rav Huna's ruling: consecrating a field full of trees
items.text_en: Rav Huna's ruling: consecrating a field full of trees
items.desc_en: Rav Huna states that if one consecrates a field full of trees, when redeeming, he redeems the trees at their market value and then redeems the land at the fixed rate of a homer of barley seed for fifty shekels. This implies Rav Huna holds that one consecrates with a generous eye, including both land and trees.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that one who consecrates a field full of trees redeems the trees at market value and the land at the fixed rate, implying that one consecrates with a generous eye (עין יפה).

items.text: First objection and resolution: the Mishnah's phrase 'sandy land'
items.text_en: First objection and resolution: the Mishnah's phrase 'sandy land'
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman objects to Rav Huna from the Mishnah, which says one gives the fixed rate even for orchards, implying the land alone is redeemed at that rate. Rav Huna responds that he meant the land is 'fit for orchards' (i.e., the fixed rate applies to the land, and trees are redeemed separately). A further objection is raised from a baraita that includes vineyards, cane fields, and tree fields in the fixed rate, but Rav Huna answers that there too one redeems and then redeems again.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman objects to Rav Huna from the Mishnah, which states that one gives the fixed rate even for orchards (pardesot sabasti), implying the land alone is redeemed at that rate.
Rav Huna responds that he meant the land is 'fit for orchards' (i.e., the fixed rate applies to the land, and trees are redeemed separately).
A further objection is raised from a baraita that includes vineyards, cane fields, and tree fields in the fixed rate.
Rav Huna answers that there too one redeems and then redeems again (podeh ve-chozer u-podeh).

items.text: ברייתא על הקדשת שלושה אילנות
items.text_en: Second objection: the baraita of three trees
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects from a baraita: if one consecrates three trees planted within ten per se'ah, he consecrates the land and trees between them, and redeems the whole at the fixed rate. If fewer or more trees, or consecrated sequentially, he does not consecrate the land. The baraita's latter clause says that even if he consecrated trees first and then land, he redeems trees at value and land at the fixed rate. The Gemara notes that if one tries to answer that here too he redeems and then redeems again, the baraita's latter clause explicitly says that, implying the first clause does not allow that.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא המפרטת דין הקדשת שלושה אילנות במטע עשרה לבית סאה, ומדייקה שהסיפא אומרת 'פודה וחוזר ופודה' אך הרישא לא, מה שמקשה על רב הונא.
