sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects from a baraita: if one consecrates three trees planted within ten per se'ah, he consecrates the land and trees between them, and redeems the whole at the fixed rate.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה על רב הונא מברייתא: המקדיש שלושה אילנות במטע עשרה לבית סאה, הקרקע והאילנות שביניהם קדושים, ופודה הכל יחד בחמישים שקל, בניגוד לשיטתו שפודה אילנות בשוויים בנפרד.

sub.desc_en: The baraita continues: if fewer or more trees, or consecrated sequentially, he does not consecrate the land or the trees between them.
sub.desc: הברייתא מפרטת שאם האילנות צפופים או מרווחים מדי, או שהוקדשו בזה אחר זה, לא קדשו לא קרקע ולא אילנות שביניהם, וממילא פודים אותם בשוויים.

sub.desc_en: The baraita's latter clause says that even if he consecrated trees first and then land, he redeems trees at value and land at the fixed rate.
sub.desc: הברייתא מוסיפה שגם אם הקדיש את האילנות ואחר כך את הקרקע, פודה את האילנות בשוויים ואת הקרקע בחמישים שקל, מה שמחזק את הקושיה על רב הונא.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that if one tries to answer that here too he redeems and then redeems again, the baraita's latter clause explicitly says that, implying the first clause does not allow that.
sub.desc: הגמרא דוחה את האפשרות שגם ברישא מדובר בפודה וחוזר ופודה, שהרי מהסיפא שמפורש 'פודה וחוזר ופודה' משמע שברישא לא מדובר כך, ולכן הברייתא אינה מתיישבת עם רב הונא.

items.text: יישוב הברייתא כרבי שמעון
items.text_en: Resolution: the baraita follows Rabbi Shimon, and a further difficulty
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the baraita follows Rabbi Shimon, who holds that one consecrates with a stingy eye, so the land alone is consecrated. However, the Gemara then questions: if it is Rabbi Shimon, why does the latter clause say that if he consecrated trees first and then land, he redeems trees at value and land at the fixed rate? Rabbi Shimon should follow the redemption status, and since the trees were consecrated first, they should be redeemed together with the land. The Gemara supports this with a baraita where Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yehudah hold that a field purchased from one's father and then consecrated after the father's death is considered an ancestral field, following the redemption status.
items.desc: הגמרא מיישבת את הברייתא כרבי שמעון הסובר שמקדיש בעין רעה, ולכן רק אילנות מסוימים מוקדשים. אך מקשה על כך מהסיפא, שכן רבי שמעון הולך אחר זמן הפדיון, ולכן היה ראוי שהאילנות ייפדו עם הקרקע. הגמרא מביאה ברייתא על דין לוקח שדה מאביו והקדישה, ובה נחלקו רבי מאיר ורבי יהודה ורבי שמעון.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the baraita follows Rabbi Shimon, who holds that one consecrates with a stingy eye, so only the land is consecrated, not the trees.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת שהברייתא היא כרבי שמעון, הסובר שהמקדיש מקדיש בעין רעה, ולכן אין האילנות נכללים בקרקע.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions: if the baraita is Rabbi Shimon, why does the latter clause say that if he consecrated trees first and then land, he redeems trees at value and land at the fixed rate?
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה על פירוש זה מהסיפא של הברייתא, שבה אפילו אם הקדיש אילנות ואחר כך קרקע, פודה את האילנות בשוויים ואת הקרקע בקצבה, מה שלא מתיישב עם שיטת רבי שמעון.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Rabbi Shimon should follow the status at the time of redemption, so the trees should be redeemed together with the land.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה שאם הברייתא כרבי שמעון, היה עליו ללכת אחר זמן הפדיון ולפדות את האילנות יחד עם הקרקע, שהרי שמענו שרבי שמעון הולך אחר הפדיון.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yehudah and Rabbi Shimon hold that a field purchased from one's father and consecrated before the father's death is considered an ancestral field at redemption, following the redemption status.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא המוכיחה שרבי שמעון ורבי יהודה הולכים אחר זמן הפדיון, שכן לוקח שדה מאביו והקדישה ואחר כך מת אביו נחשבת כשדה אחוזה, משום שבשעת הפדיון ראויה להיות שדה אחוזה.

sub.desc_en: The baraita concludes with Rabbi Meir's alternative derivation: a field purchased from one's father and consecrated after the father's death is considered an ancestral field.

items.text: Interpretation of the verse for Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Interpretation of the verse for Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon derive from the verse that a field acquired by purchase is not considered an ancestral field even if the father dies afterward, unlike Rabbi Meir. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak clarifies that they interpret the verse 'from the field of his possession' to mean a field not fit to be an ancestral field.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the verse excludes a field that becomes an ancestral field after the father's death from the law of a purchased field.

The Gemara questions how Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon, who hold that even if the father dies afterward it remains an ancestral field, derive their position from the verse, since the verse seems only to support Rabbi Meir.
The Gemara suggests that the difference lies in whether the redemption follows the status at the time of consecration or at the time of redemption.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves that Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon found a different interpretation of the verse.
The Gemara explains that the extra wording 'משדה' (from the field of) teaches that the field is one not fit to be an ancestral field, supporting Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon's position.

items.text: Laws of consecrating and selling rocky land and trees
items.text_en: Laws of consecrating and selling rocky land and trees
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa rules that if one consecrates rocky land (טְרָשִׁין), it is redeemed at its value, not by a fixed amount, because it is not fit for sowing. If not redeemed, it goes to the priests in the Jubilee. If sold, it can be redeemed in less than two years. For trees, if consecrated, they are redeemed at their value and do not go to the priests; if sold, they are not redeemable in less than two years and do not return to the owner in the Jubilee.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa rules that if one consecrates rocky land (טְרָשִׁין), it is redeemed at its value, not by a fixed amount, because it is not fit for sowing.
Rav Pappa adds that if not redeemed, rocky land goes to the priests in the Jubilee, because the Torah says 'field' which includes any type.
Rav Pappa rules that if one sold rocky land, it can be redeemed in less than two years, and if not redeemed, it returns to the owner in the Jubilee.
Rav Pappa rules that if one consecrated trees, they are redeemed at their value and do not go to the priests in the Jubilee.
Rav Pappa rules that if one sold trees, they are not redeemable in less than two years and do not return to the owner in the Jubilee.

items.text: Question on consecrating trees without land
items.text_en: Question on consecrating trees without land
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why trees consecrated without the land are redeemed at their value, suggesting they should be consecrated along with the land. It cites the Nehardeans' principle that selling a palm tree includes the land from its base to the depths, but notes this applies only when claiming ownership.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why trees consecrated without the land are redeemed at their value, suggesting they should be consecrated along with the land and redeemed together.

The Gemara objects that if one claims the trees were consecrated without the land, the Nehardeans' principle that selling a palm includes the land from base to depths would apply, but notes this only holds when claiming ownership.

items.text: The law of a purchased field: fixed value and the fifth
items.text_en: The law of a purchased field: fixed value and the fifth
items.desc_en: The Tosefta teaches that for a purchased field (שְׂדֵה מִקְנָה), one pays its value, not a fixed amount. Rabbi Eliezer uses a verbal analogy to argue for a fixed amount. The Gemara debates whether the Sages accept the verbal analogy and whether they require an additional fifth. Rava concludes they do not, based on two explicit verses about the fifth. A baraita supports Rava's conclusion but not his reasoning, comparing it to valuations.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma states that for a purchased field (שְׂדֵה מִקְנָה), one pays its value, not a fixed amount, citing the verse 'בְּמִכְסַת' (according to the valuation).

Rabbi Eliezer argues via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'וְחִשַּׁב' (and he shall calculate) that a purchased field also requires a fixed amount, like the valuation of a consecrated ancestral field.
The Gemara raises a question: do the Sages accept Rabbi Eliezer's verbal analogy and also require an additional fifth (חומש), or do they reject the analogy and not require the fifth?

Rava concludes that the Sages do not accept the verbal analogy, because the Torah explicitly mentions the fifth (חומש) for an ancestral field and for a house, forming two verses that come as one (שני כתובים הבאים כאחד), which cannot teach other cases.
The Gemara notes that even for those who hold that two verses can teach, the fifth appears in too many contexts (maaser, pure animal, impure animal) to serve as a consistent model.
A baraita supports Rava's conclusion (no fifth for a purchased field) but not his reasoning, comparing it to valuations (ערכין) which also do not add a fifth.

items.text: The goring ox that kills a slave or a free person
items.text_en: The goring ox that kills a slave or a free person
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a forewarned ox that kills a slave pays a fixed 30 shekels regardless of the slave's value, while for a free person it pays the victim's value. The Gemara notes this applies only to a forewarned ox, not a tam, and explains that even according to Rabbi Akiva, the mishnah focuses on the forewarned case because the tam case is not applicable.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a forewarned ox that kills a slave pays a fixed 30 shekels, while for a free person it pays the victim's value, and for injury it pays full damages.

The Gemara notes that the Mishnah specifies a forewarned ox, implying a tam is excluded, and questions whether this contradicts Rabbi Akiva's view that a tam also pays full damages for injuring a person.

The Gemara resolves that even according to Rabbi Akiva, the Mishnah focuses on the forewarned case because the tam case is not applicable to killing a slave or free person, so it teaches the forewarned case for clarity.

items.text: The fixed payment for seduction and rape
items.text_en: The fixed payment for seduction and rape
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who seduces or rapes pays a fixed 50 shekels regardless of the woman's status. The Gemara questions why it is fixed, and Rav Zeira explains that otherwise people would say the payment varies by status. Abaye objects with a parallel from the slave case, and Rav Zeira responds.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who seduces or rapes pays a fixed 50 shekels regardless of the woman's status, while compensation for shame and blemish varies.
The Gemara asks why the payment is fixed, since the Torah says 'fifty shekels' for all cases.
Rav Zeira explains that otherwise people would say the payment varies by the woman's status, implying the Torah fixed it to avoid such talk.
Abaye objects by drawing a parallel from the slave case, where the fixed 30 shekels for a gored slave would similarly invite such talk, yet the Torah did not vary it.
Rav Zeira begins his response to Abaye's objection, though the full resolution is cut off at the section boundary.

items.text: Conclusion of the Gemara's discussion on the seducer's payment
items.text_en: Conclusion of the Gemara's discussion on the seducer's payment
items.desc_en: Abaye and Rava each offer a proof from Scripture that the fifty-shekel payment for seduction is only for the pleasure of intercourse, and that additional payments for shame and damage are separate. Abaye cites the phrase 'תחת אשר עינה' to imply shame and damage, and Rava cites 'ונתן האיש השוכב עמה' to show that the fifty is for the benefit of lying, implying another payment for shame and damage.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the seduction payment is fifty shekels regardless of the woman's status, implying it covers only the pleasure of intercourse.
Abaye objects that the same logic would absurdly apply to a slave's value, which is fixed at thirty regardless of health.
Abaye answers that the verse 'תַּחַת אֲשֶׁר עִנָּהּ' implies the fifty shekels are only for the pleasure, with separate payments for shame and damage.
Rava answers that the verse 'וְנָתַן הָאִישׁ הַשֹּׁכֵב עִמָּהּ' shows the fifty shekels are for the benefit of lying, implying another payment for shame and damage.

items.text: Opening Mishnah on the defamer (מוציא שם רע)
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah on the defamer (מוציא שם רע)
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that the law of the defamer applies to both lenient and stringent cases: whether he defames a high priest's daughter or a minor Israelite girl, he pays one hundred sela. It then states that the one who speaks with his mouth is more severe than the one who acts, as the decree against our ancestors in the wilderness was sealed only because of evil speech.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that the law of the defamer (מוציא שם רע) applies equally to lenient and stringent cases, giving the example that whether he defames a high priest's daughter or a minor Israelite girl, he pays one hundred sela.

The Mishnah concludes that the one who speaks with his mouth is more severe than the one who acts, citing that the decree against the ancestors in the wilderness was sealed only because of evil speech (לשון הרע), as it says 'they tested Me these ten times'.

items.text: Gemara's first question and Rava's answer on the severity of speech
items.text_en: Gemara's first question and Rava's answer on the severity of speech
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's proof that speech is more severe than action, suggesting that the defamer is punished because he causes the girl's death. Rava answers that the verse says 'כי הוציא שם רע' — it is because of the evil name he brought out, not because of the death penalty.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's proof that speech is more severe than action, suggesting that the defamer is punished because he causes the girl's death penalty.
Rava answers that the verse says 'כי הוציא שם רע' — the punishment is for the evil name he brought out, not for the death penalty.

items.text: Gemara's second question and Resh Lakish's answer on the decree in the wilderness
items.text_en: Gemara's second question and Resh Lakish's answer on the decree in the wilderness
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's claim that the decree was sealed because of evil speech, suggesting it was because their measure of sin was not yet full. Resh Lakish answers that the verse 'וינסו אותי זה עשר פעמים' indicates that it was specifically for this (evil speech) that the decree was sealed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's claim that the decree was sealed because of evil speech, suggesting it was because their measure of sin was not yet full, citing Rav Hamnuna's principle that God does not punish until the measure is full.
Resh Lakish answers that the verse 'וַיְנַסּוּ אוֹתִי זֶה עֶשֶׂר פְּעָמִים' (they tested Me these ten times) indicates that it was specifically for this (evil speech) that the decree was sealed.

items.text: Baraita of Rabbi Elazar ben Parta and resolution by Rabbah citing Resh Lakish
items.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Elazar ben Parta and resolution by Rabbah citing Resh Lakish
items.desc_en: A baraita quotes Rabbi Elazar ben Parta who learns the power of evil speech from the spies, who spoke against trees and stones. The Gemara questions this, citing Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa's interpretation that the spies said 'חזק הוא ממנו' implying God cannot remove His vessels. Rabbah citing Resh Lakish resolves that the verse 'וימתו האנשים מוצאי דבת הארץ רעה' shows they died specifically for the evil report about the land.

sub.text: Baraita of Rabbi Elazar ben Parta
sub.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Elazar ben Parta
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar ben Parta cites a baraita teaching the great power of evil speech (לשון הרע) from the spies, who spoke against trees and stones, implying how much worse it is against a person.

The Gemara objects that the spies' sin might not be ordinary evil speech but rather Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa's interpretation that they said 'חזק הוא ממנו' (He is stronger than us), implying God cannot remove His vessels.
Rabbah citing Resh Lakish resolves that the verse 'וימתו האנשים מוצאי דבת הארץ רעה' shows the spies died specifically for the evil report about the land, not for their heretical statement.

items.text: Baraita of Rabbi Yehuda listing the ten trials in the wilderness
items.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Yehuda listing the ten trials in the wilderness
items.desc_en: A baraita of Rabbi Yehuda enumerates the ten trials with which the Israelites tested God: two at the sea, two at the water, two at the manna, two at the quail, one at the calf, and one at the wilderness of Paran. The Gemara elaborates on each, citing verses and stories, including the incident at the sea where the angel of the sea initially refused to release the Egyptians.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda's baraita enumerates the ten trials with which the Israelites tested God in the wilderness.
The Gemara identifies the first trial at the sea as the complaint at the descent, citing the verse 'המבלי אין קברים במצרים' (Were there no graves in Egypt?).

sub.text: Rav Huna and Rabbah bar Mari
sub.text_en: Rav Huna and Rabbah bar Mari
sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the second trial at the sea as the complaint at the ascent, citing Rav Huna that Israel were of little faith and Rabbah bar Mari that they feared the Egyptians would also emerge.
The Gemara recounts the dialogue where God commands the angel of the sea to release the Egyptians, and the angel objects that a slave cannot take back a gift from his master.

The angel further objects that a slave cannot sue his master, and God appoints the Kishon River as guarantor, after which the sea releases the Egyptians, as the verse 'וירא ישראל את מצרים מת על' (Israel saw the Egyptians dead on the seashore).

The Gemara identifies the two trials at the water: at Marah, where the people could not drink and complained against Moses, citing the verse 'ויבאו מרתה' (they came to Marah) and 'וילן העם על משה' (the people murmured against Moses).

The Gemara identifies the second trial at the water as at Rephidim, where there was no water and the people quarreled with Moses, citing the verse 'ויחנו ברפידים' (they encamped at Rephidim) and 'וירב העם עם משה' (the people strove with Moses).
The Gemara begins to introduce the two trials at the manna, citing the relevant verse.

items.text: Opening: Biblical examples of disobedience
items.text_en: Opening: Biblical examples of disobedience
items.desc_en: The Gemara opens by citing instances where the Israelites disobeyed God's commands regarding the quail and the calf, and the sin of the spies in the wilderness of Paran.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan: God's protection of the tongue
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan: God's protection of the tongue
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan quotes Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra, explaining why the tongue is uniquely protected by walls of bone and flesh, as it can cause great harm through slander.

items.text: Lashon hara as heresy and cause of leprosy
items.text_en: Lashon hara as heresy and cause of leprosy
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra teach that speaking lashon hara is akin to denying God, and that it brings leprosy upon the speaker, as derived from verses and the Mishnah.

items.text: Reish Lakish: The snake and the severity of lashon hara
items.text_en: Reish Lakish: The snake and the severity of lashon hara
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish delivers multiple teachings: the metzora is a motzi shem ra, the snake's lack of benefit from its bite parallels the slanderer, and lashon hara magnifies sins to heaven. Rav Chisda and Mar Ukva add that the slanderer deserves stoning and that God cannot dwell with him.

items.text: Remedies for lashon hara: Torah study or humility
items.text_en: Remedies for lashon hara: Torah study or humility
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chama bar Chanina and Rabbi Acha bar Chanina debate the remedy for one who speaks lashon hara: Torah study for a scholar, humility for an ignoramus, though Rabbi Acha says there is no remedy for one who has already spoken it.

items.text: Lashon hara compared to three cardinal sins
items.text_en: Lashon hara compared to three cardinal sins
items.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches that lashon hara is as severe as idolatry, forbidden relations, and murder, based on the common word 'gedolah'. The Gemara questions the derivation and adds that a three-tongued slander kills three people.

items.text: The tongue's lethal power: a series of derivations
items.text_en: The tongue's lethal power: a series of derivations
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chama bar Chanina and the Gemara compare the tongue to a hand and an arrow, showing that lashon hara kills at a distance and even in heaven, and Rava concludes that the tongue can bring life or death.

items.text: Defining lashon hara: Rava and Abaye's dispute
items.text_en: Defining lashon hara: Rava and Abaye's dispute
items.desc_en: Rava defines lashon hara as saying 'there is fire in so-and-so's house,' but Abaye objects that this is merely revealing information; rather, it is saying 'where else would fire be found but in so-and-so's house?' Rabba adds that if said in the owner's presence, it is not lashon hara, but Abaye disagrees, citing chutzpah.

items.text: Rabbah bar Rav Huna on speech in the presence of three
items.text_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna on speech in the presence of three
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna states that any matter said in the presence of three people is not considered lashon hara, because the information will inevitably spread. He explains the reasoning: your friend has a friend, and that friend's friend has a friend.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna states that any matter said in the presence of three is not lashon hara, because each person has a friend and that friend has a friend.

items.text: Rav Dimi's teaching on praising someone publicly
items.text_en: Rav Dimi's teaching on praising someone publicly
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi explains a verse about blessing a friend loudly in the morning, which is actually a curse: if someone praises a host publicly, others may hear and force the host to provide hospitality again. Rav Dimi's brother, Rav Safra, teaches that one should never speak of a friend's goodness, because it can lead to harm.

sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi interprets the verse about blessing a friend loudly in the morning as a curse, because praising a host publicly leads to others forcing him to host again.

sub.text: Rav Dimi's brother Rav Safra's teaching
sub.text_en: Rav Dimi's brother Rav Safra's teaching
sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi's brother, Rav Safra, teaches that one should never speak of a friend's goodness, because it can lead to harm.

items.text: Rav Safra's illness and the teaching about not praising
items.text_en: Rav Safra's illness and the teaching about not praising
items.desc_en: Some say Rav Dimi's brother, Rav Safra, fell ill. Rav Safra claimed he fulfilled all rabbinic teachings, but was challenged about the rule not to speak of a friend's goodness. He admitted he had not heard it, but would have fulfilled it if he had.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces an alternative version of the story: Rav Dimi's brother, Rav Safra, fell ill, and Rav Safra went to visit him.
Rav Safra declares that he has fulfilled all the teachings of the rabbis.
The rabbis challenge Rav Safra, asking whether he fulfills the rule that one should never speak of a friend's goodness, as it leads to his harm.
Rav Safra admits he had not heard this teaching, but asserts that if he had heard it, he would have fulfilled it.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's list of seven sins that cause leprosy
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's list of seven sins that cause leprosy
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani quotes Rabbi Yochanan: leprosy comes for seven sins: lashon hara, bloodshed, vain oath, forbidden sexual relations, arrogance, theft, and stinginess. Each is supported by a biblical verse.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yochanan states that leprosy comes for seven sins: lashon hara, bloodshed, vain oath, forbidden sexual relations, arrogance, theft, and stinginess.
A verse from Psalms is cited to support that lashon hara causes leprosy: 'Him who slanders his neighbor in secret, I will destroy.'
A verse from II Samuel is cited to support that bloodshed causes leprosy: 'And let there not be cut off from the house of Joab one who has a discharge or is a leper.'
A verse from II Kings is cited to support that a vain oath causes leprosy: Naaman's leprosy clung to Gehazi after his false oath.

sub.text: Supporting verse for forbidden sexual relations
sub.text_en: Supporting verse for forbidden sexual relations
sub.desc_en: A verse from Genesis is cited to support that forbidden sexual relations cause leprosy: God afflicted Pharaoh with plagues because of Sarah.
A verse from II Chronicles is cited to support that arrogance causes leprosy: King Uzziah's leprosy shone on his forehead after his pride led him to trespass.
A verse from Leviticus is cited to support that theft causes leprosy, with a Tanna's explanation: one who gathers money not his own will have the priest scatter his possessions.

A verse from Leviticus is cited to support that stinginess causes leprosy, with the Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael explaining: 'one whose house is designated for him alone' (i.e., he does not share with others).

items.text: The priestly garments and their atonement
items.text_en: The priestly garments and their atonement
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: Rabbi Yochanan said leprosy comes for these sins, but Rabbi Anani bar Sason taught that the priestly garments atone for sins. Each garment atones for a specific sin: the tunic for bloodshed, the trousers for forbidden relations, the turban for arrogance, the belt for heart-thoughts, the breastplate for justice, the ephod for idolatry, the robe for lashon hara, and the forehead-plate for brazenness.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: Rabbi Yochanan said leprosy comes for these sins, but Rabbi Anani bar Sason taught that the priestly garments atone for sins.
The tunic atones for bloodshed and the trousers atone for forbidden relations, as derived from verses.
The turban atones for arrogance and the belt atones for heart-thoughts, as per Rabbi Chanina's principle and the verse.
The breastplate atones for justice, the ephod for idolatry, and the robe for lashon hara (evil speech), as derived from verses.
The forehead-plate atones for brazenness, as derived from the verse about the forehead.

items.text: Resolution: leprosy vs. atonement based on deeds
items.text_en: Resolution: leprosy vs. atonement based on deeds
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction: if one's deeds are effective (i.e., they are righteous), leprosy comes as punishment; if not, the priestly garments atone.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction between leprosy and priestly garments by distinguishing: if one's deeds are effective (righteous), leprosy comes as punishment; if not, the priestly garments atone.

items.text: Rabbi Simon's teaching on atonement for bloodshed and lashon hara
items.text_en: Rabbi Simon's teaching on atonement for bloodshed and lashon hara
items.desc_en: Rabbi Simon quoting Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says that two sins have no atonement through sacrifices but have atonement through other means: bloodshed through the heifer whose neck is broken, and lashon hara through the incense. The incense atones for lashon hara because it is offered in secret, corresponding to the secretive nature of lashon hara.

sub.text: Rabbi Simon quoting Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Simon quoting Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Simon in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi states that two sins—bloodshed and lashon hara—have no atonement through sacrifices but have atonement through other means, with bloodshed atoned by the heifer whose neck is broken.

sub.text: Supporting baraita and Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita and Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.desc_en: The gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Chanina learns that incense atones, and the Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael specifies that incense atones for lashon hara because it is offered in secret, corresponding to the secretive nature of lashon hara.

items.text: Resolution of contradictions regarding bloodshed and lashon hara
items.text_en: Resolution of contradictions regarding bloodshed and lashon hara
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: bloodshed and lashon hara appear in both lists (sins causing leprosy and sins atoned by garments/incense). It resolves: for bloodshed, if the murderer is known, he is liable to death (so no atonement needed), but if unknown, the heifer atones. For lashon hara, if done in private, the incense atones; if done in public, leprosy comes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: bloodshed appears in both lists (sins causing leprosy and sins atoned by garments/incense), and lashon hara also appears in both lists.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction for bloodshed: if the murderer is known (but no warning was given, so no death penalty), leprosy comes; if unknown, the heifer atones.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction for lashon hara: if done in private, the incense atones; if done in public, leprosy comes.

items.text: Conclusion of previous discussion: public vs. private
items.text_en: Conclusion of previous discussion: public vs. private
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the previous statement applies specifically to public rebuke.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the previous discussion applies specifically to public rebuke (בפרהסיא).

items.text: Why the leper is isolated and brings bird offerings
items.text_en: Why the leper is isolated and brings bird offerings
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nadav asks Rabbi Chanina why the Torah commands the leper to dwell alone. The answer is that the leper separated husband from wife and friend from friend. Rabbi Yehuda ben Levi asks why the leper brings two birds; the Holy One says he acted like a chatterer, so he brings a chirping offering.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nadav asks Rabbi Chanina why the Torah commands the leper to dwell alone outside the camp.
Rabbi Chanina answers that the leper separated husband from wife and friend from friend, so the Torah decrees he dwell alone.
Rabbi Yehuda ben Levi asks why the leper brings two birds for his purification.
The Holy One says the leper acted like a chatterer, so he brings a chirping offering.

items.text: The prohibition of hatred in the heart and the mitzvah of rebuke
items.text_en: The prohibition of hatred in the heart and the mitzvah of rebuke
items.desc_en: The Sages teach that the verse 'You shall not hate your brother in your heart' refers only to hatred in the heart, not to physical harm. From the verse 'rebuke, you shall rebuke' we learn that one must rebuke a friend for a bad deed, and if not accepted, rebuke again, but not to the point of shaming him.

sub.desc_en: The Sages teach that the verse 'You shall not hate your brother in your heart' refers only to hatred in the heart, not to physical harm, and that one must rebuke a friend for a bad deed, but not to the point of shaming him.

items.text: The difficulty of giving and receiving rebuke
items.text_en: The difficulty of giving and receiving rebuke
items.desc_en: Rabbi Tarfon doubts there is anyone in his generation who can accept rebuke, citing the hypocrisy of pointing out a speck while having a beam. Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya doubts there is anyone who knows how to rebuke properly. Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri testifies that he rebuked Rabbi Akiva many times, yet only increased his love for him, fulfilling the verse that rebuking a wise man leads to love.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Tarfon expresses doubt that anyone in his generation can accept rebuke, citing the hypocritical response of pointing out a beam in the rebuker's eye.
Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya expresses doubt that anyone in his generation knows how to rebuke properly.
Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri testifies that he rebuked Rabbi Akiva many times, yet it only increased his love, fulfilling the verse that rebuking a wise man leads to love.

items.text: Rebuke for its own sake vs. humility not for its own sake
items.text_en: Rebuke for its own sake vs. humility not for its own sake
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda the son of Rabbi Shimon asks which is greater: rebuke for its own sake or humility not for its own sake. The answer is that humility not for its own sake is greater because it leads to humility for its own sake. An example is given of Rav Huna and Chiyya bar Rav sitting before Shmuel, where Chiyya complained privately rather than rebuking Shmuel publicly to avoid shaming him.

items.text: The limits of rebuke: striking, cursing, or rebuking
items.text_en: The limits of rebuke: striking, cursing, or rebuking
items.desc_en: Rav, Shmuel, and Rabbi Yochanan debate the extent of rebuke: Rav says until striking, Shmuel until cursing, Rabbi Yochanan until rebuking. This is supported by a Tannaitic dispute. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that all three derive their positions from the story of Saul and Jonathan, with each focusing on a different aspect of the verse. The Gemara reconciles why the one who says rebuking does not require striking or cursing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: To what extent does the obligation of rebuke (תוכחה) extend?
Rav (רב) says rebuke extends until striking.
Shmuel (שמואל) says rebuke extends until cursing.
Rabbi Yochanan (רבי יוחנן) says rebuke extends until rebuking (נזיפה).
A Tannaitic dispute (תנאי) parallels the three positions: Rabbi Eliezer (רבי אליעזר) says until striking, Rabbi Yehoshua (רבי יהושע) says until cursing, and Ben Azzai (בן עזאי) says until rebuking.

items.text: How much a guest may change his host's arrangements
items.text_en: How much a guest may change his host's arrangements
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel debate how far a guest may deviate from his host's practices: Rav says until striking, Shmuel until his utensils are turned backwards. The Gemara clarifies that all agree on striking the guest himself or turning his utensils, but they disagree about striking the host's wife. The reason is that a guest damages and is damaged. Rav Yehuda cites a verse that one should not change his lodging, and Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina cites another verse; the difference is a chance guest.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: To what extent may a guest not change his host's arrangements?
Rav says: until striking (the guest himself).
Shmuel says: until his utensils are turned backwards.
The Gemara clarifies: All agree on striking the guest himself.
All also agree on turning his utensils backwards.
They disagree about striking the host's wife.
Rav reasons: Since the guest is not pained by the host's wife, what does he care?
Shmuel reasons: He may come to be driven away (from the host's house).
The Gemara explains: A guest damages and is damaged (by the host).
Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav cites a verse: 'To the place where his tent was at first' — one should not change his lodging.
Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina cites another verse: 'And he went on his journeys.'
The difference between them is a chance guest (who happens by).

items.text: One should not change his profession or his father's profession
items.text_en: One should not change his profession or his father's profession
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan derives from the verse about Hiram that one should not change his profession or his father's profession, as Hiram's mother was from Dan and his father was a coppersmith, and the verse associates him with Oholiav from the tribe of Dan.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan opens by asking from where one learns that a person should not change his profession or his father's profession.
He answers by citing the verse about Hiram, whose mother was from the tribe of Naphtali and whose father was a coppersmith from Tyre.
Mar adds that Hiram's mother was from the tribe of Dan, and the verse associates him with Oholiav from the tribe of Dan.

items.text: The threshold of suffering
items.text_en: The threshold of suffering
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar defines the ultimate suffering as when a garment is woven for him but does not fit. Rava Ze'ira objects, citing a greater suffering: even if they intended to mix hot water but gave cold, or vice versa. Mar the son of Ravina adds even if his shirt is turned. Rava adds even if he reached for three coins but got two. The Gemara specifies that two coins becoming three is not suffering. The reason is that one who goes forty days without suffering has received his world.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: What is the ultimate threshold of suffering?
Rabbi Elazar answers: Any garment woven for him that does not fit.
Rava Ze'ira objects, citing a greater suffering: even if they intended hot water but gave cold, or vice versa.
Mar the son of Ravina adds: even if his shirt is turned.
Rava adds: even if he reached for three coins but got two.
The Gemara specifies: only three becoming two is suffering, but two becoming three is not, because there is no trouble to throw them away.

sub.text: Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.text_en: Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains: because the school of Rabbi Yishmael taught that one who goes forty days without suffering has received his world.

items.text: Opening statement on punishment
items.text_en: Opening statement on punishment
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that punishment is prepared for the wicked.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a general statement that punishment is prepared for the wicked.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's teaching on the patriarchs
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's teaching on the patriarchs
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer HaGadol teaches that even the patriarchs could not withstand God's rebuke, citing a verse.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer HaGadol teaches that even the patriarchs could not withstand God's rebuke, citing a verse from Samuel.

items.text: Dispute about the relationship between generation and leader
items.text_en: Dispute about the relationship between generation and leader
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda Nesi'ah and the Rabbis argue whether the generation determines the leader or vice versa. The Gemara questions the practical difference, citing the examples of Jehoiakim and Zedekiah to show that the leader and generation can be mismatched.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute between Rabbi Yehuda Nesi'ah and the Rabbis over whether the generation determines the leader or the leader determines the generation, citing the verse from Psalms.
The Gemara questions the practical difference between the two positions, noting that examples of Jehoiakim and Zedekiah show that leader and generation can be mismatched.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan cites Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai's explanation that God considered destroying the world for Jehoiakim but was appeased by his generation, and for Zedekiah's generation but was appeased by Zedekiah himself, demonstrating the mismatch.

items.text: Resolution of the dispute
items.text_en: Resolution of the dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the dispute is about the strength or weakness of the generation relative to the leader.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda Nesia and the Rabbis concerns the relative strength or weakness (תוקפא וניחותא) of the generation and its leader, not their merit.

items.text: Conclusion of the previous chapter
items.text_en: Conclusion of the previous chapter
items.desc_en: The standard formula marking the end of a chapter: 'We have returned to you, Yesh BaArakhin.'

sub.desc_en: The standard formula marking the end of the previous chapter: 'We have returned to you, Yesh BaArakhin.'

items.text: Mishnah: Principles of valuation
items.text_en: Mishnah: Principles of valuation
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the assessment of a vow depends on the vow-maker's financial ability, the age of the person being valued, the value of the person, and the time of valuation. It gives examples: a poor person who vows the value of a rich person pays the poor person's rate, and vice versa. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi adds that in the case of a rich person who vows his own value and a poor person accepts it, the poor person pays the rich rate.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating the general principles of valuation: affordability depends on the vow-maker, years on the subject, sex on the valuated, and the value at the time of the vow.
The Mishnah elaborates on affordability: a poor person who vows the value of a rich person pays the poor rate, and a rich person who vows the value of a poor person pays the rich rate.
The Mishnah contrasts offerings: if one vows to bring the offering of a specific leper, the offering depends on the leper's financial status, not the vow-maker's.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi argues that even in valuations, a poor person who accepts a rich person's vow to donate his own value must pay the rich rate, similar to the offering case.

items.text: Gemara: Clarifications and challenges on the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarifications and challenges on the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's phrasing, noting that 'the ability of the hand' should refer to the one making the vow, not the one being valued. It then discusses the scriptural basis for the poor person paying the poor rate, and challenges the Mishnah's statement about offerings, citing a verse that limits the poor offering to the poor person himself. Rabbi Yitzchak and Rav Adda bar Ahava offer interpretations, and the Gemara questions the case where the donor is rich.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's phrasing: the phrase 'the ability of the hand should refer to the one making the valuation, not the one being valued.
The Gemara answers: the Mishnah uses the term 'vow' for both affordability and years, so it says 'the years in the subject of the vow'.

The Gemara asks: what is the reason for the Mishnah's ruling that a poor person who valuated a wealthy person gives the poor rate? It answers: the verse 'according to the means of him who vowed' makes it dependent on the one who vows.

The Gemara challenges the Mishnah's statement about offerings: a poor person who vows to provide the offering of a leper brings the poor offering even if the donor is rich, but the verse limits the poor offering to the poor person himself.
Rabbi Yitzchak (Rabbi Yitzchak) answers: the case is where the donor is poor, but perhaps the mercy is on the leper, not the donor, as it is written 'he'.
Rav Adda bar Ahava (Rav Adda bar Ahava) says: the verse 'and his means do not suffice' includes the one who vows.
The Gemara questions: if the donor is rich, does he bring the offering in wealth?
The Gemara asks: if so, what is the meaning of 'but in the offerings is not so'?

items.text: Exclusion of a poor metzora whose vow-maker is poor
items.text_en: Exclusion of a poor metzora whose vow-maker is poor
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that one verse excludes a poor metzora whose vow-maker is poor, and another excludes a poor metzora whose vow-maker is rich. It was necessary to teach both, lest one think that since one case is included, the other is also included.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that one verse excludes a poor metzora whose vow-maker is poor, and another excludes a poor metzora whose vow-maker is rich, and both were necessary.

items.text: Derivation from valuations: poor person valuing a rich person
items.text_en: Derivation from valuations: poor person valuing a rich person
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that in the case of valuations, a poor person who vows the value of a rich person pays the poor person's valuation. One might think the same applies here, but the verse 'אם דל הוא' teaches otherwise.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara derives from valuations that a poor person who vows the value of a rich person pays the poor person's valuation, but the verse 'אם דל הוא' teaches that in the case of a metzora, the poor person pays according to the rich person's means.

items.text: Rabbi's opinion and the exclusion of a poor metzora whose vow-maker is rich
items.text_en: Rabbi's opinion and the exclusion of a poor metzora whose vow-maker is rich
items.desc_en: According to Rabbi, who holds that in valuations we follow the obligation of the person, the verse is not needed for the previous exclusion. Instead, it excludes a poor metzora whose vow-maker is rich, lest one think that since Rabbi says we follow the person's obligation, the metzora would be considered poor.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: According to Rabbi, who holds that in valuations we follow the person's obligation, the verse is not needed for the previous exclusion — what does it exclude?
The Gemara answers: It excludes a poor metzora whose vow-maker is rich, lest one think that since Rabbi says we follow the person's obligation, the metzora would be considered poor.

items.text: Mishnah: Changes in wealth and their effect on valuations and offerings
items.text_en: Mishnah: Changes in wealth and their effect on valuations and offerings
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a person was poor and became rich, or rich and became poor, he pays the valuation of a rich person. Rabbi Yehuda adds that even if he was poor, became rich, and then became poor again, he pays the valuation of a rich person. However, for offerings, this is not the case; even if his father died and left him a fortune, or his ship came in, the Temple has no claim.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that a person who was poor and became rich, or rich and became poor, pays the valuation of a rich person.
Rabbi Yehuda adds that even if a person was poor, became rich, and then became poor again, he pays the valuation of a rich person.
The Mishnah concludes that for offerings, even if a poor person inherits wealth or his ship arrives with treasure, the Temple has no claim on that wealth.

items.text: Gemara: Scriptural sources for the Mishnah's rulings
items.text_en: Gemara: Scriptural sources for the Mishnah's rulings
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the scriptural basis: for a poor person who became rich, the verse is 'אשר תשיג יד הנודר'; for a rich person who became poor, the verse is 'על פי אשר תשיג'. Rabbi Yehuda derives his ruling from the verse 'ואם מך הוא מערכך', which implies that he must be in his poverty from beginning to end.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the scriptural sources for the Mishnah's rulings: for a poor person who became rich, the verse is 'אֲשֶׁר תַּשִּׂיג יַד הַנֹּדֵר'; for a rich person who became poor, the verse is 'עַל פִּי אֲשֶׁר תַּשִּׂיג'.
Rabbi Yehuda derives his ruling from the verse 'וְאִם מָךְ הוּא מֵעֶרְכֶּךָ', which implies that he must be in his poverty (מָךְ) from beginning to end.

items.text: Challenge and resolution regarding the word 'הוא' in the context of a metzora
items.text_en: Challenge and resolution regarding the word 'הוא' in the context of a metzora
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yehuda's logic by comparing to the verse 'דל הוא', which would similarly require poverty from beginning to end. However, a baraita shows that for a metzora's offerings, the ruling follows the sin-offering (Rabbi Shimon), the guilt-offering (Rabbi Yehuda), or the birds (Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov), all derived from the same verse. The word 'הוא' is then explained according to Rabbi and the Rabbis for their respective exclusions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yehuda's logic by asking whether the verse 'דל הוא' (he is poor) would similarly require poverty from beginning to end.

The Gemara objects by citing a baraita where Rabbi Shimon, Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov disagree about which offering determines the metzora's status, showing that the word 'הוא' does not impose a fixed poverty requirement.

Rav Yehuda citing Rav resolves that all three Tannaim derive their positions from the same verse 'אשר לא תשיג ידו בטהרתו', each focusing on a different aspect: Rabbi Shimon on the atoning element (sin-offering), Rabbi Yehuda on the enabling element (guilt-offering), and Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov on the factor that brings purity (birds).
The Gemara concludes that the word 'הוא' in the metzora context serves Rabbi and the Rabbis for their respective exclusions as previously established.

items.text: Challenge from the word 'והוא' in the context of witnesses
items.text_en: Challenge from the word 'והוא' in the context of witnesses
items.desc_en: The Gemara further challenges by considering the word 'והוא' in the context of witnesses, which would imply that the witness must be valid from beginning to end. However, a baraita shows that if a witness knew testimony before becoming a relative, deaf, blind, or insane, he is disqualified, indicating that the word is not interpreted that way.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: if the word 'הוּא' in the context of the poor person implies a continuous state, then the word 'הוּא' in the verse about witnesses (וְהוּא עַד) should also require the witness to be valid from beginning to end.

The Gemara objects: if you say that is indeed the case, a baraita shows that a witness who knew testimony before becoming a relative, deaf, blind, or insane is disqualified, proving that the word 'הוּא' is not interpreted to require continuous validity.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Cases of changing status
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Cases of changing status
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists cases where a person's condition changes (e.g., from healthy to deaf and back) and rules that if the beginning and end are valid, the person is valid for testimony. This sets up the discussion.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the verse and the principle of 'והוא עד'
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the verse and the principle of 'והוא עד'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the verse 'or he saw... if he does not tell' depends on seeing and telling, and the word 'והוא' (and he) is used to teach that the witness must be specifically designated. A baraita illustrates that if one says 'I adjure all of you' without specifying, they are not liable, but if he says 'everyone who knows', they are liable.

items.text: Discussion of a rich heir and a dying father
items.text_en: Discussion of a rich heir and a dying father
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a case where a father dies and leaves a large sum (ריבוא) to his son, making the son rich. Rabbi Abahu clarifies that the father 'leaves' the money, and the Gemara explains that this refers to when the father was dying, as most dying people die.

items.text: Case of a ship at sea and Rabbi Eliezer's opinion
items.text_en: Case of a ship at sea and Rabbi Eliezer's opinion
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a case where a ship at sea brings wealth, and Rav Chisda explains it refers to a ship that is rented out. The Gemara questions why the rental income is not considered, and answers that rental is only paid at the end. It then identifies the Mishnah as following Rabbi Eliezer, who says a farmer is given his team and a donkey driver his donkey.

items.text: Mishnah: Principles of valuations based on the subject's age and gender
items.text_en: Mishnah: Principles of valuations based on the subject's age and gender
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that the years are determined by the one who vows (e.g., a child vowing for an elder pays the elder's rate), and the valuations are determined by the subject (e.g., a man vowing for a woman pays the woman's rate). It also rules that the valuation is based on the time of the vow, even if the subject's age changes later.

items.text: Gemara: Comparing valuations to monetary payments
items.text_en: Gemara: Comparing valuations to monetary payments
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that compares valuations to monetary payments, but concludes that valuations are not paid at the time of payment but at the time of the vow, based on the verse 'as your valuation so it shall stand'.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara: Age thresholds and the principle of 'year' for leniency and stringency
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara: Age thresholds and the principle of 'year' for leniency and stringency
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the 30th day is considered below, and the 5th and 20th years are considered below, based on a gezerah shavah from the year of sixty. Rabbi Eliezer adds that extra days beyond the years require a month and a day. The Gemara explains that the gezerah shavah is available because the word 'year' is superfluous.

items.text: Gemara: The superfluous 'year' and disagreement with Rabbi
items.text_en: Gemara: The superfluous 'year' and disagreement with Rabbi
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the gezerah shavah is based on a superfluous 'year', and suggests that the Mishnah does not follow Rabbi, who holds that 'until' includes the endpoint. A baraita is cited where Rabbi interprets 'from the first day until the seventh day' to include both endpoints.

items.text: Opening dispute on the inclusion of head and feet in the plague of leprosy
items.text_en: Opening dispute on the inclusion of head and feet in the plague of leprosy
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the phrase 'from his head to his feet' excludes the head and feet themselves. Rabbi offers a different derivation using the terms 'first' and 'seventh'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the phrase 'from his head to his feet' excludes the head and feet themselves from the plague of leprosy.
The Gemara answers with a verse, and Rabbi offers an alternative derivation using the terms 'first' and 'seventh' to include the head and feet.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of Rabbi's position
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of Rabbi's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that even according to Rabbi, the verses are balanced: the phrase 'from a month old to five years' and 'from five to twenty years' are both needed to establish the age categories.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that even according to Rabbi, the verses are balanced against each other, and the extra verse is needed to resolve the ambiguity.

items.text: Source for excluding head and feet
items.text_en: Source for excluding head and feet
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that 'head' excludes the head itself and 'feet' excludes the feet. Two answers are given: one based on the difference between signs on the body and signs on the head, and another based on the verse 'to all the sight of the priest's eyes'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the rule that 'his head' excludes the head itself.
The Gemara provides two alternative derivations: either the signs of the body differ from those of the head, or the verse 'to all that appears to the priest' teaches the exclusion.

Another answer: the verse 'to all the sight of the priest's eyes' (ויקרא יג:יב) teaches that only what is visible to the priest is considered, excluding the head and feet which are not typically seen together.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's opinion on the age of a one-year-old
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's opinion on the age of a one-year-old
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer argues that a child must be a month and a day older than the year to be considered a year old, using a gezerah shavah from the term 'above' in the context of a month. The Gemara objects that this would imply only one day, but the gezerah shavah would then be superfluous.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer states that a child must be a month and a day older than the years to be considered a year old, and a supporting baraita (תניא) cites his use of a גזירה שוה (verbal analogy) from the word 'למעלה' (above) in the context of a month.
The Gemara objects that if the גזירה שוה (verbal analogy) were applied strictly, it would require only one extra day, rendering the analogy superfluous.

items.text: Baraita on the definition of 'year' in various contexts
items.text_en: Baraita on the definition of 'year' in various contexts
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the 'year' mentioned in sacrifices, houses in walled cities, the two years of a sold field, the six years of a Hebrew slave, and the years for a son and daughter are all calculated from time to time (i.e., a full 365-day period). The Gemara provides scriptural derivations for each.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by listing six contexts where 'year' is calculated from time to time (a full 365-day period).
Rav Acha bar Yaakov derives that the year for sacrifices is from time to time from the verse 'כֶּבֶשׂ בֶּן שְׁנָתוֹ' (a lamb in its year), emphasizing 'שְׁנָתוֹ' (its own year) not a calendar year.

The Gemara derives that the year for houses in walled cities is from time to time from the verse 'עַד תֹּם שְׁנַת מִמְכָּרוֹ' (until the completion of the year of its sale), emphasizing 'מִמְכָּרוֹ' (its sale) not a calendar year.

The Gemara derives that the two years for a sold ancestral field are from time to time from the verse 'בְּמִסְפַּר שְׁנֵי תְבוּאֹת' (by the number of crop years), implying that one may eat three crops in two full years.

The Gemara derives that the six years for a Hebrew slave are from time to time from the verse 'שֵׁשׁ שָׁנִים יַעֲבֹד וּבַשְּׁבִיעִית' (six years he shall serve, and in the seventh), implying that even a partial seventh year counts as a full year.

items.text: Dispute between Rav Giddel and Rav Yosef on the application of 'from time to time'
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav Giddel and Rav Yosef on the application of 'from time to time'
items.desc_en: Rav Giddel says the rule applies to valuations (arakhin), while Rav Yosef says it applies to the laws of a child born by caesarean section (yotze dofen). Abaye asks if they disagree, and Rav Yosef clarifies they do not; each stated a different application. The Gemara supports this with Rav's ruling that the entire chapter follows 'from time to time'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the practical application of the rule that a year for a son or daughter is calculated from time to time (מעת לעת).
Rav Giddel says in the name of Rav that the rule applies to valuations (ערכין).
Rav Yosef says the rule applies to the chapters of a child born by caesarean section (יוצא דופן).
Abaye asks Rav Yosef whether he and Rav Giddel disagree with each other.
Rav Yosef replies that they do not disagree; each stated a different application.
The Gemara supports Rav Yosef's claim by arguing that if they disagreed, the one who said 'for valuations' would not also accept 'for yotze dofen'.
The Gemara cites Rav's ruling that the entire chapter follows the principle of 'from time to time' (מעת לעת), implying both applications are valid.
The Gemara asks why Rav Giddel, who said 'for valuations', did not also mention 'yotze dofen'.
The Gemara answers that Rav Giddel only mentioned valuations because they are analogous to the other cases in the baraita, which are all explicitly written in the Torah.
The Gemara objects that if the rule for 'yotze dofen' were also explicitly written, then the baraita's phrase 'that of a son and that of a daughter' would be redundant.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's phrase 'that which is in a male and that which is in a female'
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's phrase 'that which is in a male and that which is in a female'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah distinguishes between male and female valuations, noting that a female's value declines with age while a male's does not. Ḥizkiyya answers with a folk saying about an old man versus an old woman in the house.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah distinguishes between male and female valuations, noting that a female's value declines with age while a male's does not.
Ḥizkiyya answers with a folk saying: an old man in the house is a burden, but an old woman in the house is a treasure, explaining why a female's value declines less.

items.text: Conclusion of the previous chapter
items.text_en: Conclusion of the previous chapter
items.desc_en: The Gemara marks the end of the previous chapter with the phrase 'We have returned to you, the chapter of Hasagat Yad'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara marks the end of the previous chapter with the phrase 'We have returned to you, the chapter of Hasagat Yad'.

items.text: Mishnah: Vows of weight and hand-weight
items.text_en: Mishnah: Vows of weight and hand-weight
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that one who says 'my weight is upon me' gives his weight in the specified metal, and relates a story of a woman from Yarmatya who vowed her daughter's weight in gold. For 'the weight of my hand upon me', Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei dispute the method of estimation.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the rule that one who says 'my weight is upon me' gives his weight in the specified metal, and illustrates with a story of a woman from Yarmatya who vowed her daughter's weight in gold.
Rabbi Yehuda states that for 'the weight of my hand upon me', one fills a barrel with water up to the elbow and adds donkey meat, bones, and sinews until the barrel is full.
Rabbi Yosei objects that it is impossible to precisely match meat to meat and bones to bones, and instead proposes evaluating how much the hand is fit to weigh.

items.text: Gemara: Clarifying the Mishnah's rule on unspecified metal
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarifying the Mishnah's rule on unspecified metal
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda explains that if one specified a metal, he gives that metal; otherwise he may discharge his vow with any item. Rav Ḥaba and Rav Pappa add that in places where certain items are used as weights, one may fulfill the vow with those items, even if they are not standard currency.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the mishna's phrase 'if silver, silver, and if gold, gold' means.
Rav Yehuda explains that if one specified silver or gold, he gives that metal; otherwise he may exempt himself with any material.
Rav Ḥaba cites a statement that in a place where pitch is weighed, one may fulfill the vow even with pitch, and clarifies that this applies even if some measure by volume.
Rav Pappa adds that in a place where onions are weighed, one may fulfill the vow even with onions, despite the custom of adding extra onions after weighing.

items.text: Gemara: Resolving the apparent contradiction in the Mishnah's story
items.text_en: Gemara: Resolving the apparent contradiction in the Mishnah's story
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah cites a story that seems to contradict its own rule. It resolves that the Mishnah is incomplete and should read: if the person is distinguished, even without specification, we assess according to his honor; the story illustrates this.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah cites a story that seems to contradict its own rule.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah is incomplete and should read: if the person is distinguished, even without specification, we assess according to his honor; the story illustrates this.

items.text: Gemara: Dispute on the interpretation of 'my height' vs. 'full my height'
items.text_en: Gemara: Dispute on the interpretation of 'my height' vs. 'full my height'
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda distinguishes between 'my height' (a non-bending rod) and 'full my height' (a bending rod). A baraitha contradicts this, stating both require a non-bending rod. The Gemara explains that Rav Yehuda follows Rabbi Akiva's principle of interpreting extra language, as demonstrated in a Mishnah about selling a cistern.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda distinguishes between 'קומתי עלי' (my height upon me) requiring a non-bending rod and 'מלא קומתי עלי' (full my height upon me) requiring a bending rod.
The Gemara raises an objection from a baraitha that states both 'קומתי עלי' and 'מלא קומתי עלי' require a non-bending rod, contradicting Rav Yehuda's distinction.
The Gemara answers that Rav Yehuda follows Rabbi Akiva's principle of interpreting extra language, citing a Mishnah where Rabbi Akiva requires a path because of extra language.
The Gemara explains that since the extra language is unnecessary, it comes to add (לטפויי מילתא קאתי), and similarly Rav Yehuda's distinction adds a requirement.

items.text: Gemara: Inquiry about the term 'my standing'
items.text_en: Gemara: Inquiry about the term 'my standing'
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an unresolved question: what is the halakha if one says 'my standing' (עוֹמְדֵי) upon me?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an unresolved question about the halakha if one says 'my standing' (עוֹמְדֵי) upon me.

items.text: Unresolved questions about dimensions
items.text_en: Unresolved questions about dimensions
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises unresolved questions (teiku) about the meaning of terms like 'rochbo' (its width), 'yeshivato' (its seating), 'ovyo' (its thickness), and 'hikkifu' (its circumference) in the context of valuations.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei on measuring hand and foot
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei on measuring hand and foot
items.desc_en: A baraita presents a dispute: Rabbi Yehuda says one fills a barrel with water up to the elbow (for hand) or knee (for foot), then adds donkey meat, sinews, and bones until full, citing a verse. Rabbi Yosei objects that exact matching is impossible; Rabbi Yehuda responds that we estimate, and Rabbi Yosei retorts that if we estimate, we could just measure the limb directly.

items.text: Contradiction regarding the definition of 'hand' in different contexts
items.text_en: Contradiction regarding the definition of 'hand' in different contexts
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: for hand, the baraita says up to the elbow, but for sanctification of hands and feet in the Temple, it is up to the wrist (perek). The Gemara resolves that Torah law defines 'hand' as up to the wrist, but for vows we follow common language. It then questions this, citing tefillin where 'yadecha' means the upper arm (kiborit), and explains that Torah law for tefillin is the entire upper arm, while for sanctification it is a halakha l'Moshe miSinai.

items.text: Contradiction regarding the definition of 'foot' and resolution via halitza
items.text_en: Contradiction regarding the definition of 'foot' and resolution via halitza
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: for foot, the baraita says up to the knee, but a verse about 'raglayim' excludes those with swollen feet (ba'alei kavin). The Gemara resolves that for vows we follow common language, but Torah law excludes ba'alei kavin. It then questions this with halitza, where 'raglo' includes up to the knee. The resolution is that the verse 'me'al raglov' implies above the foot but not above the knee.

items.text: Rav Papa and Rav Ashi on the anatomy of the leg
items.text_en: Rav Papa and Rav Ashi on the anatomy of the leg
items.desc_en: Rav Papa deduces that the isteveria (shin bone) goes down to the ground, because if it were severed, the term 'me'al' would apply to the severed part. Rav Ashi argues that even if severed, the part attached to the leg is considered part of the leg.

items.text: Mishnah: Appraising the value of a hand
items.text_en: Mishnah: Appraising the value of a hand
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that for a vow of 'dmei yadai alai', we appraise the person's value with the hand and without the hand, noting this is a stringency of vows over valuations.

items.text: Gemara: How to appraise the hand
items.text_en: Gemara: How to appraise the hand
items.desc_en: Rava says we appraise like for damages (omeid shel nizakin). Abaye objects that the contexts differ (a worthless person vs. a worthy one). Abaye then proposes appraising how much a person would pay for a slave who works with one hand vs. two hands, clarifying that the other hand is not severed but disabled (muktevet).

items.text: Rava's dilemmas about repeated appraisals
items.text_en: Rava's dilemmas about repeated appraisals
items.desc_en: Rava raises three dilemmas: (1) If appraised by a court of three (for damages) and then says 'dmei alai', is that appraisal valid? (2) If appraised by ten and then says 'dmei alai' again, is a new appraisal needed due to potential appreciation? (3) If he says 'dmei alai' without appraisal and then repeats it, what is the law? The text breaks off mid-dilemma.

items.text: Unresolved questions about assessment for sequential and simultaneous vows
items.text_en: Unresolved questions about assessment for sequential and simultaneous vows
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises three unresolved questions (תיקו) about how to assess a person's value when he vows sequentially ('this after that') versus simultaneously ('two valuations upon me in one utterance'), and whether an assessment made without the person's knowledge (מאליו) is valid.

items.text: Proof from the Mishnah regarding assessment of the dead
items.text_en: Proof from the Mishnah regarding assessment of the dead
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to resolve one of the questions from a Mishnah: if one says 'my value upon me' and dies, heirs do not pay, because the dead have no value. If assessment without knowledge were valid, every dead person would be worth at least four zuz. The Gemara distinguishes: assessment without knowledge is valid for valuations, but not for 'my value' vows.

items.text: Mishnah: Stringencies of valuations over vows
items.text_en: Mishnah: Stringencies of valuations over vows
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that valuations (ערכין) are more stringent than vows (נדרים) in that if one says 'my valuation upon me' and dies, heirs pay, whereas for 'my value upon me' they do not. It also discusses cases of limbs: a limb that is not vital (e.g., hand) yields nothing, but a vital organ (e.g., head) requires full valuation. Partial vows are also addressed.

items.text: Gemara: Analysis of the Mishnah's first clause and the status of loans
items.text_en: Gemara: Analysis of the Mishnah's first clause and the status of loans
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Tosefta that also notes stringencies of vows over valuations. It then questions whether the Mishnah's ruling that heirs pay for a valuation implies that an oral loan is collectible from heirs, and answers that this is a loan written in the Torah. It further clarifies that the case is when the debtor stood in court, and explains why 'my value' is not paid: it requires assessment, whereas valuation does not.

items.text: Rav Giddel's ruling on 'valuation of my hand'
items.text_en: Rav Giddel's ruling on 'valuation of my hand'
items.desc_en: Rav Giddel says in the name of Rav that one who says 'valuation of my hand upon me' pays its value (דמיה). The Gemara reconciles this with the Mishnah which says 'he said nothing' – that is for the Rabbis, but Rav follows Rabbi Meir. It then explains why a new statement is needed: to counter the assumption that here the person mistakenly thought 'hand' has a valuation, unlike a vessel.

items.text: Reason for full valuation on vital organs and the general rule
items.text_en: Reason for full valuation on vital organs and the general rule
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why one who says 'valuation of my head' pays full valuation: the Torah says 'valuations of souls' (נפשות), and the head is where the soul resides. The general rule 'a thing on which life depends' includes from the knee upward.

items.text: Dispute on 'half my valuation' and the rule for partial vows
items.text_en: Dispute on 'half my valuation' and the rule for partial vows
items.desc_en: A Tosefta records a dispute: for 'half my valuation upon me', the Sages say he gives half, but Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda says he is flogged and gives full valuation. Rav Pappa explains the flogging is a decree lest one confuse 'half his valuation' with 'valuation of his half', which is a vital matter. For 'half my value' and 'value of my half', the Gemara explains the latter gives full value because the verse says 'a vow by your valuation of souls'.

items.text: Dispute on half-valuation of a vessel and the case of 'valuation of so-and-so'
items.text_en: Dispute on half-valuation of a vessel and the case of 'valuation of so-and-so'
items.desc_en: A Tosefta records a dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages about one who vows half the valuation of a vessel. Rava and Abaye explain that the Sages here follow both Rabbi Meir (no vain utterance) and Rabbi Shimon (one does not donate in an unusual manner – half is unusual). The Gemara then clarifies the Mishnah's case of 'valuation of so-and-so upon me' – it refers to one who stood in court, and the latter clause about 'value of so-and-so' is necessary to teach that if the vower dies, heirs pay.

items.text: Gemara's explanation of the Mishnah's first clause
items.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the Mishnah's first clause
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that even though the animal was not appraised, once the owner stood in court his property becomes liable, and the appraisal is merely a clarification.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves a potential misunderstanding: even though the animal was not appraised, once the owner stood in court his property becomes liable, and the appraisal is merely a clarification (גלויי מילתא בעלמא).

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah distinguishes between saying "this ox is for a burnt-offering" (if it dies, one is exempt) and "this ox is upon me for a burnt-offering" (if it dies, one is liable).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents two cases: saying 'this ox is for a burnt-offering' exempts one if the ox dies, while saying 'this ox is upon me for a burnt-offering' makes one liable to pay.

items.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Rav's distinction
items.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Rav's distinction
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Rav limits the Mishnah's liability case to when one says "the value of this ox is upon me for a burnt-offering"; if one says "this ox is upon me for a burnt-offering," since he specified "this" and it died, he is not liable, as he meant "upon me to bring it."

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Rav limits the Mishnah's liability case to when one says "the value of this ox is upon me for a burnt-offering"; if one says "this ox is upon me for a burnt-offering," since he specified "this" and it died, he is not liable, as he meant "upon me to bring it."

items.text: Objection from a baraita
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that seems to contradict Rabbi Chiyya bar Rav, and the Gemara answers that the baraita also refers to a case where one said "the value of."

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that states that if one says 'this ox is an elevation-offering' and it dies, he is not liable, but if he says 'this ox is upon me as an elevation-offering' and it dies, he is liable, seemingly contradicting Rabbi Chiyya bar Rav's distinction.
The Gemara answers that the baraita, like the mishnah, also refers to a case where the speaker said 'the value of' (דמי), so it does not contradict Rabbi Chiyya bar Rav.

items.text: Refining the distinction between the baraita's clauses
items.text_en: Refining the distinction between the baraita's clauses
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the baraita's latter clause explicitly says "the value of," so the first clause must also involve "the value of," but with a different nuance: in the first clause the animal itself is consecrated for its value, while in the latter clause the value is consecrated only when it comes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the baraita's latter clause explicitly says 'דְּמֵי' (the value of), so the first clause must not involve 'דְּמֵי'.
The Gemara explains that the latter clause indeed says 'דְּמֵי' (the value of), but the first clause also involves 'דְּמֵי' with a different nuance: the animal itself is consecrated for its value.

The Gemara resolves that both clauses involve 'דְּמֵי' (the value of), but in the first clause the animal is consecrated for its value, while in the latter clause the value is consecrated only when it comes.

items.text: Attribution to Rabbi Meir
items.text_en: Attribution to Rabbi Meir
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how one can consecrate something not yet in existence, and Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav answers that the baraita follows Rabbi Meir, who holds that one can consecrate something not yet in the world.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that one cannot consecrate something not yet in existence.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav answers that the baraita follows Rabbi Meir, who holds that one can consecrate something not yet in the world.

items.text: Alternative version and additional case
items.text_en: Alternative version and additional case
items.desc_en: An alternative tradition records Rav Pappa asking Abaye (or Rami bar Chama asking Rav Chisda) whether the baraita indeed follows Rabbi Meir, and the answer is affirmative. A related case is cited: if one rents a house and it becomes leprous, the renter is exempt unless he demolishes it.

sub.desc_en: An alternative tradition records Rav Pappa asking Abaye (or Rami bar Chama asking Rav Chisda) whether the baraita indeed follows Rabbi Meir, who holds that one can consecrate an object not yet in existence.
Abaye responds affirmatively, implying that the baraita must follow Rabbi Meir, as no other Tanna holds this view.
A related case is cited: if one rents a house and it becomes leprous, the renter is exempt unless he demolishes it, illustrating a parallel principle of liability.

items.text: Clarifying the mishnah's statement about the resident dedicating the house
items.text_en: Clarifying the mishnah's statement about the resident dedicating the house
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a resident can dedicate a house he rents, since he does not own it. It reinterprets the mishnah to refer to the landlord dedicating the house, and then addresses the problem of the landlord living in the dedicated house and paying rent to the Temple, which would involve misuse of sacred property. The Gemara resolves this by suggesting the landlord stipulates that the future rent will be consecrated, but this raises the issue of consecrating something not yet in existence, which is attributed to Rabbi Meir's view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a resident can dedicate a house he rents, since he does not own it, citing the verse 'איש כי יקדיש ביתו קדש' (a man who dedicates his house) which implies only his own property.
