The Gemara reinterprets the mishnah to mean that the landlord dedicates the house, and the resident pays rent to the Temple.

The Gemara objects that if the landlord dedicates the house, he cannot live in it without committing מעילה (misuse of sacred property), and paying rent would be problematic because the rent would go to חולין (non-sacred use).
The Gemara suggests that the landlord stipulates that future rent will be consecrated, but then objects that one cannot consecrate something not yet in existence.
Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav resolves that the mishnah follows Rabbi Meir, who holds that one can consecrate something not yet in existence.

sub.text: Alternative version: Rav Pappa to Abaye / Rav Mari bar Chama to Rav Chisda
sub.text_en: Alternative version: Rav Pappa to Abaye / Rav Mari bar Chama to Rav Chisda
sub.desc_en: An alternative version records Rav Pappa asking Abaye (or Rav Mari bar Chama asking Rav Chisda) whether the mishnah follows Rabbi Meir, and the response is a rhetorical question: 'And if not, whose view would it be?'

items.text: Mishnah: Mortgaging for valuations and offerings, and coercion for willingness
items.text_en: Mishnah: Mortgaging for valuations and offerings, and coercion for willingness
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that those liable for valuations are mortgaged, those liable for sin-offerings and guilt-offerings are not mortgaged, but those liable for burnt-offerings and peace-offerings are mortgaged. It adds that even though atonement is not achieved until the person is willing, as it says 'for his acceptance', we coerce him until he says 'I am willing', and similarly for divorce.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah continues: Even though atonement is not achieved until he is willing, as it says 'for his acceptance', we coerce him until he says 'I am willing', and similarly for divorce.

items.text: Gemara: Exceptions to the rule of mortgaging for sin-offerings and burnt-offerings
items.text_en: Gemara: Exceptions to the rule of mortgaging for sin-offerings and burnt-offerings
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa notes that sometimes those liable for sin-offerings are mortgaged, and those liable for burnt-offerings are not. The Gemara explains that sin-offerings of a nazirite are mortgaged because if he shaves after any of the three offerings, he is released, so he might neglect to bring it. Burnt-offerings of a woman after childbirth are not mortgaged because the verse gives her priority, but Rava says the verse only gives priority for reading, not for sacrifice. The exception is the burnt-offering of a leper, as Rabbi Yishmael says his burnt-offering also delays his atonement.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa opens by stating that sometimes those liable for sin-offerings are mortgaged, and those liable for burnt-offerings are not.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rav Pappa's first case
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rav Pappa's first case
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that sin-offerings of a nazirite are mortgaged because if he shaves after any of the three offerings, he is released, so he might neglect to bring it.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rav Pappa's second case
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rav Pappa's second case
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that burnt-offerings of a woman after childbirth are not mortgaged because the verse gives her priority.

sub.text: Gemara's objection to the second case
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection to the second case
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the verse only gives the woman priority for reading, not for sacrifice, citing Rava's statement.

sub.text: Gemara's resolution with the burnt-offering of a leper
sub.text_en: Gemara's resolution with the burnt-offering of a leper
sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the exception is the burnt-offering of a leper, as Rabbi Yishmael says his burnt-offering also delays his atonement.

items.text: The requirement of willingness for offerings and the scope of coercion
items.text_en: The requirement of willingness for offerings and the scope of coercion
items.desc_en: A baraitha teaches that the verse 'he shall offer it' implies coercion, but 'for his acceptance' shows it must be willing, so we coerce until he says 'I am willing'. Shmuel states that a burnt-offering requires the owner's knowledge, citing the same verse. The Gemara questions what Shmuel adds, and explains that he teaches that even if a friend designates the offering, the owner's knowledge is needed, as he might not want atonement through something not his own.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the verse 'יַקְרִיב אוֹתוֹ' implies coercion, but 'לִרְצוֹנוֹ' shows willingness is required, so we coerce until he says 'I am willing'.
Shmuel states that a burnt-offering requires the owner's knowledge, citing the verse 'לִרְצוֹנוֹ'.
The Gemara questions what Shmuel adds, since the baraita already teaches the same principle.
The Gemara explains that Shmuel teaches that even if a friend designates the offering, the owner's knowledge is needed, as he might not want atonement through something not his own.

items.text: Beginning of an objection regarding a vow to bring another's offering
items.text_en: Beginning of an objection regarding a vow to bring another's offering
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to raise an objection from a baraitha about someone who says 'the sin-offering and guilt-offering of so-and-so are upon me', which will challenge the previous discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraitha about someone who says 'the sin-offering and guilt-offering of so-and-so are upon me', which will challenge the previous discussion.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Distinction between chatat and olah regarding da'at
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Distinction between chatat and olah regarding da'at
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that for a chatat, if the owner was aware (da'at) the sacrifice is valid, but if unaware it is invalid; for an olah, it is valid regardless. This sets up the Gemara's discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule: for a chatat, awareness matters; for an olah, it does not.

items.text: Shmuel and Ulla's dispute: Time of separation vs. time of atonement
items.text_en: Shmuel and Ulla's dispute: Time of separation vs. time of atonement
items.desc_en: Shmuel explains the Mishnah refers to the time of atonement, while he himself speaks of the time of separation. Ulla argues that the distinction between chatat and olah applies only at the time of separation, but at atonement both require da'at.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel explains that the baraita refers to the time of atonement (שעת כפרה), while his own statement refers to the time of separation (שעת הפרשה).
Ulla argues that the distinction between חטאת (sin-offering) and עולה (burnt-offering) applies only at the time of separation, but at the time of atonement both require da'at (awareness).

items.text: Objection from a baraita and resolution
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita and resolution
items.desc_en: A baraita is brought that seems to contradict both Shmuel and Ulla, stating that for all sacrifices, da'at is required. Shmuel and Ulla each reinterpret the baraita to align with their views. Rav Pappa concludes that the two sources are not contradictory, and the amoraim indeed disagree.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that states that for all sacrifices, including a sin-offering and a guilt-offering, if designated without da'at (awareness) the owner does not fulfill his obligation, contradicting Shmuel and Ulla.
Shmuel resolves the objection by interpreting the baraita as referring to the time of designation (שעת הפרשה), not the time of atonement.
Ulla resolves the objection by interpreting the baraita as referring to the time of atonement (שעת כפרה), consistent with his own view.
Rav Pappa concludes that the two baraitot are not contradictory because they refer to different times, and the amoraim indeed disagree.

items.text: Clarification of Shmuel's statement
items.text_en: Clarification of Shmuel's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Shmuel's phrase 'at the time of separation' might be interpreted as including even that time, and his statement teaches that despite the earlier objection, his view stands.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara qualifies that Shmuel's statement 'at the time of designation' might mean 'even at the time of designation,' teaching that the first Mishnah is not a refutation.
The Gemara resolves that Shmuel's statement teaches that despite the earlier objection, his view stands.

items.text: Digression: Annulment of a protest (moda'a) on a get
items.text_en: Digression: Annulment of a protest (moda'a) on a get
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet rules that if one makes a protest before giving a get, the protest is valid. The Gemara clarifies that this applies even if he later appeared to consent, and the Mishnah's phrase 'until he says' implies he must explicitly annul the protest.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet rules that if one makes a protest (מודעא) before giving a get, the protest is valid.
The Gemara questions why this ruling is necessary, as it seems obvious.
The Gemara explains that the ruling is needed for a case where the husband was forced and then appeared to consent, lest one think the protest is annulled.
The Gemara proves from the Mishnah's phrasing 'עד שיאמר' (until he says) rather than 'עד שיתן' (until he gives) that the husband must explicitly annul the protest.

items.text: Conclusion of previous chapter
items.text_en: Conclusion of previous chapter
items.desc_en: The Gemara marks the end of the previous chapter with the phrase 'Hadran alach ha'omer mishkali'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the previous chapter and transitions to a new Mishnah.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara: Procedure for publicizing sale of orphans' and consecrated property
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara: Procedure for publicizing sale of orphans' and consecrated property
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the appraisal of orphans' property is announced for 30 days, consecrated property for 60 days, with announcements morning and evening. The Gemara explains the timing (when workers go out and come in) and the content of the announcement, including the purpose (for a woman's ketubah or a creditor's debt).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the appraisal of orphans' property is announced for 30 days, consecrated property for 60 days, with announcements morning and evening.
The Gemara asks why the announcements are specifically made in the morning and evening.
Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav explains that the times correspond to when workers go out and come in, so they can inspect the property or inquire about it.
A baraita supports Rav's explanation, repeating the Mishnah's rule and specifying the times as when workers go out and come in.
The Gemara describes the content of the announcement: the field's boundaries, its quality, its appraised value, and that it is for sale to pay a woman's ketubah or a creditor's debt.
The Gemara asks why the announcement specifies that the sale is for the purpose of paying a woman's ketubah or a creditor's debt.
The Gemara explains that the specification is because some buyers prefer a creditor (who is lenient with money) and some prefer a woman (who pays in installments).

items.text: Opening Tannaitic dispute on announcement periods
items.text_en: Opening Tannaitic dispute on announcement periods
items.desc_en: The baraita presents a dispute between Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, and the Sages regarding the number of days for announcing the sale of orphans' property (30 or 60 days) and consecrated property (60 or 90 days). Rav Chisda cites Avimi that the halakha follows the opinion of sixty days for orphans.

items.text: Clarification of Rav Chisda's statement
items.text_en: Clarification of Rav Chisda's statement
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak questions Rabbi Chiya bar Avin about the details of Rav Chisda's ruling: whether it is sixty or thirty days, and whether it applies to orphans or consecrated property. Rabbi Chiya bar Avin clarifies it is sixty days for orphans, aligning with Rabbi Meir, but Rav Chisda explains that the sixty days include only specific days (Mondays and Thursdays), resulting in only eighteen actual days of announcement.

items.text: Explanation of the calculation
items.text_en: Explanation of the calculation
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the sixty-day period is counted only on Mondays and Thursdays, which are market days, so the actual number of announcement days is eighteen. Nevertheless, because the process is prolonged, people hear about it.

items.text: Dispute on when to seize orphans' property
items.text_en: Dispute on when to seize orphans' property
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Rav Asi rules that courts only seize orphans' property if usury is consuming it. Rabbi Yochanan adds cases of a promissory note with usury or a woman's ketubah due to loss of sustenance. The Gemara explains why Rav Asi excludes the ketubah case: the Sages instituted that the wife's earnings offset her sustenance, but sometimes her earnings are insufficient.

items.text: Challenge from the Mishnah and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge from the Mishnah and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Asi from the Mishnah which states that courts do get involved in orphans' property for announcements, implying they seize property even without usury. It considers various explanations: the creditor is a gentile who accepted Jewish law, or the case involves a ketubah. After a back-and-forth, it concludes that the Mishnah deals with a gentile creditor who accepted judgment but not the prohibition of usury.

items.text: Second challenge from a baraita on inferior land
items.text_en: Second challenge from a baraita on inferior land
items.desc_en: Another baraita states that creditors collect from orphans' property only from inferior land. The Gemara again challenges Rav Asi, and after similar analysis, resolves it with the same answer about a gentile creditor who accepted judgment but not the usury prohibition.

items.text: Third challenge and final resolution
items.text_en: Third challenge and final resolution
items.desc_en: A baraita mentions giving a woman her ketubah and a creditor his debt from orphans' property. The Gemara challenges Rav Asi regarding the ketubah, but resolves that the case is where the debtor admitted the debt. It then concludes that all the previous cases are also where the debtor admitted.

items.text: Case of collecting ketubah for a divorcee
items.text_en: Case of collecting ketubah for a divorcee
items.desc_en: Marimar collected a ketubah for a divorcee from orphans' property. Ravina challenges him based on Rav Asi and Rabbi Yochanan's rulings that only a widow's ketubah is collected due to loss of sustenance, not a divorcee's. Marimar responds that they learned Rabbi Yochanan's ruling for a divorcee as well, due to the concern for 'chen' (favor).

items.text: Rav Nachman's practice and the underlying dispute
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's practice and the underlying dispute
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman initially did not seize orphans' property, but after hearing Rav Huna's statement that orphans who consume what is not theirs should follow their debtors, he changed his practice. The Gemara explains the initial reluctance: Rav Papa says it is because paying a debt is a mitzvah and orphans are not obligated in mitzvot; Rav Huna bar Yehoshua says it is due to concern that the debtor might have hidden assets. The difference between them is in cases where the debtor admitted or was excommunicated and died in that state. A ruling from the academy states that the halakha follows Rav Huna bar Yehoshua.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and initial question
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and initial question
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the appraisal of orphans' property requires a 30-day announcement, and for consecrated property 60 days, with announcements morning and evening. The Gemara asks: what case are we dealing with? If a gentile creditor, would he obey? Rather, it must be a Jewish creditor.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the appraisal of orphans' property requires a 30-day announcement, and for consecrated property 60 days, with announcements morning and evening.
The Gemara asks what case the Mishnah deals with, rejecting the possibility of a gentile creditor who would not obey, and concluding it must be a Jewish creditor.

items.text: Challenge to Rav Pappa
items.text_en: Challenge to Rav Pappa
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that according to Rav Huna bar Yehoshua, who explains the Mishnah as dealing with a debtor who admits, it is fine. But for Rav Pappa, who holds that a creditor can collect without announcement, this is difficult.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Pappa by noting that Rav Huna bar Yehoshua's explanation of the Mishnah works, but Rav Pappa's position is difficult.

items.text: Rav Pappa's two answers
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's two answers
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa offers two answers: either the Mishnah deals with a ketubah, which requires announcement due to the woman's favor (חינא), or it deals with a gentile creditor who accepted Jewish law. The Gemara objects: if he accepted, why not wait until the orphans grow up? The answer: he accepted for this debt but not for that delay.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa offers his first answer: the Mishnah's announcement requirement applies to a ketubah, because of the woman's favor (חינא).
Rav Pappa offers his second answer: the Mishnah deals with a gentile creditor who accepted Jewish law for adjudication.
The Gemara objects: if the gentile accepted Jewish law, why not wait until the orphans grow up before collecting?
The Gemara resolves: the gentile accepted Jewish law for this debt but not for the delay of waiting until the orphans mature.

items.text: Second Mishnah and challenge to Rav Pappa
items.text_en: Second Mishnah and challenge to Rav Pappa
items.desc_en: A second Mishnah states that a creditor can collect on condition to give the woman her ketubah and the creditor his debt. The Gemara asks: if a gentile creditor, would he obey? Rather, it must be a Jewish creditor. For Rav Huna bar Yehoshua it's fine, but for Rav Pappa, while the ketubah is explained by חינא, the creditor remains difficult.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of a second Mishnah
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of a second Mishnah
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a second Mishnah that states a creditor can collect on condition to give the woman her ketubah and the creditor his debt.
The Gemara asks: if it deals with a gentile creditor, would he obey?
The Gemara concludes it must be a Jewish creditor.
The Gemara notes that for Rav Huna bar Yehoshua it is fine, but for Rav Pappa the creditor remains difficult.

items.text: Resolution for the second Mishnah
items.text_en: Resolution for the second Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves: it always deals with a gentile creditor who accepted Jewish law, but only for this debt and not for waiting until the orphans grow up.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah always deals with a gentile creditor who accepted Jewish law for this debt only, not for waiting until the orphans grow up.

items.text: Rava's concern for a receipt and the debate
items.text_en: Rava's concern for a receipt and the debate
items.desc_en: Rava says the reason for the announcement is concern for a receipt (שובר). Rav Huna bar Yehoshua challenges: do we worry about a receipt? The Mishnah says a woman who collects without her husband's presence must take an oath. Rabbi Acha Sar HaBirah reports a case before Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha in Antioch, who said the concern applies only to a ketubah due to חינא, but not to a creditor. Rabbah said in the name of Rav Nachman: even a creditor. The Gemara objects: if you worry about a receipt, worry there too! Rava answers: there the reason is so that one does not take another's money and go overseas.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that the reason for the announcement is concern for a receipt (שובר) that the debtor might have paid and lost.

Rav Huna bar Yehoshua challenges Rava: do we really worry about a receipt? He cites the Mishnah that a woman collecting her ketubah without her husband present must take an oath, implying no concern for a receipt.
Rabbi Acha Sar HaBirah reports a case before Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha in Antioch, who ruled that the concern for a receipt applies only to a ketubah due to חינא (favor), but not to a creditor.

sub.text: Rabbah in the name of Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Rabbah in the name of Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: Rabbah says in the name of Rav Nachman that even a creditor is subject to the concern for a receipt.
The Gemara objects: if you worry about a receipt in the case of a creditor, then you should also worry about a receipt in the case of a woman collecting her ketubah without her husband present.
Rava answers that there the reason is different: to prevent a person from taking another's money and going overseas, not due to concern for a receipt.

items.text: Rava's halakhic ruling and the Nehardeans' position
items.text_en: Rava's halakhic ruling and the Nehardeans' position
items.desc_en: Rava rules: we do not seize orphans' property for a debt, but if the creditor says 'give' (specifying a field or sum), we seize and do not appoint a guardian; if unspecified, we seize and appoint a guardian. The Nehardeans say: in all cases we seize and appoint a guardian, except for a field found not to be his, as we do not establish witnesses as liars. Rav Ashi concludes: therefore we do not seize, but if we do, we appoint a guardian, following the Nehardeans' exception.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that we do not seize orphans' property for a debt, but if the creditor specifies a field or sum, we seize without appointing a guardian; if unspecified, we seize and appoint a guardian.
The Nehardeans say that in all cases we seize and appoint a guardian, except for a field found not to be the debtor's, as we do not establish witnesses as liars.
Rav Ashi concludes that therefore we do not seize, but if we do, we appoint a guardian, following the Nehardeans' exception.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute: If one consecrates all his property while his wife has a ketubah, Rabbi Eliezer says that when he divorces her he must vow to forbid her benefit (so she cannot collect from the consecrated property), while Rabbi Yehoshua says he need not. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds a similar case of a guarantor for a ketubah.

items.text: Gemara's initial explanation of the dispute
items.text_en: Gemara's initial explanation of the dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: What is the basis of their dispute? It explains: Rabbi Eliezer holds that a person does make a 'kinunya' (scheme) against consecrated property, meaning he might divorce his wife to reclaim the property, so a vow is needed to prevent that. Rabbi Yehoshua holds that a person does not make such a scheme.

items.text: Challenge from Rav Huna's ruling and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge from Rav Huna's ruling and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: Rav Huna said that a dying man who consecrated all his property and said 'I have a maneh in the hand of so-and-so' is believed, because we assume one does not scheme against consecrated property. Does this align with the tannaitic dispute? The Gemara answers: The dispute is only regarding a healthy person, but for a dying person, everyone agrees that one does not scheme against consecrated property, because a person does not sin for no benefit.

items.text: Alternative explanation: dispute over vows made in public
items.text_en: Alternative explanation: dispute over vows made in public
items.desc_en: An alternative explanation: Everyone agrees that a healthy person does not scheme against consecrated property. The dispute here is about a vow made in public (נדר שהודר ברבים) — one opinion holds it can be dissolved, the other that it cannot. Another version: the dispute is about a vow made with the knowledge of the public (על דעת רבים).

items.text: Challenge from Ameimar and resolution: dispute over release of consecrated property
items.text_en: Challenge from Ameimar and resolution: dispute over release of consecrated property
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: Ameimar said a vow made in public can be dissolved, but one made with the knowledge of the public cannot. Does this align with the tannaitic dispute? Moreover, Rabbi Yehoshua says 'he does not need' — he should have said 'it does not help'! Rather, the dispute here is about the possibility of releasing consecrated property (שאלה דהקדש).

items.text: Support from a baraita linking to Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
items.text_en: Support from a baraita linking to Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon says: These are the words of Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel. Beit Shammai say: A mistaken consecration is consecration (so the vow is needed), while Beit Hillel say: A mistaken consecration is not consecration (so no vow is needed).

items.text: Story of Moshe bar Atzri and Abaye's advice
items.text_en: Story of Moshe bar Atzri and Abaye's advice
items.desc_en: The Gemara relates: Moshe bar Atzri was a guarantor for his daughter's ketubah, and his son Rav Huna was a Torah scholar in financial distress. Abaye said: Is there no one to advise Rav Huna to divorce his wife so she can claim her ketubah from her father, and then remarry her? Rava objected: But we learned 'he must vow'! Abaye replied: Does everyone who divorces do so in court? Eventually it was revealed that Rav Huna was a priest (so he could not remarry her). Abaye commented: Poverty follows the poor.

items.text: Contradiction in Abaye's statements and resolution
items.text_en: Contradiction in Abaye's statements and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions: Does Abaye really say this? He also said: Who is a cunning wicked person? One who advises selling property (to avoid creditors), like Rabban Gamliel. The Gemara resolves: His son is different, and a Torah scholar is different. Then it asks: But why not let the guarantor claim that a guarantor for a ketubah is not legally bound?

items.text: The status of a kablan (guarantor) when the borrower has no assets
items.text_en: The status of a kablan (guarantor) when the borrower has no assets
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the case of Rav Huna, who was a kablan, can be reconciled with the dispute about whether a kablan is liable only if the borrower has assets. Two answers are given: either Rav Huna had assets that were lost, or a father naturally guarantees for his son. The Gemara then clarifies the halakhic distinctions between an arev (surety) for a ketubah and a kablan for a debt, concluding that in all cases the guarantor is liable even if the borrower has no assets, except for an arev for a ketubah, who is never liable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rav Huna's case as a kablan (guarantor) fits with the dispute over whether a kablan is liable only if the borrower has assets.
First answer: Rav Huna had assets that were later lost (flooded), so the borrower originally had assets.
Second answer: A father naturally guarantees for his son, so Rav Huna's guarantee was unconditional.
A baraita is cited to clarify the halakhic distinctions between an arev (surety) for a ketubah and a kablan for a debt, with a dispute about the intermediate cases.

The Gemara rules that in all cases the guarantor is liable even if the borrower has no assets, except for an arev for a ketubah, who is never liable because he performed only a מצוה (commandment) and lost nothing.

items.text: The case of a purchaser of property and the ketubah
items.text_en: The case of a purchaser of property and the ketubah
items.desc_en: A man sold his property and was divorcing his wife. Rav Yosef asked Rav Pappa whether a purchaser (of the property) is liable for the ketubah, similar to an arev or hekdesh. Rav Pappa dismissed the question. The Nehardeans ruled that only explicitly taught cases apply. Rav Mesharshiya explains that hekdesh is liable due to profit, and an arev due to performing a mitzvah, but a purchaser knowingly takes on the risk.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a case: a man sold his property and was divorcing his wife.

sub.text: Rav Yosef's question to Rav Pappa
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef's question to Rav Pappa
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef asks Rav Pappa whether a purchaser of the property is liable for the ketubah, given that an arev and hekdesh are already taught.
Rav Pappa dismisses the question, implying the Tanna enumerated cases like a peddler and we should not add more.
The Nehardeans rule that only explicitly taught cases apply; what is not taught is not applied.
Rav Mesharshiya explains the Nehardeans' reasoning: hekdesh is liable due to profit, an arev due to performing a mitzvah, but a purchaser knowingly takes on the risk and thus is not liable.

items.text: Mishnah: Consecrating property with debts, and the Gemara's discussion
items.text_en: Mishnah: Consecrating property with debts, and the Gemara's discussion
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one consecrates his property while owing a ketubah or debt, the creditors cannot collect from the consecrated property; rather, the redeemer redeems it with the intent to pay them. The Gemara explains why the Mishnah repeats 'podeh podeh'—to prevent the notion that consecrated property can be released without redemption. It then notes that the Mishnah disagrees with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who limits redemption to when the debt equals the consecrated value, while the Rabbis allow it up to half.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one consecrates his property while owing a ketubah or debt, the creditors cannot collect from the consecrated property; rather, the redeemer redeems it with the intent to pay them.
The Gemara asks why the Mishnah repeats the phrase 'הפודה פודה' (the redeemer redeems).
The Gemara answers that the repetition is due to Rabbi Avahu's teaching, to prevent the notion that consecrated property can be released without redemption.
The Gemara notes that the Mishnah disagrees with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who limits redemption to when the debt equals the consecrated value.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Yehuda citing Rav Sheshet
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Yehuda citing Rav Sheshet
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehuda in the name of Rav Sheshet states that the Rabbis allow redemption even when the debt is only up to half the consecrated value.

items.text: Mishnah: Provisions for those liable for valuations, and the Gemara's reasoning
items.text_en: Mishnah: Provisions for those liable for valuations, and the Gemara's reasoning
items.desc_en: The Mishnah details that those liable for valuations are given basic necessities like food, clothing, bedding, and tools, but not to their family. It specifies allowances for craftsmen and discusses how to handle multiple types of tools. The Gemara begins to ask for the scriptural source for these provisions.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that those liable for valuations are given basic provisions (food, clothing, bedding, sandals, tefillin) for themselves, but not for their family.
The Mishnah details that a craftsman receives two tools of each type, and Rabbi Eliezer adds that a farmer gets his yoke and a donkey driver his donkey.

The Mishnah rules that when one has many of one tool type and few of another, he is given two from the abundant type and all from the scarce type, and one who consecrates his property has his tefillin redeemed for him.
The Gemara asks for the scriptural source for these provisions.

items.text: Exemption of wife and children from consecration
items.text_en: Exemption of wife and children from consecration
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the biblical source for the Mishnah's ruling that one who consecrates his property does not exempt his wife and children. The verse 'And if he be poor from your valuation' implies that only the person himself is exempted, not his wife and children.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse 'וְאִם מָךְ הוּא מֵעֶרְכֶּךָ' (And if he be poor from your valuation) and explains that it means 'keep him alive from your valuation' — the exemption applies only to the person himself.
The Gemara asks for the reason why the Mishnah exempts the wife and children from consecration.
The Gemara answers that the verse says 'הוּא מֵעֶרְכֶּךָ' (he from your valuation), implying that only the person himself is exempted, not his wife and children.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's ruling on a farmer's team
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's ruling on a farmer's team
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer rules that if the person is a farmer, he is given his team of oxen. The Rabbis object that these are not tools of his trade but rather property, so they are not exempted.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer rules that if the person is a farmer, he is given his team of oxen.
The Rabbis object that these are not tools of his trade but rather property, so they are not exempted.

items.text: One who has only one type of tool
items.text_en: One who has only one type of tool
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah needs to state that if he has only one type of tool, it is left for him. It explains that one might think that previously he could borrow, but now no one will lend to him, so the Mishnah teaches that it is still left for him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah needs to state that if he has only one type of tool, it is left for him, since obviously he can continue using it as before.
The Gemara answers that one might think that previously he could borrow tools, but now no one will lend to him, so the Mishnah teaches that the tool is still left for him.

items.text: One who consecrates his property is given his tefillin
items.text_en: One who consecrates his property is given his tefillin
items.desc_en: The Gemara relates a case where a man sold his property and came before Rav Yemar, who ruled that they should give him his tefillin. The Gemara questions why this is necessary, as it is already in the Mishnah. It explains that one might think that only in consecration does one think he is performing a mitzvah, but in selling, one would not sell his own mitzvah, so the ruling teaches otherwise.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states that one who consecrates his property is given his תפילין (phylacteries).
The Gemara relates a case where a man sold his property and came before רב יימר (Rav Yemar), who ruled that they should remove his תפילין (phylacteries) and give them to the buyer.
The Gemara asks what this incident teaches us, since the mishnah already rules that תפילין (phylacteries) are taken.

The Gemara explains that one might think that only in consecration does one intend to include his תפילין (phylacteries) because he thinks he is performing a מצוה (commandment), but in a sale a person would not sell an item used for a מצוה (commandment) of his body; therefore the incident teaches that even in a sale, תפילין (phylacteries) are included.

items.text: Mishnah: Exemptions for wife's clothing and new items
items.text_en: Mishnah: Exemptions for wife's clothing and new items
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that one who consecrates his property or evaluates himself does not include his wife's clothing, his children's clothing, dyed items for them, or new sandals bought for them. It adds that although slaves are sold with their clothing for enhancement, and similarly for a cow or pearl, the Temple only takes the item at its current place and time.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who consecrates his property or evaluates himself does not include his wife's clothing, his children's clothing, dyed items for them, or new sandals bought for them.
The Mishnah adds that although slaves are sold with their clothing for enhancement, and similarly for a cow or pearl, the Temple only takes the item at its current place and time.

items.text: Gemara: Derivation from verses
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation from verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from the verse 'And he shall give your valuation on that day' that one should not delay a pearl for a light item, and from 'Holy to the Lord' that unspecified consecrations are for the Temple treasury.

sub.desc_en: The baraita derives from the verse 'וְנָתַן אֶת הָעֶרְכְּךָ בַּיּוֹם הַהוּא' that one should not delay a pearl for a light item, and from 'קֹדֶשׁ לַה׳' that unspecified consecrations are for the Temple treasury (בדק הבית).

items.text: Conclusion of the chapter
items.text_en: Conclusion of the chapter
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the chapter with the phrase 'We have returned to you, the valuation of orphans.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the chapter with the standard formula 'We have returned to you, the valuation of orphans.'

items.text: Mishnah: Restrictions on consecrating near Jubilee
items.text_en: Mishnah: Restrictions on consecrating near Jubilee
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not consecrate a field less than two years before the Jubilee, nor redeem it less than one year after the Jubilee. Months are not calculated for the Temple, but the Temple does calculate months.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rules for consecrating and redeeming fields near the Jubilee year, including that months are not calculated for the Temple but the Temple does calculate months.

items.text: Contradiction and resolution by Rav and Shmuel
items.text_en: Contradiction and resolution by Rav and Shmuel
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita that allows consecration before and after Jubilee but not in the Jubilee year itself. Rav and Shmuel explain that the Mishnah means one may not consecrate to be redeemed by deduction less than two years before Jubilee, so a person should be careful not to consecrate less than two years before. They then dispute whether a field consecrated in the Jubilee year itself is consecrated.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita that permits consecration before and after Jubilee but forbids it in the Jubilee year itself, and if one consecrates it is not consecrated.

Rav and Shmuel both explain that the Mishnah means one may not consecrate to be redeemed by deduction less than two years before Jubilee, so a person should be careful not to consecrate less than two years before.

It was stated: Rav and Shmuel dispute whether a field consecrated in the Jubilee year itself is consecrated, with Rav ruling it is consecrated and requires fifty shekels, and Shmuel ruling it is not consecrated at all.

items.text: Rav Yosef's objection and Shmuel's position
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's objection and Shmuel's position
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef objects to Shmuel's position regarding consecration in the Jubilee year, arguing that a kal vachomer cannot be applied here because the Mishnah (Rabbi Yehuda) states that if the Jubilee arrives and the field was not redeemed, the priests enter and give its value. The Gemara concludes that Shmuel follows Rabbi Shimon, who says the priests enter but do not give payment.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef objects to Shmuel's position by arguing that a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument) can be applied to the case of sale, but not to consecration in the Jubilee year.

Rav Yosef further objects that in the case of consecration, a kal vachomer cannot apply, because the Mishnah (Rabbi Yehuda) states that if the Jubilee arrives and the field was not redeemed, the priests enter and give its value.
The Gemara resolves that Shmuel follows Rabbi Shimon, who holds that the priests enter but do not give payment, thus avoiding the objection.

items.text: Rav's position on the Jubilee year
items.text_en: Rav's position on the Jubilee year
items.desc_en: Rav holds that the Jubilee year is included in the calculation, so the field returns to the owner at the Jubilee and the priests receive nothing extra.

items.text: Scriptural basis for Rav and Shmuel
items.text_en: Scriptural basis for Rav and Shmuel
items.desc_en: Rav derives his view from the phrase 'from the year of Jubilee', interpreting it as including the Jubilee year itself. Shmuel counters that the phrase means 'from the year after the Jubilee'.

items.text: Difficulty with Shmuel's interpretation
items.text_en: Difficulty with Shmuel's interpretation
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that for Rav, the verse's distinction between 'from the year of Jubilee' and 'after the Jubilee' is consistent, but for Shmuel, 'after the Jubilee' would have to mean 'after after'.

items.text: Challenge from a baraita and Rav's response
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraita and Rav's response
items.desc_en: A baraita states that one may not consecrate a field in the Jubilee year itself, and if one does, it is not consecrated. Rav explains that it is not consecrated for redemption by reduction, but it is consecrated and one gives fifty shekels.

items.text: Contradiction from Rav and Shmuel's own ruling
items.text_en: Contradiction from Rav and Shmuel's own ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara points out that the baraita implies that before the Jubilee one can redeem by reduction, but Rav and Shmuel both say one cannot consecrate for redemption by reduction with less than two years remaining.

items.text: Rav's resolution: the baraita follows the Rabbis
items.text_en: Rav's resolution: the baraita follows the Rabbis
items.desc_en: Rav answers that the baraita follows the Rabbis, while he follows Rabbi, who interprets 'first' and 'seventh' as including the year itself, and similarly 'in the year' includes the Jubilee year.

items.text: Challenge from the pundyon and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge from the pundyon and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the pundyon (a coin) in Rabbi's ruling, and concludes that for Shmuel, Rabbi follows the Rabbis, not Rabbi Yehuda, because if he followed Rabbi Yehuda he would require a selah and two pundyon.

items.text: Final challenge from a baraita about redemption after the Jubilee
items.text_en: Final challenge from a baraita about redemption after the Jubilee
items.desc_en: A baraita states that one cannot redeem after the Jubilee with less than a year. For Shmuel this is straightforward, but for Rav the Gemara questions what 'after the Jubilee' means, and then clarifies that it does not mean literally after the Jubilee.

items.text: Clarification of the Mishnah's statement about redeeming after the Jubilee
items.text_en: Clarification of the Mishnah's statement about redeeming after the Jubilee
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions what the Mishnah's statement that one cannot redeem a field less than a year after the Jubilee teaches, suggesting it might be about not counting months with the sanctuary. It concludes that the Mishnah is explaining the reason: because months are not counted with the sanctuary.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions what the Mishnah's statement about redeeming after the Jubilee teaches, suggesting it might be informing us that months are not counted with the sanctuary.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah is not teaching a new rule but explaining the reason: since months are not counted with the sanctuary, one cannot redeem less than a year after the Jubilee.

items.text: Source for not counting months with the sanctuary
items.text_en: Source for not counting months with the sanctuary
items.desc_en: A baraisa provides a scriptural source for the rule that months are not counted with the sanctuary, derived from the verse "and the priest shall reckon unto him the money according to the years that remain." It then asks about a case where one consecrates a field in the middle of a year, and derives from the same verse that if one wishes to treat months as a year, one may do so.

sub.desc_en: A baraita (תנו רבנן) is cited, deriving from the verse 'וְחִשַּׁב לוֹ הַכֹּהֵן אֶת הַכֶּסֶף עַל פִּי הַשָּׁנִים הַנּוֹתָרוֹת' that one counts years, not months, with the sanctuary.

A secondary question is raised: from where do we know that if one wishes, one may count months toward a year — for example, if the field was dedicated in the middle of the 48th year of the Jubilee cycle.
The answer cites the same verse 'וְחִשַּׁב לוֹ הַכֹּהֵן' — teaching that the priest calculates in any case, allowing flexibility to include partial years as a full year.

items.text: Mishnah: Payment for a field consecrated during or before the Jubilee
items.text_en: Mishnah: Payment for a field consecrated during or before the Jubilee
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who consecrates his field during the Jubilee period pays fifty shekels of silver per a beit kor of barley seed. It details that deep pits or high rocks ten handbreadths high are not measured with the field, but less than that are. If consecrated two or three years before the Jubilee, one pays a sela and a pundion per year, and if one offers to pay year by year, we do not listen to him; rather, he pays all at once. The difference between the owner and others is that the owner pays an additional fifth.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the fixed rate for redeeming a field dedicated during the Jubilee, and that deep pits or high rocks of ten tefachim are not measured with the field while shallower ones are.

The Mishnah continues: when a field is dedicated two or three years before the Jubilee, the redeemer pays a set amount per year, cannot pay yearly installments, and the distinction between the original owner ( בעלים ), who adds a fifth, and any other person, who does not.

items.text: Gemara: Clarification of the Mishnah's measure
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarification of the Mishnah's measure
items.desc_en: A baraisa clarifies that the Mishnah's measure of a kor is for seed, not produce, and that it is a hand's throw, not a thick or thin measure. Levi taught that it is neither thick nor thin, but average.

sub.desc_en: A Tanna taught: the measure is a kor of seed, not a kor of produce, and a hand-drop, not a line-drop; and Levi taught: it must be average, neither too thick nor too thin.
Levi taught that the seed must be of medium quality, not too plump and not too thin.

items.text: Gemara: Discussion of pits and rocks in the field
items.text_en: Gemara: Discussion of pits and rocks in the field
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why pits and rocks are not measured with the field, suggesting they should be consecrated separately. It considers the possibility that they are not a beit kor, but a baraisa teaches that the term "field" includes any size. Mar Ukva bar Chama explains that the pits are filled with water and thus not fit for sowing, which is supported by the parallel with rocks. The Gemara then asks about less than ten handbreadths, and answers that such features are called 'nganei d'ara' (cavities of the land) and 'shidrei d'ara' (ridges of the land) and are considered part of the field.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why pits and rocks in the field are not consecrated separately as independent items.
The Gemara objects that even if the pits are not a beit kor, a baraisa teaches that the term 'field' includes any size.
Mar Ukva bar Chama explains that the pits are filled with water and thus not fit for sowing, supported by the parallel with rocks.
The Gemara asks why pits less than ten handbreadths deep are also not measured with the field.
The Gemara answers that such features are called 'nganei d'ara' (cavities of the land) and 'shidrei d'ara' (ridges of the land) and are considered part of the field.

items.text: Gemara: Source for paying per year and the requirement to pay all at once
items.text_en: Gemara: Source for paying per year and the requirement to pay all at once
items.desc_en: A baraisa derives from the verse "and it shall be deducted from your valuation" that even if the sanctuary consumed the field for one or two years, or even if it was not consumed but was before him, he pays a sela and a pundion per year. Another baraisa derives from the verse "and the priest shall reckon unto him the money" that if the owners say they will pay year by year, we do not listen to them; rather, the money must be paid all at once. The difference between the owner and others is that the owner pays an additional fifth.

sub.desc_en: A baraita derives from the verse 'וְנִגְרַע מֵעֶרְכֶּךָ' that even if the sanctuary consumed the field for one or two years, or even if it was not consumed but was before him, the owner pays a sela and a pundion per year.

Another baraita derives from the verse 'וְחִשַּׁב לוֹ הַכֹּהֵן אֶת הַכֶּסֶף' that if the owners say they will pay year by year, we do not listen to them; rather, the money must be paid all at once, and the difference between the owner and others is that the owner pays an additional fifth.

items.text: Mishnah: Laws of redemption and the Jubilee
items.text_en: Mishnah: Laws of redemption and the Jubilee
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one consecrated a field and redeemed it, it does not leave his hand in the Jubilee. If his son redeemed it, it leaves to his father in the Jubilee. If another or one of the relatives redeemed it from him, it leaves to the priests in the Jubilee. If a priest redeemed it and it is under his hand, he cannot claim it as his own because it leaves to the priests; rather, it leaves his hand and is divided among all his fellow priests.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule for a field consecrated and redeemed by the owner, his son, or another person.
The Mishnah adds that if a priest redeemed the field, it does not become his but is divided among all priests in the Jubilee.

items.text: Who is excluded from redeeming a field?
items.text_en: Who is excluded from redeeming a field?
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita interpreting the verses to exclude a son from redeeming a field sold by his father, but includes a brother. A debate ensues: the son should be included because he stands in his father's place for testimony and Hebrew slave, while the brother should be included because he stands in his brother's place for yibbum. The Gemara rejects the brother's claim because yibbum only applies where there is no son.

sub.desc_en: The baraita interprets the verses to exclude a son from redeeming a field sold by his father, but includes a brother.
The Gemara asks why the son is included and the brother excluded, and answers that the son stands in his father's place for testimony and Hebrew slave.
The Gemara objects that the brother should be included because he stands in his brother's place for yibbum, but rejects this because yibbum only applies where there is no son.

items.text: Refining the comparison: Hebrew slave vs. yibbum
items.text_en: Refining the comparison: Hebrew slave vs. yibbum
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the son's inclusion is based on Hebrew slave, since the same objection (yibbum only without a son) applies there too. The Gemara responds that the comparison to Hebrew slave is valid because the same objection is already raised there.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: why not derive the opposite from the Hebrew slave, since there the son inherits two roles (testimony and slavery) while here only one (yibbum)?
The Gemara answers: the comparison to Hebrew slave is valid because the same objection (yibbum only without a son) applies there too, so the son's inclusion is consistent.

items.text: Does a daughter prevent the field from going to priests?
items.text_en: Does a daughter prevent the field from going to priests?
items.desc_en: Rabba bar Avuh asks whether a daughter can prevent her father's field from going to the priests in the Jubilee. The Gemara suggests a proof from the school of Rabbi Yishmael: anyone who is considered 'another' in place of a son does not prevent it, and a daughter is like 'another' in place of a son regarding inheritance.

items.text: Does a wife prevent the field from going to priests?
items.text_en: Does a wife prevent the field from going to priests?
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks whether a wife can prevent her husband's field from going to the priests. The Gemara considers two possibilities: the husband prevents it because he inherits from her, or the son prevents it because he takes inherited property even if not yet in hand. The question remains unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers: Come hear, from the school of Rabbi Yishmael: Whatever is 'another' in place of a son — and this also, in place of a son, is like 'another'.

items.text: Field consecrated less than two years before Jubilee
items.text_en: Field consecrated less than two years before Jubilee
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks Rav Chisda whether a field consecrated less than two years before the Jubilee goes out to the priests. Rav Chisda answers that only a field subject to reduction (i.e., consecrated at least two years before) goes out, but Rami bar Chama objects that the verse applies to any field not redeemed, and this field is subject to redemption.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks Rav Chisda whether a field consecrated less than two years before the Jubilee goes out to the priests.
Rav Chisda answers that only a field subject to reduction (בת גירעון, i.e., consecrated at least two years before) goes out to the priests, not one consecrated less than two years before.
The Gemara objects that the verse applies to any field not redeemed, and this field is subject to redemption (בת גאולה), so it should also go out to the priests.

items.text: Priest who redeems a field does not keep it
items.text_en: Priest who redeems a field does not keep it
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that if a priest redeems a field that would go to the priests in the Jubilee, he cannot keep it for himself. The verse 'achuzato' teaches that it is the inheritance of the priests collectively, not his personal possession. The field leaves his hand and is divided among his fellow priests.

items.text: Dispute: Do priests pay for the field in the Jubilee?
items.text_en: Dispute: Do priests pay for the field in the Jubilee?
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute: Rabbi Yehuda says priests enter and pay its value; Rabbi Shimon says they enter without paying; Rabbi Eliezer says they do not enter at all, and the field is called 'retushin' until a later Jubilee. The Gemara explains the sources: Rabbi Yehuda learns from 'kodesh' of consecrating a house (payment required), Rabbi Shimon learns from 'kodesh' of the lambs of Shavuot (free), and Rabbi Yehuda argues that we derive from consecrated property of the Temple.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states Rabbi Yehuda's position: when the Jubilee arrives and the field was not redeemed, the priests enter and pay its value.
The Mishnah presents Rabbi Shimon's position: the priests enter without paying.
The Mishnah presents Rabbi Eliezer's position: the priests do not enter at all, and the field is called 'retushin' until a later Jubilee.
The Gemara asks what is Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning, and explains that he derives from a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) of the word 'קדש' from the case of consecrating a house.
The Gemara explains the analogy: just as there (consecrating a house) payment is required, so too here the priests must pay.
The Gemara explains Rabbi Shimon's reasoning: he derives from the lambs of Shavuot (כבשי עצרת) that the priests receive without payment.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yehuda could also learn from the lambs of Shavuot, and answers that he derives from consecrated property of the Temple (קדשי בדק הבית).

items.text: Opening dispute: Rabbi Shimon's position on redeeming consecrated property
items.text_en: Opening dispute: Rabbi Shimon's position on redeeming consecrated property
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Shimon agrees that one does not redeem consecrated property of the Temple treasury from consecrated property of the altar, and explains that he derives this from the principle that one derives a matter that is a gift to the priests from another matter that is a gift to the priests, not from a matter that is not a gift to the priests.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that Rabbi Shimon agrees one does not redeem consecrated property of the Temple treasury from consecrated property of the altar.

The Gemara explains that Rabbi Shimon derives his position from the principle that one derives a matter that is a gift to the priests from another matter that is a gift to the priests, not from a matter that is not a gift to the priests.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's ruling
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's ruling
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer states that one does not enter (the field) and does not give (money to redeem it), implying that the field is not redeemed and does not return to the original owner.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer rules that one does not enter the field and does not give money to redeem it, implying the field is not redeemed and does not return to the original owner.

items.text: Rabbah's explanation of Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning
items.text_en: Rabbah's explanation of Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning
items.desc_en: Rabbah explains that Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning is based on a verse: 'And if he does not redeem the field... it shall not be redeemed again, and if he sells the field... it shall be when it goes out in the Jubilee' — implying that if not redeemed, it goes out to the priests.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah explains that Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning is based on the verse 'And if he does not redeem the field... it shall not be redeemed again, and if he sells the field... it shall be when it goes out in the Jubilee' — implying that if not redeemed, it goes out to the priests.

items.text: Abaye's objection and alternative explanation
items.text_en: Abaye's objection and alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Abaye objects that Rabbah's reading cuts the verse improperly, and instead explains that Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning is based on a baraita: the word 'again' teaches that the field is not redeemed in the sense of returning to its original status, but it is redeemed in the sense of being like a purchased field. The Gemara clarifies that this refers to the second Jubilee, and that this applies to Rabbi Eliezer's view, not to Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects that Rabbah's reading of the verse is like a sharp knife cutting the verse improperly.
Abaye explains that Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning is based on a baraita: the word 'עוֹד' teaches that the field is not redeemed to its original status, but it is redeemed as a purchased field.
The Gemara asks when this applies, and rejects the possibility of the first Jubilee because the field would still be ancestral land.
The Gemara concludes that it must refer to the second Jubilee.
The Gemara asks which rabbi this applies to, and rejects Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon because the field would go to the priests.
The Gemara concludes that this applies to Rabbi Eliezer, and thus his reasoning is derived from this baraita.

items.text: Clarifying the context of the baraita
items.text_en: Clarifying the context of the baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the baraita deals with a field that went out to the priests, a priest consecrated it, and the original owners came to redeem it. One might think they cannot redeem it, but the word 'again' teaches that it is not redeemed in the original sense but is redeemed as a purchased field.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions what Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon would derive from the word 'עוֹד' (again) in the verse.

The Gemara explains that the baraita deals with a field that went out to the priests, a priest consecrated it, and the original owners came to redeem it; one might think they cannot redeem it, but the word 'עוֹד' teaches that it is not redeemed in the original sense but is redeemed as a purchased field.

items.text: Derivation from the verse 'to the one who bought it' and the necessity of both verses
items.text_en: Derivation from the verse 'to the one who bought it' and the necessity of both verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that from the verse 'in the year of Jubilee the field shall return to the one from whom it was bought' one might think it returns to the treasurer, but the verse 'to the one who has the inheritance of the land' teaches otherwise. The Gemara then explains the necessity of both verses: 'it shall not be redeemed' and 'to the one who bought it' — each addresses a different case where one might think the field returns to the original owner, and the other verse prevents that.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites the verse 'in the year of Jubilee the field shall return to the one who bought it' and teaches that one might think it returns to the treasurer, but the verse 'to the one who has the inheritance of the land' teaches otherwise.

The Gemara asks why the verse 'to the one who bought it' is needed, and the baraita answers that it applies to a field that went to the priests, was sold by a priest, consecrated by the buyer, and redeemed by another — one might think it returns to the original owners, so the verse teaches it returns to the buyer.

The Gemara states that both verses 'it shall not be redeemed' and 'to the one who bought it' are necessary, because each addresses a different case where one might think the field returns to the original owner, and the other verse prevents that.

The Gemara explains that if only 'it shall not be redeemed' were written, one might think that since the field does not return at all, in the case where it does return it should go to the first owner, so the verse 'to the one who bought it' is needed.

The Gemara explains that if only 'to the one who bought it' were written, one might think that since the owners do not pay money, in the case where they do pay they should keep it, so the verse 'it shall not be redeemed' is needed.

The Gemara concludes that if only 'it shall not be redeemed' were written without 'עוֹד' (again), one might think it is never redeemed, so the verse writes 'עוֹד' to teach that it is not redeemed in the manner it was before, but it is redeemed to be before him as a purchased field.

items.text: Rava's conclusion on the verse
items.text_en: Rava's conclusion on the verse
items.desc_en: Rava concludes that the verse 'and the field shall be when it goes out in the Jubilee' means 'when it goes out from the hand of another' — i.e., from the priest, not returning to the original owner.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the question by citing the verse 'וְהָיָה הַשָּׂדֶה בְּצֵאתוֹ בַיּוֹבֵל' (and the field shall be when it goes out in the Jubilee), interpreting 'בְּצֵאתוֹ' as 'when it goes out from the hand of another' — i.e., from the priest, not returning to the original owner.

items.text: Opening question: owners in second Jubilee
items.text_en: Opening question: owners in second Jubilee
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether owners in the second Jubilee are considered like 'others' (non-owners) or not, based on the verse 'it shall not be redeemed'.

items.text: First answer: 'it shall not be redeemed' implies non-redeemable
items.text_en: First answer: 'it shall not be redeemed' implies non-redeemable
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially interprets 'it shall not be redeemed' as meaning the field is never redeemable, but the verse 'still' suggests it can be redeemed if it becomes like a field of purchase.

items.text: Objection: first Jubilee vs second Jubilee
items.text_en: Objection: first Jubilee vs second Jubilee
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if the verse applies to the first Jubilee, why is it not redeemable? It is already an inherited field. So it must refer to the second Jubilee, and to whom? If to Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon (who say owners in second Jubilee are like others), it goes to priests; but if to Rabbi Eliezer (who says they are like owners), it stays with owners.

items.text: Resolution: Rabbi Eliezer's view on second Jubilee
items.text_en: Resolution: Rabbi Eliezer's view on second Jubilee
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Eliezer indeed holds owners in second Jubilee are like others, based on the verse 'still' implying redeemability even after the first Jubilee.

items.text: Mishna: field purchased from father, then father dies
items.text_en: Mishna: field purchased from father, then father dies
items.desc_en: The Mishna discusses a field bought from a father; if the father dies after consecration, it is like a field of inheritance; if before, like a field of purchase. Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda/Shimon disagree.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda and Shimon: field is like inherited
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda and Shimon: field is like inherited
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda and Shimon argue the field is like an inherited field because the verse 'if from a field of purchase which is not of his inheritance' excludes fields that are eligible for inheritance.

items.text: Gemara: field of purchase never goes to priests in Jubilee
items.text_en: Gemara: field of purchase never goes to priests in Jubilee
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that a field of purchase never goes to priests in Jubilee, because no one consecrates what isn't theirs. Priests and Levites consecrate and redeem forever, before and after Jubilee.

items.text: Baraisa: proof for field from father after his death
items.text_en: Baraisa: proof for field from father after his death
items.desc_en: A Baraisa teaches: from where do we know that one who buys a field from his father, consecrates it, then the father dies — it is before him like a field of inheritance? From the verse 'and if from a field of purchase which is not from a field of inheritance' — a field not fit for inheritance, this one is fit.

items.text: Rabbi Meir's alternative proof
items.text_en: Rabbi Meir's alternative proof
items.desc_en: Rabbi Meir argues: from where for one who buys from his father, the father dies, then he consecrates — that it is before him like a field of inheritance? From the verse 'and if from a field of purchase which is not from a field of inheritance' — a field that is not a field of inheritance, this one is not, so it is like a field of purchase.

items.text: Gemara: dispute over fruit ownership vs body ownership
items.text_en: Gemara: dispute over fruit ownership vs body ownership
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda/Shimon is about whether fruit ownership is like body ownership (Rabbi Meir) or not (Rabbi Yehuda/Shimon).

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: fruit ownership equals body ownership for all
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: fruit ownership equals body ownership for all
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak clarifies: for Rabbi Shimon and Yehuda, fruit ownership is like body ownership, contradicting the earlier suggestion. The real dispute is about the timing of consecration relative to the father's death.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer: field redeemed in second Jubilee goes to priests
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer: field redeemed in second Jubilee goes to priests
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer says: if a field is redeemed by owners in the second Jubilee, it goes to priests in the Jubilee. The Gemara notes this implies owners in second Jubilee are like others.

items.text: Alternative version: Rabbi Eliezer says priests don't enter until another redeems
items.text_en: Alternative version: Rabbi Eliezer says priests don't enter until another redeems
items.desc_en: An alternative version: Rabbi Eliezer says priests do not enter the field until another redeems it. The Gemara infers that owners in second Jubilee are like others.

items.text: Mishna: field consecrated after father's death vs before
items.text_en: Mishna: field consecrated after father's death vs before
items.desc_en: The Mishna repeats: one who buys a field from his father, consecrates it after the father dies — it is like a field of inheritance; if before — like a field of purchase. Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda/Shimon disagree.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda and Shimon: field is like inherited (again)
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda and Shimon: field is like inherited (again)
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda and Shimon reiterate: the field is like an inherited field because the verse excludes fields that are not eligible for inheritance.

items.text: Gemara: field of purchase never goes to priests in Jubilee (repeat)
items.text_en: Gemara: field of purchase never goes to priests in Jubilee (repeat)
items.desc_en: The Gemara repeats: a field of purchase never goes to priests in Jubilee, because no one consecrates what isn't theirs. Priests and Levites consecrate and redeem forever.

items.text: Baraisa: proof for field from father after his death (repeat)
items.text_en: Baraisa: proof for field from father after his death (repeat)
items.desc_en: The Baraisa repeats: from where do we know that one who buys a field from his father, consecrates it, then the father dies — it is before him like a field of inheritance? From the verse 'and if from a field of purchase which is not from a field of inheritance'.

items.text: Rabbi Meir's alternative proof (repeat)
items.text_en: Rabbi Meir's alternative proof (repeat)
items.desc_en: Rabbi Meir repeats his proof: from where for one who buys from his father, the father dies, then he consecrates — that it is before him like a field of inheritance? From the verse 'and if from a field of purchase which is not from a field of inheritance' — a field that is not a field of inheritance, this one is not, so it is like a field of purchase.

items.text: Gemara: dispute over fruit ownership vs body ownership (repeat)
items.text_en: Gemara: dispute over fruit ownership vs body ownership (repeat)
items.desc_en: The Gemara again suggests the dispute is about fruit ownership vs body ownership.

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: fruit ownership equals body ownership for all (repeat)
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: fruit ownership equals body ownership for all (repeat)
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak clarifies: for Rabbi Shimon and Yehuda, fruit ownership is like body ownership. The real dispute is about the timing of consecration relative to the father's death.

items.text: Gemara's explanation of the verse for a purchased field
items.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the verse for a purchased field
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the Torah uses the phrase 'from a field of his possession' (משדה אחזתו) for a purchased field, deducing that it excludes a field that is fit to be a hereditary field.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the verse uses the phrase 'from a field of his possession' (משדה אחזתו) for a purchased field, when it could have used simpler wording.
The Gemara answers that the phrase excludes a field that is fit to be a hereditary field (שדה אחוזה), i.e., a purchased field that could have been inherited.

items.text: Gemara's question about priests and Levites consecrating forever
items.text_en: Gemara's question about priests and Levites consecrating forever
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah states that priests and Levites consecrate forever, since even Israelites can consecrate. It resolves that the Mishnah's phrasing is due to the structure of the earlier clause about before and after the Jubilee.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah specifies that priests and Levites may consecrate fields forever, since even Israelites can do so.
The Gemara suggests that according to Shmuel, who holds that in the Jubilee year itself consecration does not take effect, the Mishnah teaches that priests and Levites may consecrate even then.
The Gemara objects that according to Rav, who holds that consecration does take effect in the Jubilee year, the Mishnah's specification of priests and Levites is still unnecessary.

The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah's phrasing is stylistic: because the first clause uses 'before the Jubilee and after the Jubilee', the latter clause mirrors it with 'whether after the Jubilee or before the Jubilee'.
The Gemara adds that because the first clause states 'they do not consecrate nor redeem', the latter clause states 'they consecrate and redeem' for stylistic parallelism.

items.text: Conclusion of the chapter
items.text_en: Conclusion of the chapter
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the chapter with the phrase 'We return to you, Ein Makdishin'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara marks the conclusion of the previous chapter with the formula 'we return to you, chapter 'Ein Makdishin'.

items.text: Mishnah: The owner opens redemption and a story about a consecrated field
items.text_en: Mishnah: The owner opens redemption and a story about a consecrated field
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that when one consecrates his field when the Jubilee is not in effect, the owner is given the first opportunity to redeem it, adding a fifth. It recounts a story where a man consecrated his field due to its poor quality and offered to redeem it with an issar, but Rabbi Yosei said he said 'with an egg' because consecrated property can be redeemed with money or its equivalent.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule: when one consecrates his field when the Jubilee is not in effect, the owner is told 'open you first' because owners add a fifth, while others do not.

The Mishnah recounts a story where a man consecrated his field due to its poor quality, offered to redeem it with an issar, but Rabbi Yosei corrected that he said 'with an egg' because consecrated property can be redeemed with money or its equivalent, and the man was told 'I have reached you,' losing an issar but keeping his field.

items.text: Gemara: Clarifying 'they say' and the reason for the owner's fifth
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarifying 'they say' and the reason for the owner's fifth
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's use of 'they say' when a baraita says 'they force', and resolves that initially they say, and if he does not listen they force. It then asks why the Mishnah states that the owner adds a fifth, suggesting it is because the field is dear to him and the mitzvah of redemption is with the owner.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's use of 'אומרין' (they say) when a baraita uses 'כופין' (they force), implying a contradiction.
The Gemara answers that 'אומרין' (they say) in the Mishnah actually means 'כופין' (they force), equating the two terms.
The Gemara offers an alternative resolution: initially they say (אומרין), and if he does not listen, they force (כופין).
The Gemara questions why the Mishnah specifies that the owner adds a fifth, suggesting a simpler reason.
The Gemara suggests that the owner redeems the field because it is dear to him (חביבה עליה טפי).
The Gemara adds that the mitzvah of redemption (מצות גאולה) is with the owner, so he is the primary redeemer.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah gives two reasons: the field is dear to the owner, and the mitzvah of redemption is with him, and additionally the owner adds a fifth.

items.text: Gemara: Dispute between Rabbi Yosei and the Rabbis about payment method
items.text_en: Gemara: Dispute between Rabbi Yosei and the Rabbis about payment method
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes the dispute in the story, initially suggesting it is about whether money-equivalent is like money, but concludes that all agree it is like money. The dispute is actually about redeeming with an item whose fifth is worth less than a perutah: the first Tanna allows an issar, while Rabbi Yosei allows even an egg. The Gemara notes that the anonymous ruling follows the Rabbis.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the dispute between Rabbi Yosei and the Rabbis is about whether money-equivalent (שווה כסף) is considered like money (ככסף).

The Gemara rejects the initial proposal, noting that it is established that all agree money-equivalent is like money, and instead redefines the dispute as about redeeming with an item whose fifth is worth less than a perutah (פרוטה).
The Gemara explains that the first Tanna (תנא קמא) permits redemption with an issar (איסר) whose fifth is worth a perutah, while Rabbi Yosei permits even an egg (ביצה) whose fifth is worth less.
The Gemara concludes that the anonymous ruling (סתמא) in the Mishnah follows the Rabbis (רבנן), who hold that the owner loses only an issar and retains his field.

items.text: Mishnah: Bidding process for redeeming a consecrated field
items.text_en: Mishnah: Bidding process for redeeming a consecrated field
items.desc_en: The Mishnah details the process when multiple people bid to redeem a consecrated field, with each bidder being penalized if they retract. It concludes that if the owner and another bid the same amount, the owner is preferred because he adds a fifth.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the bidding process for redeeming a consecrated field, where each bidder who retracts is penalized up to ten sela'im.
The Mishnah continues detailing the penalties for each retracting bidder, culminating in the sale of the field for its value to cover the ten-sela deficit.
The Mishnah concludes that when the owner and another bid the same amount, the owner is preferred because he adds a fifth (חומש).

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Owner's right to add a fifth and the rule of 'higga'tikha'
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Owner's right to add a fifth and the rule of 'higga'tikha'
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that when the owner bids, he adds a fifth to the highest bid. If a non-owner bids, the owner can preempt by paying the bid plus a fifth; otherwise, the bidder acquires the field and the owner says 'higga'tikha' (you have reached me).

items.text: Rav Chisda's distinction: simultaneous vs. sequential bidding
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's distinction: simultaneous vs. sequential bidding
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda explains that the Mishnah's rule applies only when the forty-year-old bidder is still present; if not, the payment is divided equally among the bidders.

items.text: Gemara's challenge: why not collect from the next age-group?
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge: why not collect from the next age-group?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that when a forty-year-old backs out, we seize his property up to ten selas. It asks why we don't collect from the fifty-year-old instead, and similarly for other age groups, and answers that the older bidder is not present.

items.text: Further challenge: the case of the ten-year-old
items.text_en: Further challenge: the case of the ten-year-old
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the Mishnah's ruling that when a ten-year-old backs out, we sell the field and collect the remainder from him. It argues that if no twenty-year-old is present, the Mishnah should say 'we collect from him' rather than 'from the ten-year-old's property,' implying a contradiction.

items.text: Rav Chisda's resolution: simultaneous vs. sequential
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's resolution: simultaneous vs. sequential
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between cases where all bidders back out at once (divide equally) and where they back out one after another (seize from each). A baraita supports this distinction.

items.text: Alternative formulation of the contradiction and resolution
items.text_en: Alternative formulation of the contradiction and resolution
