items.desc_en: Some raise a contradiction between the Mishnah (sell and collect from the ten-year-old) and a baraita (divide equally). Rav Chisda again resolves it by the same distinction: simultaneous vs. sequential.

items.text: Why the owner's fifth is preferred over a non-owner's addition to principal
items.text_en: Why the owner's fifth is preferred over a non-owner's addition to principal
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah says the owner's bid with a fifth takes precedence over a non-owner's bid with a larger principal. It answers that the fifth is profit for the Temple, so it is preferred; in a case where the fifth goes to the owner, the principal is more important.

items.text: Why the Mishnah omits the owner's dinar/ prutah
items.text_en: Why the Mishnah omits the owner's dinar/ prutah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah states that the owner pays thirty-one and a dinar, but earlier it said the owner pays thirty. Rava explains that the owner adds a prutah, and the Mishnah was imprecise.

items.text: Rav Chisda on adding a fifth when the field was appraised
items.text_en: Rav Chisda on adding a fifth when the field was appraised
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda says the Mishnah's rule that no fifth is added applies only when the field was not appraised by three; if it was, a fifth is added. A baraita with Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel is analyzed, concluding that Rav Chisda's view aligns with Beit Shammai's stringency.

items.text: Clarifying the owner's option and the role of the dinar
items.text_en: Clarifying the owner's option and the role of the dinar
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the owner's right to preempt is conditional on his willingness. Rav Sheshet clarifies that the Mishnah means the owner may initially pay the amount that reaches thirty-one and a dinar.

items.text: Opening scenario from previous Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening scenario from previous Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case where if someone says 'at twenty-one,' the owners have priority, and if not, the other party says 'I have reached you.' This serves as a lead-in to the new Mishnah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a scenario where if someone says 'at twenty-one,' the owners have priority, and if not, the other party says 'I have reached you.'

items.text: Mishnah: Limits on declaring cherem
items.text_en: Mishnah: Limits on declaring cherem
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a person may declare cherem from his flock, cattle, Canaanite slaves, and ancestral field, but if he declares all of them, they are not cherem, according to Rabbi Eliezer. Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya argues that if one cannot consecrate all property to God, certainly one should spare his own property.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a person may dedicate some of his flock, cattle, Canaanite slaves, and ancestral field, but not all; Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah disagree.
Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya argues that if one cannot consecrate all property to God, certainly one should spare his own property.

items.text: Gemara: Derivation of the law from verses
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation of the law from verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks the source for the Mishnah's law. It cites a baraita that derives from the verse 'from all that is his' that not all property can be consecrated, and from 'but' (אך) that if one does consecrate all, it is not valid. The Gemara explains why multiple exclusions are necessary, covering different categories like slaves, fields, and movable property.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source of the Mishnah's law that one cannot consecrate all his property.
A baraita is cited, deriving from the verse 'from all that is his' that not all property can be consecrated, and similarly for people, animals, and ancestral fields.
Rabbi Eliezer adds that the word 'אך' (but) teaches that if one does consecrate all, it is not valid.
Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya argues a fortiori: if one cannot consecrate all to Heaven, certainly one should spare his own property.
The Gemara explains why multiple exclusions are necessary: each exclusion covers a different category (slaves, fields, movable property) that would otherwise be subject to consecration.

items.text: Derivation regarding children and Hebrew slaves
items.text_en: Derivation regarding children and Hebrew slaves
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the verse mentions 'behemah' (animal). It explains that this teaches that only items one can sell can be consecrated, excluding Hebrew slaves and ancestral fields. However, a minor daughter can be sold, so the verse further specifies 'behemah' to mean only items that can be sold permanently, excluding a daughter who is released at majority.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Torah specifies 'behemah' (animal) in the verse about herem, and introduces a supporting baraita.
The baraita teaches that the word 'behemah' excludes items one cannot sell, such as Hebrew slaves and ancestral fields, from being consecrated as herem.
The Gemara objects that a minor daughter can be sold, so the baraita's exclusion seems incomplete.
The baraita resolves that 'behemah' further specifies only items that can be sold permanently, excluding a daughter who is released at majority.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya and Tanna Kamma
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya and Tanna Kamma
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's statement seems identical to the Tanna Kamma. It explains the difference lies in the enactment of Usha, which limits one from spending more than a fifth of his property. A story is told about someone who wanted to spend more and was stopped by Rabbi Yeshevav and Rabbi Akiva.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's statement appears identical to the Tanna Kamma — what is the difference between them?
The Gemara answers: The difference lies in the enactment of Usha (אושא) cited by Rabbi Ila, which limits one from spending more than a fifth (חומש) of his property.
A story is told about someone who wanted to spend more than a fifth, and his colleagues — identified as Rabbi Yeshevav and Rabbi Akiva — did not allow him.

items.text: Mishnah: What cannot be declared cherem
items.text_en: Mishnah: What cannot be declared cherem
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one cannot consecrate his son, daughter, Hebrew slaves, or acquired field, as they are not his. Rabbi Yehuda says priests and Levites cannot consecrate; Rabbi Shimon says priests cannot, but Levites can. Rabbi comments that Rabbi Yehuda's view applies to land, and Rabbi Shimon's to movable property.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that one who dedicates his son, daughter, Hebrew slaves, or purchased field — they are not dedicated, because a person cannot dedicate what is not his.
Rabbi Yehuda states that both priests and Levites may not dedicate their property.
Rabbi Shimon says priests may not dedicate because dedicated property is theirs, but Levites may dedicate because dedicated property is not theirs.

Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi rules that Rabbi Yehuda's view applies to land, citing the verse 'כי אחזת עולם היא להם' (for it is their perpetual possession), and Rabbi Shimon's view applies to movable property, since dedicated property is not theirs.

items.text: Gemara: Analysis of Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon's positions
items.text_en: Gemara: Analysis of Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon's positions
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Yehuda's view: priests cannot consecrate because cherem belongs to them, but Levites should be able to consecrate movable property. The Gemara answers that the verse equates movable property to land. For Rabbi Shimon, the Gemara explains that Levites can consecrate movable property, and clarifies that Rabbi's statement means Rabbi Shimon agrees with Rabbi Yehuda regarding land.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Yehuda's position: priests cannot dedicate because חרמים (dedicated property) belongs to them, but Levites should be able to dedicate movable property.
The Gemara answers that the verse equates movable property to land, so Levites cannot dedicate movable property either.
The Gemara questions Rabbi Shimon's position: priests cannot dedicate as stated, but why can Levites dedicate land?
The Gemara answers that when Rabbi Shimon says Levites may dedicate, he means only movable property.
The Gemara objects that from Rabbi's statement, it implies Rabbi Shimon also allows dedicating land.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi's statement means Rabbi Shimon agrees with Rabbi Yehuda regarding land, disagreeing only about movable property.

items.text: Rabbi Chiya bar Avin's ruling on movable cherem
items.text_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Avin's ruling on movable cherem
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Avin states that if one consecrates movable property, it is given to any priest he wishes, as derived from the verse 'Every cherem in Israel.'

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Avin rules that one who dedicates movables may give them to any priest he wishes, as derived from the verse 'כל חרם בישראל'.

items.text: Source for giving herem fields to the priest of that watch
items.text_en: Source for giving herem fields to the priest of that watch
items.desc_en: The Gemara establishes that a person who dedicates his fields as herem gives them to the priest of the watch serving at that time, derived from a verbal analogy with the law of a convert's stolen property. It then cites a baraita that clarifies the verse 'to God, to the priest' means the priest of that watch, and rejects the possibility that it could be any priest, using another verse to specify the priest of that watch.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara establishes that one who dedicates his fields as חרם (herem) gives them to the priest of the current watch, derived from a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) with the law of a convert's stolen property.
The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from the verse 'לַה׳ לַכֹּהֵן' (to God, to the priest) that God acquires the herem and gives it to the priest of that watch.
The Gemara raises an objection: perhaps the verse means any priest the owner chooses, not specifically the priest of that watch.
The Gemara resolves the objection by citing another verse that specifies the priest of that watch, rejecting the possibility of any priest.

items.text: Field that goes out to priests in Jubilee and the question of Shabbat
items.text_en: Field that goes out to priests in Jubilee and the question of Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a field that goes out to the priests in the Jubilee year is given to the watch that encounters the Jubilee. An inquiry is raised: if the Jubilee occurs on Shabbat, to which watch is it given? Rav Chiyya bar Ami in the name of Chulfana answers that it is given to the outgoing watch. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak cites a baraita that both Jubilee and the Sabbatical year release at the same time, but Jubilee at its beginning and the Sabbatical at its end.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a field which goes out to the priests in the Jubilee year is given to the priestly watch that encounters the Jubilee.
The Gemara raises an inquiry: if the Jubilee occurs on Shabbat, to which watch is the field given?

sub.text: Rav Chiyya bar Ami in the name of Chulfana
sub.text_en: Rav Chiyya bar Ami in the name of Chulfana
sub.desc_en: Rav Chiyya bar Ami in the name of Chulfana answers that the field is given to the outgoing watch.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak citing a baraita
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak citing a baraita
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak cites a baraita that both Jubilee and the Sabbatical year release at the same time, but Jubilee at its beginning and the Sabbatical at its end.

items.text: Challenge and resolution regarding Jubilee's timing
items.text_en: Challenge and resolution regarding Jubilee's timing
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the baraita's claim that Jubilee begins at the start of the year, since the verse says the shofar is sounded on Yom Kippur. It resolves that the baraita follows Rabbi Yishmael the son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, who holds that the Jubilee takes effect from Rosh Hashanah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the baraita's claim about Jubilee beginning at the start of the year is contradicted by the verse placing the shofar blast on Yom Kippur.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita follows Rabbi Yishmael the son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, who holds that Jubilee takes effect from Rosh Hashanah, not Yom Kippur.

items.text: Chizkiya bar Bilvati's question and the dispute about analogy
items.text_en: Chizkiya bar Bilvati's question and the dispute about analogy
items.desc_en: Chizkiya bar Bilvati heard this and went to ask Rabbi Avahu: why not draw an analogy from movable property to land? The Gemara responds that this is a dispute among Tannaim: some draw the analogy and some do not, and the ruling follows those who do not draw the analogy.

sub.text: Chizkiya bar Bilvati's question to Rabbi Avahu
sub.text_en: Chizkiya bar Bilvati's question to Rabbi Avahu
sub.desc_en: Chizkiya bar Bilvati asks Rabbi Avahu why we do not draw an analogy from movable property to land regarding the distribution of herem.
The Gemara responds that this is a dispute among Tannaim: some draw the analogy and some do not, and the ruling follows those who do not draw the analogy.

items.text: Mishnah: Laws of herem of priests and redemption
items.text_en: Mishnah: Laws of herem of priests and redemption
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that herem of priests has no redemption but is given to priests like terumah. Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira says that unspecified herem goes to the Temple treasury, while the Sages say it goes to priests. The Mishnah then discusses the laws of one who dedicates his consecrated animals as herem, distinguishing between a vow and a freewill offering, and the redemption of a firstborn animal.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that herem of priests has no redemption but is given to priests like terumah.
Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira states that unspecified herem goes to the Temple treasury, citing the verse 'כל חרם קדש קדשים הוא לה׳'.

The Sages argue that unspecified herem goes to priests, and explain that the verse 'כל חרם קדש קדשים הוא לה׳' teaches that herem applies to both קדשי קדשים (most holy things) and קדשים קלים (lesser holy things).

sub.text: Mishnah's rule on dedicating consecrated animals
sub.text_en: Mishnah's rule on dedicating consecrated animals
sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one who dedicates his consecrated animals as herem, if it was a vow, pays their full value.

sub.text: Mishnah's rule on freewill offering and firstborn
sub.text_en: Mishnah's rule on freewill offering and firstborn
sub.desc_en: The Mishnah explains that for a freewill offering, one pays the benefit value, and for a firstborn animal, one appraises how much a person would pay to give it to his grandson or nephew.

items.text: Opening baraita on herem
items.text_en: Opening baraita on herem
items.desc_en: The baraita states that herem of priests has no redemption and is given to the priest. While in the owner's possession, it is like consecrated property; once given to a priest, it becomes ordinary.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that priestly herem has no redemption and is given to the priest; while in the owner's possession it is like consecrated property, but once given to a priest it becomes ordinary.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira's view
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira interprets the verse 'like a field of herem' given his view that unspecified herem goes to the Temple treasury. It explains that he uses the verse to teach that a priest who consecrates his own herem field cannot keep it, and draws an analogy to a Israelite's ancestral field.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira interprets the verse 'like a field of herem' given his view that unspecified herem goes to the Temple treasury.
The Gemara answers that the verse teaches that a priest who consecrates his own herem field cannot keep it, citing a baraita that derives this from the verse.

The Gemara explains the analogy: just as an Israelite's ancestral field leaves his hand and is divided among priests, so too a priest's herem field leaves his hand and is divided among his fellow priests.
The Gemara notes that the Rabbis derive their law from the words 'herem' and 'the herem', but Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira does not derive anything from those words.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira's source for herem applying to all sacrifices
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira's source for herem applying to all sacrifices
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira derives that herem applies to both sacred and less sacred offerings from Rabbi Yishmael's teaching.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where does Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira derive that herem applies to both קדשי קדשים (most sacred offerings) and קדשים קלים (lesser sacred offerings)?
The Gemara answers: he holds like Rabbi Yishmael, who derives this from the verses 'תקדיש' and 'לא יקדיש'.

items.text: Rav's ruling and the contradiction with the Mishnah
items.text_en: Rav's ruling and the contradiction with the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rav rules like Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira, but the Gemara questions why he abandons the Rabbis and the Mishnah. It resolves that Rav had a different version of the Mishnah, and his statement means the law follows Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira according to that version.

sub.desc_en: Rav rules that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira regarding unspecified dedications.
The Gemara objects: would Rav abandon the majority opinion of the Rabbis to follow Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira?
The Gemara answers that the baraita teaches the opposite version of the dispute.
The Gemara objects further: would Rav abandon the Mishnah to follow a baraita?
The Gemara answers that Rav also teaches the Mishnah in the opposite version.
The Gemara questions why one would reverse the Mishnah based on the baraita rather than the reverse.
The Gemara answers that Rav had a tradition from his teachers that the Mishnah should be taught that way.
The Gemara objects: if the Mishnah is reversed, Rav should have said the law follows the Rabbis, not Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira.
The Gemara resolves: Rav means that according to the reversed version you taught, the law follows Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira.

items.text: Incident in Pumbedita and Rav Yehuda's ruling
items.text_en: Incident in Pumbedita and Rav Yehuda's ruling
items.desc_en: A man dedicated his property in Pumbedita; Rav Yehuda instructed him to redeem it with four zuz and throw them into the river, showing that unspecified herem goes to the Temple treasury. The Gemara explains that this follows Shmuel's view that redemption is valid even with a small amount, and that in the present time it is permitted initially.

sub.desc_en: A man dedicated his property in Pumbedita; Rav Yehuda instructed him to redeem it with four zuz and throw them into the river, showing that unspecified herem goes to the Temple treasury.
The Gemara asks in accordance with whose opinion Rav Yehuda ruled, and answers that it follows Shmuel, but questions whether Shmuel permits this לכתחילה (the ideal standard).

The Gemara explains that Shmuel's restriction applies only when the Temple stood, but nowadays it is permitted even לכתחילה (the ideal standard); the requirement for four zuz rather than a peruta is for publicity.

items.text: Ulla's opposing view
items.text_en: Ulla's opposing view
items.desc_en: Ulla states that if he were there, he would give all the property to the priests, indicating that unspecified herem goes to the priests.

sub.desc_en: Ulla states that if he were present at the incident in Pumbedita, he would give all the property to the priests, indicating that unspecified herem goes to the priests.

items.text: Baraita on laws dependent on the Jubilee
items.text_en: Baraita on laws dependent on the Jubilee
items.desc_en: A baraita lists laws that apply only when the Jubilee is in effect, including the Hebrew slave, the field of herem, walled cities, and the resident alien. The Gemara explains the scriptural basis and resolves a contradiction regarding the Pumbedita incident by distinguishing between land in Israel and movables outside Israel.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that the Hebrew slave (עבד עברי) applies only when the Jubilee is in effect, citing the verse 'עַד שְׁנַת הַיּוֹבֵל יַעֲבֹד עִמָּךְ'.
The baraita continues, listing that the field of herem (שדה החרם) and walled cities (בתי ערי חומה) also apply only when the Jubilee is in effect, each with a scriptural proof.
Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai adds that the field of herem (שדה חרמין) applies only when the Jubilee is in effect, citing the verse 'וְהָיָה הַשָּׂדֶה בְּצֵאתוֹ בַיּוֹבֵל קֹדֶשׁ לַה' כִּשְׂדֵה הַחֵרֶם'.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar adds that the resident alien (גר תושב) applies only when the Jubilee is in effect.
Rav Bivi explains the scriptural basis for the resident alien's dependence on the Jubilee, using a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'טוֹב' (good) appearing in two verses.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction with the Pumbedita incident by distinguishing between land (מקרקעי) in Israel and movables (מטלטלי) outside Israel, ruling that land outside Israel is treated like movables in Israel.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on Rabbi Yishmael's teaching
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on Rabbi Yishmael's teaching
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents Rabbi Yishmael's resolution of contradictory verses about consecrating firstborn animals: one may consecrate it as a dedication of value but not as an altar sacrifice. The Gemara explains that the Rabbis use the verses for a negative commandment and the obligation to consecrate, while Rabbi Yishmael holds that the firstborn is inherently sacred.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael states the contradiction between the verse 'תַּקְדִּישׁ' (you shall consecrate) and the verse 'לֹא יַקְדִּישׁ' (he shall not consecrate) regarding a firstborn animal.
Rabbi Yishmael resolves the contradiction: one may consecrate the firstborn as a dedication of value (הקדש עילוי) but not as an altar sacrifice (הקדש מזבח).
The Gemara explains that the Rabbis interpret the verse 'לֹא יַקְדִּישׁ' as a negative commandment (לאו) and the verse 'תַּקְדִּישׁ' as the obligation to consecrate the firstborn, citing a baraita.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yishmael holds the firstborn is inherently sacred from the womb (קדושתו מרחם), so there is no need to consecrate it.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who sells a field during the Jubilee period may not redeem it for less than two years, based on the verse 'according to the number of years of crops he shall sell to you'. It adds that a year of blight, mildew, or the Sabbatical year does not count toward the two years, but if the buyer left it fallow or uncultivated, it does count. Rabbi Eliezer says that if the field was sold before Rosh Hashanah and was full of produce, the buyer may eat three harvests in two years.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the rule that one who sells a field during the Jubilee period may not redeem it for less than two years, citing the verse 'according to the number of years of crops he shall sell to you'.
The Mishnah states that a year of blight, mildew, or the Sabbatical year does not count toward the two years, but if the buyer left it fallow or uncultivated, it does count.
Rabbi Eliezer adds that if the field was sold before Rosh Hashanah and was full of produce, the buyer may eat three harvests in two years.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's language
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's language
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah says 'he is not permitted to redeem' rather than 'he does not redeem', implying that there is a prohibition involved. It explains that even the seller is subject to a positive commandment, and even the buyer is also subject to a positive commandment, as the verse requires 'years you shall purchase'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah says 'אֵינוֹ מוּתָּר לִגְאוֹל' (not permitted to redeem) rather than 'אֵינוֹ גּוֹאֵל' (he does not redeem), implying that there is a prohibition involved, even if one merely offers to pay the money.

The Gemara explains that not only the seller stands in violation of a positive commandment (based on the verse 'בְּמִסְפַּר שְׁנֵי תְבוּאֹת יִמְכׇּר לָךְ'), but even the buyer stands in violation, because the verse requires 'שָׁנִים תִּקְנֶה' (by years you shall acquire), which is not fulfilled.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel regarding sale in the Jubilee year itself
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel regarding sale in the Jubilee year itself
items.desc_en: An explicit dispute is cited: Rav says the sale is valid but the field returns at the Jubilee, while Shmuel says it is not sold at all. Shmuel's reasoning is a kal vachomer: if a field already sold goes out at the Jubilee, then one not yet sold should certainly not be sold. The Gemara questions Rav's rejection of this kal vachomer by citing a similar kal vachomer regarding selling one's daughter as a maidservant when she is a na'arah, and resolves that in that case she cannot be resold, whereas here the field can be resold after the Jubilee.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports a dispute: Rav says the sale is valid but the field reverts at the Jubilee, while Shmuel says it is not sold at all, based on a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) from a field already sold that goes out at the Jubilee.

The Gemara objects that Rav does not accept such a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument), citing a baraita that uses the same logic to forbid selling one's daughter as a maidservant when she is a נערה (adolescent).
The Gemara distinguishes: in the daughter case, she cannot be sold again after the Jubilee, but here the field can be sold again after the Jubilee, so Rav's position is consistent.
The Gemara resolves the objection: in the daughter case she cannot be resold, but here the field can be resold after the Jubilee, so the kal vachomer does not apply.

items.text: Challenge from a baraita and Rav's response
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraita and Rav's response
items.desc_en: A baraita is brought that teaches that one may sell close to the Jubilee, but in the Jubilee year itself one may not sell, and if one sold, it is not sold. Rav explains that 'not sold' means not sold for the count of years of crops, but it is sold and returns at the Jubilee. The Gemara objects that if it is sold, it should remain in the buyer's possession until after the Jubilee, and then he could eat two years of crops and return it, but a baraita says that if he ate one year before the Jubilee, he completes another year after the Jubilee. The Gemara resolves that in that case he entered for eating, but here he did not enter for eating.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited that derives from the verse 'אַחַר הַיּוֹבֵל שָׁנִים תִּקְנֶה' that one may sell close to the Jubilee, but in the Jubilee year itself one may not sell, and if one did sell, it is not sold.
Rav explains that the baraita means it is not sold for the purpose of counting years of produce, but it is sold and reverts at the Jubilee.

The Gemara objects: if the sale is valid, let it remain in the buyer's possession until after the Jubilee, and then let him eat two years of produce and return it, citing a baraita that if he ate one year before the Jubilee, they complete another year after the Jubilee.

The Gemara distinguishes: in the baraita, the buyer entered for consumption (he intended to eat the produce), but here the buyer did not enter for consumption (since the sale was in the Jubilee year itself, he knew the field would revert immediately).

items.text: Rav Anan's report and Rav Yosef's resolution
items.text_en: Rav Anan's report and Rav Yosef's resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Anan reports that he heard two rulings from Shmuel: one about the field in the Jubilee year, and another that a slave sold to gentiles or outside the land goes free. He was unsure which ruling holds that the sale is reversible and which that it is not. Rav Yosef resolves the doubt by citing a baraita that a slave sold outside the land goes free and requires a second bill of manumission from the second master, indicating that the sale is irreversible, so Shmuel's ruling about the field must be that it is not sold and the money is returned.

sub.desc_en: Rav Anan reports that he heard two rulings from Mar Shmuel: one is the previous ruling about the field, and the other is that one who sells his slave to gentiles or outside the land goes free.
Rav Anan notes that one ruling holds that the sale is reversible (the field case) and the other that it is not reversible (the slave case), but he does not know which is which.

Rav Yosef resolves the doubt by citing a baraita about selling a slave outside the land: the slave goes free and needs a second get shichrur (bill of manumission), implying the sale is not reversible, so Shmuel's ruling here is that the field is not sold and the money is returned.

items.text: Rav and Shmuel's dispute about the sale of a field to a non-Jew
items.text_en: Rav and Shmuel's dispute about the sale of a field to a non-Jew
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rav's position that the sale is void and money returns, suggesting it might be a gift like in the case of one who betroths his sister. Abaye asks why the buyer is penalized rather than the seller, and Rav Yosef explains with a metaphor that the one who creates the prohibition is penalized.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Shmuel's position that the sale is void and money returns, suggesting it might be a gift like in the case of one who betroths his sister.
Abaye objects to Rav Yosef, asking why the buyer is penalized rather than the seller.
Rav Yosef answers with a metaphor that the one who creates the prohibition (the buyer) is penalized, not the seller.

items.text: Clarification of the Mishnah's case of a blighted year
items.text_en: Clarification of the Mishnah's case of a blighted year
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah mentions a blighted year when even if the field was left fallow it counts as a year of produce; it explains that the case of plowing is necessary, lest one think the owner could pay the value and redeem immediately.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah needs to mention a blighted year, since even if the field was left fallow it counts as a year of produce, so plowing should certainly count.
The Gemara answers that the case of plowing is necessary, lest one think the owner could pay the value and redeem immediately; the Mishnah teaches that this is not allowed.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's teaching on selling a field full of produce before Rosh Hashanah
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's teaching on selling a field full of produce before Rosh Hashanah
items.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Eliezer who derives from the verse that if one sells a field full of produce before Rosh Hashanah, the buyer cannot demand the same amount of produce at redemption; sometimes one eats three harvests in two years.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer opens with the rule that if one sells a field full of produce before Rosh Hashanah, the buyer cannot demand the same amount of produce at redemption.

Rabbi Eliezer cites the verse 'במספר שני תבואות ימכר לך' (by the number of harvests it shall be sold to you) to prove that sometimes one eats three harvests in two years, so the buyer cannot demand equal produce.

items.text: Mishnah: Laws of redemption when the field was resold
items.text_en: Mishnah: Laws of redemption when the field was resold
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that if the field was sold to a first buyer for 100 and resold for 200, the original owner redeems only from the first buyer; if sold for 200 and resold for 100, he redeems from the last buyer. Additional restrictions prohibit selling far and redeeming near, selling bad and redeeming good, borrowing to redeem, or redeeming in halves; these are stricter for a commoner than for the Temple.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the first case: if the field was sold to the first buyer for 100 and resold for 200, the original owner redeems only from the first buyer, citing the verse 'אֲשֶׁר מָכַר לוֹ' (to whom he sold it).
The Mishnah states the second case: if sold for 200 and resold for 100, the original owner redeems only from the last buyer, citing the verse 'לָאִישׁ אֲשֶׁר בְּתוֹכוֹ' (the man who is within it).

The Mishnah lists additional restrictions: one may not sell far and redeem near, sell bad and redeem good, borrow to redeem, or redeem in halves; these are stricter for a commoner than for the Temple.

items.text: Gemara: Derivation of the Mishnah's laws from verses
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation of the Mishnah's laws from verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that derives the Mishnah's first case from the verse 'to the man who sold it to him', and the second case from 'to the man who is within it'. Rabbi Dostai ben Yehuda adds cases where the field appreciated or depreciated in value, deriving that only the surplus in hand or in the land is considered.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites the verse 'לָאִישׁ אֲשֶׁר מָכַר לוֹ' to derive that when the first sale was at a lower price, the redeemer accounts only with the first buyer.
The baraita cites the verse 'לָאִישׁ אֲשֶׁר בְּתוֹכוֹ' to derive that when the first sale was at a higher price, the redeemer accounts only with the last buyer.
Rabbi Dostai ben Yehuda derives from 'וְהֵשִׁיב אֶת הָעוֹדֵף' that when the field appreciated, the redeemer accounts only for the original sale price, not the appreciated value.
Rabbi Dostai ben Yehuda derives from the same verse that when the field depreciated, the redeemer accounts only for the current lower value, not the original purchase price.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi and Rabbi Dostai and the derivation from Hebrew slave
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi and Rabbi Dostai and the derivation from Hebrew slave
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two opinions, suggesting cases of price fluctuation. It questions whether the lenient interpretation is correct, and proves from a gezerah shavah of 'redemption' from a Hebrew slave sold to a gentile that the calculation is always to the owner's benefit, extending the principle to a Hebrew slave sold to an Israelite.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the opinions of Rabbi and Rabbi Dostai ben Yehuda, suggesting cases of price fluctuation (appreciation and depreciation).
The Gemara objects: how do we know the calculation is to the owner's benefit (lenient interpretation); perhaps it is to his detriment (stringent interpretation)?
The Gemara rejects the objection, asserting that it cannot be stringent because a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) of 'גאולה' (redemption) is derived from a Hebrew slave.

The Gemara cites a baraita: for a Hebrew slave sold to a gentile who appreciated in value, the calculation is only from the original purchase price, as derived from the verse 'מכסף מקנתו' (from the money of his purchase).
The baraita continues: if the slave depreciated, the calculation is only from the current lower value, as derived from the verse 'כפי שניו' (according to his years).

The Gemara concludes that the principle of calculating to the owner's benefit applies to a Hebrew slave sold to a gentile, and extends it to a Hebrew slave sold to an Israelite via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) of 'שכיר' (hireling).

items.text: Abaye's statement (beginning of next sugya)
items.text_en: Abaye's statement (beginning of next sugya)
items.desc_en: Abaye begins a new statement, likely continuing the discussion, but the text cuts off.

sub.desc_en: Abaye begins a new statement, likely continuing the discussion, but the text cuts off.

items.text: Opening challenge: leniency or stringency for the Hebrew slave?
items.text_en: Opening challenge: leniency or stringency for the Hebrew slave?
items.desc_en: A rabbi challenges Abaye: the statement 'I am like ben Azzai in the markets of Tiberias' could be interpreted either leniently or stringently. He asks why we assume the lenient interpretation.

sub.desc_en: A rabbi challenges Abaye: the statement 'I am like ben Azzai in the markets of Tiberias' could be interpreted either leniently or stringently; why assume the lenient interpretation?

items.text: First answer: leniency from the Torah's kindness
items.text_en: First answer: leniency from the Torah's kindness
items.desc_en: Abaye argues that the lenient interpretation is correct because the Torah is lenient with the Hebrew slave, as derived from the verse 'for it is good for him with you' which requires the master to provide equal food and lodging.

sub.desc_en: Abaye argues that the lenient interpretation is correct because the Torah is lenient with the Hebrew slave, as derived from the verse 'for it is good for him with you' which requires the master to provide equal food and lodging.

items.text: Counter-argument: stringency from the severity of Sabbatical year
items.text_en: Counter-argument: stringency from the severity of Sabbatical year
items.desc_en: The Gemara counters that we should be stringent due to Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's teaching about the harsh consequences of violating the Sabbatical year. It then elaborates on the progression of punishments: from dealing in Sabbatical produce to selling movable property, fields, houses, borrowing with interest, selling one's daughter, and finally selling oneself into slavery to a gentile or idolatry.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that we should be stringent based on Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's teaching about the harshness of the Sabbatical year's dust (אבקה).
Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina teaches that dealing in Sabbatical produce leads to selling movable property, citing verses about the Jubilee year.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's teaching continued
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's teaching continued
sub.desc_en: If one does not feel the loss, he eventually sells his fields, as derived from the verse about a brother who becomes poor.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's teaching continued
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's teaching continued
sub.desc_en: If it does not come to his attention, he sells his house; the Gemara explains the difference in phrasing using Rav Huna's principle that a repeated sin becomes permitted to him.
The Gemara objects to Rav Huna's statement that a repeated sin is 'permitted,' and corrects it to 'becomes like permitted to him.'

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's teaching continued
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's teaching continued
sub.desc_en: If it does not come to his attention, he eventually borrows with interest, citing the verse prohibiting interest.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's teaching continued
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's teaching continued
sub.desc_en: If it does not come to his attention, he sells his daughter, with an explanation that selling a daughter is preferable to borrowing with interest because the debt grows.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's teaching continued
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's teaching continued
sub.desc_en: If it does not come to his attention, he sells himself, first to a Jew, then to a ger (גר), and then to a ger toshav (גר תושב).

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's teaching concluded
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's teaching concluded
sub.desc_en: The teaching concludes that 'family of the ger' refers to a gentile, and 'or to the root of the family of the ger' refers to one who is sold and becomes a servant to idolatry itself.

items.text: Rejection of stringency: redemption even for idolatry
items.text_en: Rejection of stringency: redemption even for idolatry
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the stringency argument by citing a baraita from the school of Rabbi Yishmael: even one who sells himself to idolatry is redeemed in the Jubilee, as the verse says 'an eternal redemption shall be his'. The Gemara then questions whether this leniency applies only to prevent him from sinking among the nations, but for his redemption price we should be stringent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the stringency argument by citing a baraita from the school of Rabbi Yishmael: even one who sells himself to idolatry is redeemed in the Jubilee, as the verse says 'an eternal redemption shall be his'.
The Gemara questions whether this leniency applies only to prevent him from sinking among the nations, but for his redemption price we should be stringent.

items.text: Resolution: Rav Nachman's interpretation of verses
items.text_en: Resolution: Rav Nachman's interpretation of verses
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves the issue by interpreting the verses 'if many years remain' and 'if few years remain' to mean that redemption is calculated based on the slave's financial situation: if his money increased, he is redeemed according to the purchase price; if his money decreased, according to the years remaining. Rav Yosef praises this as a Sinai-like teaching.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak cites the two verses about redemption of a Hebrew slave, one speaking of many years and one of few years.
The Gemara questions the redundancy of the two verses, since years are inherently many or few.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves that the verses refer to the slave's financial situation: if his money increased, redemption is based on the purchase price; if decreased, on the remaining years.
The Gemara objects that the verses could be interpreted literally: if two years remain, pay four; if four remain, pay two.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves the objection by noting the extra word 'בשנים' (in the years), which teaches that the calculation depends on the slave's financial gain or loss during the years.
Rav Yosef praises Rav Nachman's interpretation as being as authoritative as a Sinai tradition.

items.text: Law of not selling at a distance: derivation from verses
items.text_en: Law of not selling at a distance: derivation from verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives the law that one may not sell a field far away and redeem a nearby one, or sell a poor field and redeem a good one, from the verse 'and his hand reaches and finds'. Rava resolves a contradiction between two interpretations of 'found' by context: in the context of redemption it means present finding, while in the context of damages it means something that existed originally.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the law that one may not sell a distant field and redeem a nearby one, and cites a baraita that derives it from the verse 'והשיגה ידו' (and his hand reaches) and 'ומצא' (and finds).
The Gemara objects that the word 'מצא' (found) in the baraita seems to mean present finding, but a contradictory baraita from Rabbi Eliezer shows it means something that existed originally.

Rava resolves the contradiction by context: in the redemption context, 'מצא' parallels 'השיגה ידו' (present reaching), meaning present finding; in the damages context, it parallels 'יער' (forest), meaning something that existed originally.

items.text: Law of consecrated property: borrowing and redeeming in halves
items.text_en: Law of consecrated property: borrowing and redeeming in halves
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the verse 'and if he redeems' that one may borrow and redeem consecrated property, and may redeem in halves. Rabbi Shimon explains the rationale: since the seller of an ancestral field has enhanced power (it returns in Jubilee), his power is diminished (cannot borrow or redeem in halves); but the one who consecrates an ancestral field, whose power is diminished (it goes to priests in Jubilee), has enhanced power to borrow and redeem in halves.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where are these matters (that one may borrow and redeem consecrated property, and redeem in halves) derived?
The Sages taught a baraita: From the verse 'וְאִם גָּאֹל יִגְאַל' (and if he redeems) we learn that one may borrow and redeem, and redeem in halves.
Rabbi Shimon explains the rationale: since the seller of an ancestral field has enhanced power (it returns in Jubilee), his power is diminished (cannot borrow or redeem in halves).
Rabbi Shimon concludes: but the one who consecrates an ancestral field, whose power is diminished (it goes to priests in Jubilee), has enhanced power to borrow and redeem in halves.

items.text: Baraita dispute on borrowing and redeeming in halves
items.text_en: Baraita dispute on borrowing and redeeming in halves
items.desc_en: Two conflicting baraitot are presented: one permits borrowing and redeeming in halves, the other forbids. The Gemara resolves the contradiction by attributing the first to the Rabbis and the second to Rabbi Shimon.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited permitting borrowing and redeeming in halves.
A second baraita is cited forbidding borrowing and redeeming in halves.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by attributing the first baraita to the Rabbis and the second to Rabbi Shimon.

items.text: Mishnah: Laws of redeeming a house in a walled city
items.text_en: Mishnah: Laws of redeeming a house in a walled city
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who sells a house in a walled city may redeem it immediately or within twelve months; the transaction resembles interest but is permitted. If the seller dies, his son may redeem; if the buyer dies, redemption is from his son. The year is counted from the sale, and a leap month is included. Rabbi adds that a full year plus its intercalation is given. If not redeemed by the end of twelve months, the house is permanently acquired by the buyer, whether purchased or received as a gift.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the law that one who sells a house in a walled city may redeem it immediately or within twelve months, and this resembles interest but is permitted.
The Mishnah continues with the rules of inheritance: if the seller dies, his son may redeem; if the buyer dies, redemption is from his son; the year is counted from the sale, as per the verse.

The Mishnah concludes that the term 'תְּמִימָה' (complete) includes the intercalated month; Rabbi adds a full year plus its intercalation; if not redeemed by twelve months, the house is permanently acquired by the buyer, whether purchased or received as a gift.

items.text: Gemara: Dispute between Rabbi and Rabbis on 'days' and 'complete year'
items.text_en: Gemara: Dispute between Rabbi and Rabbis on 'days' and 'complete year'
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's counting from the sale date (not from the beginning of the year) aligns with the Rabbis, not Rabbi, who derives from 'days' that at least two days are required. The Rabbis use 'days' for a day-to-day calculation, while Rabbi derives day-to-day from 'until the completion of the year of its sale'. The Rabbis use that verse to indicate the seller's year, not the world's year. Rabbi derives 'from time to time' from 'complete', while the Rabbis use 'complete' for the intercalation. The Gemara concludes that Rabbi also derives day-to-day and from time to time from 'until the completion of the year of its sale'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that the Mishnah does not align with Rabbi, citing a baraita where Rabbi says 'days' means at least two days.
The Gemara asks what the Rabbis do with the word 'days', and answers that they require it for a day-to-day calculation.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi derives the day-to-day requirement from the verse 'until the completion of the year of its sale'.
The Gemara explains that the Rabbis use that verse to indicate the seller's own year, not the world's calendar year.

The Gemara explains that the Rabbis require 'days' for a from-time-to-time calculation, since from 'until the completion of the year of its sale' one might think only day-to-day, not from time to time.
The Gemara asks how Rabbi derives the from-time-to-time requirement, and answers that he derives it from the word 'complete' (תְּמִימָה).
The Gemara asks what the Rabbis do with 'complete', and answers that they require it for the intercalation of the year.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi also needs 'complete' for the intercalation, so how can he derive from-time-to-time from it?
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi derives both day-to-day and from-time-to-time from the verse 'until the completion of the year of its sale', leaving 'complete' for the intercalation.

items.text: Gemara: Dispute on whether the transaction is actual interest or merely resembles it
items.text_en: Gemara: Dispute on whether the transaction is actual interest or merely resembles it
items.desc_en: A baraita states that the transaction is outright interest, but the Torah permitted it. Rabbi Yochanan resolves the contradiction with the Mishnah by attributing the Mishnah to the Rabbis and the baraita to Rabbi Yehuda. A supporting baraita discusses a case where a debtor sells his field to a creditor; if the seller eats the produce it is permitted, but if the buyer eats it, it is forbidden. Rabbi Yehuda permits even when the buyer eats the produce, citing a precedent with Baytos ben Zonin. The Gemara clarifies the dispute: the Tanna Kamma forbids 'one side of interest', while Rabbi Yehuda permits it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that contradicts the Mishnah: the baraita calls the transaction outright interest (ריבית גמורה) permitted only by the Torah, while the Mishnah calls it merely resembling interest.
Rabbi Yochanan resolves the contradiction by attributing the Mishnah to the Rabbis and the baraita to Rabbi Yehuda.
A baraita is cited: when a debtor sells his field to a creditor, if the seller eats the produce it is permitted, but if the buyer eats it, it is forbidden (Tanna Kamma's view).
Rabbi Yehuda permits even when the buyer eats the produce, citing a precedent with Baytos ben Zonin.
The Sages object to Rabbi Yehuda's precedent, arguing that in the case of Baytos ben Zonin, the seller ate the produce, not the buyer.
The Gemara clarifies the dispute: the Tanna Kamma forbids 'one side of interest' (צד אחד בריבית), while Rabbi Yehuda permits it.

items.text: Rava's distinction regarding usury
items.text_en: Rava's distinction regarding usury
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the dispute between the earlier authorities is not about whether a side-pledge (צד אחד) in usury is prohibited, but about whether usury with intent to return is prohibited. One holds it is prohibited, the other permits it.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the dispute by stating that all agree a side-pledge (צד אחד) in usury is prohibited, and the disagreement is only about usury with intent to return (רבית על מנת להחזיר).

items.text: Redemption by the seller's son and buyer's son
items.text_en: Redemption by the seller's son and buyer's son
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains two seemingly obvious cases: if the seller dies, his son may redeem the house, and if the buyer dies, his son may redeem it immediately. The verses teach that redemption applies in all cases.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the mishna needs to state that if the seller dies his son may redeem the house, as this seems obvious.
The Gemara explains that the verse 'וְהָיְתָה גְּאֻלָּתוֹ' (and he shall have the right of redemption) teaches that redemption applies in any case, even by the seller's son.
The Gemara asks why the mishna needs to state that if the buyer dies the seller may redeem from the buyer's son, as this too seems obvious.
The Gemara explains that the verse 'וְהָיְתָה גְּאֻלָּתוֹ' (and he shall have the right of redemption) teaches that redemption applies in any case, even from the buyer's son.

items.text: Counting the year from the sale
items.text_en: Counting the year from the sale
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the year is counted from the time of sale, not from the beginning of the year. The verse 'עַד מְלֹאת לוֹ שָׁנָה תְמִימָה' indicates the year is for the first owner.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches that the year is counted from the time of the first sale, as derived from the verse 'עַד מְלֹאת לוֹ שָׁנָה תְמִימָה'.

items.text: Dispute over to whom the house is forfeited
items.text_en: Dispute over to whom the house is forfeited
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yochanan dispute whether the house is forfeited to the first buyer or the second buyer. Rabbi Abba bar Memel explains Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning: the first seller sold all rights that would come to him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks to whom the house is forfeited.
Rabbi Elazar rules that the house is forfeited to the first buyer.
Rabbi Yochanan rules that the house is forfeited to the second buyer.
The Gemara questions Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning, since the year is counted for the first buyer.
Rabbi Abba bar Memel explains that the first seller sold the second buyer all rights that would come to him, including the right of forfeiture.

items.text: Two houses sold in Adar I and Adar II
items.text_en: Two houses sold in Adar I and Adar II
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Memel discusses a case where two houses were sold, one on the 15th of Adar I and one on the 1st of Adar II. The year for the second house ends on the 1st of Adar of the next year, while the first house's year ends on the 15th. Ravina objects that the second buyer could argue he is earlier, but the response is that the first buyer can say the second descended to the leap month.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Memel presents a case of two walled-city houses sold on different dates in Adar I and Adar II, ruling that each buyer's redemption year ends on the anniversary of his purchase.
Ravina objects that the second buyer could argue he is earlier because he can light a fire (i.e., use the house) before the first buyer's year ends.
The response is that the first buyer can say the second buyer descended into the leap month (Adar II), so his year is shorter.

sub.text: Rabbi Abba bar Memel's second case
sub.text_en: Rabbi Abba bar Memel's second case
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Memel presents a parallel case of two lambs born on the same dates, applying the same rule for their one-year age for tithe purposes.
Ravina objects similarly that the second lamb's owner could claim he eats greens (i.e., benefits from the lamb) before the first.
The response is that the first owner can say the second descended into the leap month while he did not, so the second's year ends earlier.

items.text: Why repeat the case of two lambs?
items.text_en: Why repeat the case of two lambs?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the baraita repeats the same principle for lambs. It explains that one might think the verse 'תְּמִימָה' applies only to houses, but not to animals, so the repetition teaches that 'year' is derived from each other.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the baraita repeats the case of two lambs, since it seems identical to the previous case of two houses.

The Gemara explains that the repetition is necessary because one might think the verse 'תְּמִימָה' (complete) applies only to houses, not to animals, so the baraita teaches that the word 'year' is derived from each other through a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy).

items.text: Dispute over 'complete year'
items.text_en: Dispute over 'complete year'
items.desc_en: Rabbi and the Sages dispute the meaning of 'complete year'. Rabbi says it means 365 days like the solar year, while the Sages say it means 12 months from day to day, and if the year is intercalated, it is intercalated for him.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah is cited, introducing the dispute about the meaning of 'complete year'.
Rabbi states that the year includes its intercalation, meaning 365 days like the solar year.
A baraita is cited, elaborating Rabbi's position that a complete year is 365 days like the solar year.
The Sages state that a complete year is twelve months from day to day, and if the year is intercalated, it is intercalated for him.

items.text: The word 'לַצְּמִיתוּת' includes gifts
items.text_en: The word 'לַצְּמִיתוּת' includes gifts
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that 'לַצְּמִיתוּת' means permanently, and another interpretation includes gifts. The Gemara questions whether this follows Rabbi Meir, who says a gift is not like a sale. Rav Papa defends it, but the Sages object from the Jubilee verse, concluding it is not like Rabbi Meir.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that 'לַצְּמִיתוּת' means permanently, and another interpretation includes gifts, derived from the root 'צְמִית'.
The Sages ask Rav Papa whose opinion the baraita follows, noting it cannot be Rabbi Meir, who holds that a gift is not like a sale.
Rav Papa answers that even Rabbi Meir could agree, because the Torah explicitly uses 'לַצְּמִיתוּת' to include gifts.

sub.text: Sages to Rav Papa (or Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua)
sub.text_en: Sages to Rav Papa (or Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua)
sub.desc_en: The Sages object, citing that regarding Jubilee, where 'תָּשׁוּבוּ' includes gifts, Rabbi Meir does not include them, so this baraita is certainly not Rabbi Meir.

items.text: Consecrated house in a walled city
items.text_en: Consecrated house in a walled city
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one who consecrates a house in a walled city may redeem it forever. If another redeemed it from the Temple and the year passed, it is forfeited to the redeemer. Shmuel derives this from the verse 'לַקּוֹנֶה אוֹתוֹ', even from the Temple. The Temple itself cannot acquire it permanently because it has no descendants.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that one who consecrates a house in a walled city may redeem it forever, but if another redeemed it from the Temple and the year passed without redemption, it is forfeited to the redeemer.
Shmuel derives the rule from the verse 'לַקּוֹנֶה אוֹתוֹ' (to the one who buys it), teaching that even the Temple, as a purchaser from the original owner, can acquire the house permanently.
The gemara asks why the Temple itself should not acquire the house permanently, since it is the direct purchaser from the original owner.
The gemara answers that the verse 'לְדוֹרוֹתָיו' (to his generations) excludes the Temple, which has no descendants, so it cannot acquire the house permanently.

items.text: Why 'לֹא יֵצֵא בַּיּוֹבֵל'?
items.text_en: Why 'לֹא יֵצֵא בַּיּוֹבֵל'?
items.desc_en: Rav Safra explains that the verse 'לֹא יֵצֵא בַּיּוֹבֵל' is needed for a case where the Jubilee occurs within the year of sale. One might think it goes out in Jubilee, so the verse teaches it does not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the verse 'לֹא יֵצֵא בַּיּוֹבֵל' (it shall not go out in the Jubilee) is needed.
Rav Safra answers that the verse is needed for a case where the Jubilee occurs within the year of sale, teaching that it does not go out in the Jubilee.

items.text: Hillel's enactment to prevent hiding
items.text_en: Hillel's enactment to prevent hiding
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes that originally the seller would hide on the 12th month to cause forfeiture. Hillel enacted that the buyer deposits money in the chamber, breaks in, and the seller can take his money anytime. Rava derives from this that a conditional get given on condition that the wife gives 200 zuz is valid if she gives willingly, but not if forced.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah describes Hillel's enactment: originally the seller would hide on the 12th month to cause forfeiture, so Hillel instituted that the buyer deposits money in the chamber, breaks in, and the seller can take his money anytime.
Rava derives from Hillel's enactment that a conditional get given on condition that the wife gives 200 zuz is valid if she gives willingly, but not if forced.

items.text: Gemara's inference from Hillel's enactment
items.text_en: Gemara's inference from Hillel's enactment
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from Hillel's need to enact that a gift given under coercion is valid, implying that generally a coerced gift is not valid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from Hillel's enactment that a coerced gift is generally invalid, since Hillel needed to enact that a coerced gift is valid.

items.text: Rav Pappa's challenge to the inference
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's challenge to the inference
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa (or Rav Ashi) challenges the inference: perhaps Hillel's enactment was needed only for a gift given not in the recipient's presence, but in his presence, whether willingly or under coercion, it is a valid gift.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa (or Rav Ashi) objects that Hillel's enactment may only be needed for a gift given not in the recipient's presence, but in the recipient's presence, even a coerced gift is valid.

items.text: Rava's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rava's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rava offers a different version: Hillel's enactment was about a get given on condition that the wife give the husband 200 zuz, and if she gives it in his presence, whether willingly or under coercion, it is a valid gift; the enactment was needed only for giving not in his presence.

sub.desc_en: Rava explains that Hillel's enactment was specifically for a gift given not in the recipient's presence, but in the recipient's presence, even a coerced gift is valid.

items.text: Rav Pappa's second challenge
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's second challenge
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa (or Rav Shimi bar Ashi) challenges again: perhaps even in his presence, only a willing gift is valid, not a coerced one, and Hillel only enacted what was necessary.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa (or Rav Shimi bar Ashi) objects that perhaps even in the recipient's presence, only a willing gift is valid, and Hillel only enacted what was necessary.

items.text: Mishnah: Laws of walled cities
items.text_en: Mishnah: Laws of walled cities
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that anything inside the wall of a walled city is considered like walled city houses, except fields; Rabbi Meir includes fields. A house built into the wall is not considered a walled city house according to Rabbi Yehuda, while Rabbi Shimon says its outer wall is its wall.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah defines which areas are considered walled cities for the laws of redemption, and records disputes between Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabbi Shimon.
Rabbi Meir adds that even fields are included in the category of walled city houses.
Rabbi Yehuda rules that a house built into the wall is not considered a walled city house.
Rabbi Shimon says that the outer wall of such a house is considered its wall, making it a walled city house.

items.text: Gemara: Derivation of included structures
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation of included structures
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: Rabbi Yehuda derives from 'house' and 'which is in the city' that only houses are included, but not fields; Rabbi Meir derives from 'which is in the city' that even fields are included, and the word 'house' is used for something else.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with Rabbi Yehuda's position: the word 'בית' (house) limits the law to houses, but the phrase 'אשר בעיר' (which is in the city) includes structures like bathhouses and towers, while excluding fields.
Rabbi Meir argues that the phrase 'אשר בעיר' (which is in the city) includes even fields, and the word 'בית' (house) is used for a different derivation.

items.text: Rav Chisda's resolution of the dispute
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's resolution of the dispute
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda citing Rav Katina explains that the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda concerns the status of חולסית ומצולה (a type of pit or marsh), which a baraita states Rabbi Meir considers like houses and Rabbi Yehuda like fields.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rabbi Meir can include fields when the verse explicitly says 'house'.
Rav Chisda explains that the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda concerns specific types of land (חולסית ומצולה), with a baraita showing their respective positions.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan on the dispute about a house built in the wall
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan on the dispute about a house built in the wall
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan says that Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon both derive from the verse about Rachav: Rabbi Shimon takes it literally (the house is in the wall, so it is a walled city house), while Rabbi Yehuda says 'she dwelt in the wall' but not in a walled city.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's dispute about a house built into the wall, where Rabbi Yehuda says it is not considered a walled city house.

Rabbi Yochanan explains that both Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yehuda derive their positions from the same verse about Rahab, with Rabbi Shimon taking it literally and Rabbi Yehuda inferring that she lived in the wall, not in a walled city.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan's explanation of Rabbi Yehuda
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's explanation of Rabbi Yehuda
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that Rabbi Yehuda reads the verse as 'she dwelt in the wall' but not in a walled city, so the house is not treated as a walled city house.

items.text: Mishnah: Cities with roofs as walls and list of walled cities
items.text_en: Mishnah: Cities with roofs as walls and list of walled cities
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a city whose roofs form its wall, or that was not walled since Joshua's time, is not considered a walled city. It lists examples of walled cities: Ketzra of Tzippori, Gush Chalav, Yodfat, Gamla, Gedod, Chadid, Ono, and Jerusalem.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a city whose roofs form its wall is not considered a walled city, and lists examples of walled cities from Joshua's time.
The Mishnah lists examples of walled cities: Ketzra of Tzippori, Gush Chalav, Yodfat, Gamla, Gedod, Chadid, Ono, and Jerusalem.

items.text: Gemara: Exclusions and additional conditions
items.text_en: Gemara: Exclusions and additional conditions
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: 'wall' excludes a row of roofs, 'around' excludes Tiberias whose wall is the sea. Rabbi Eliezer bar Yosei says the verse 'which had no wall' implies even if it lacks a wall now but had one previously.

sub.desc_en: The baraita expounds the verse: 'wall' excludes a row of roofs, 'around' excludes Tiberias whose wall is the sea.
Rabbi Eliezer bar Yosei adds that the verse 'which had no wall' implies even if it lacks a wall now but had one previously.

items.text: Gemara: Clarification of the list of cities
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarification of the list of cities
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Tanna specified the locations: Gamla in the Galilee, Gedod in Transjordan, and Chadid, Ono, and Jerusalem in Judea, and asks what this adds.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Tanna's listing of cities by region, asking what the Tanna is telling us.

items.text: Abaye and Rava interpret the list of cities
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava interpret the list of cities
items.desc_en: Abaye explains that the list includes cities from different regions, while Rava argues that the list excludes cities with the same name in other lands, and that cities without duplicates needed no specification.

sub.desc_en: Abaye explains that the list of cities specifies each by its region: Gamla in the Galilee, Gedod in Transjordan, and Hadid, Ono, and Jerusalem in Judah.
Rava argues that the regional specification excludes cities with the same name in other lands, and cities without duplicates needed no such specification.

items.text: Question about Jerusalem and resolution
items.text_en: Question about Jerusalem and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Jerusalem is included since a house in Jerusalem cannot become permanently forfeited (חלוט). Rabbi Yochanan explains that the Jerusalem in the list is like Jerusalem but not identical, as houses there can become חלוט. Rav Ashi suggests there were two cities named Jerusalem.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Jerusalem can be included in the list of walled cities, since a house in Jerusalem cannot become permanently forfeited (חלוט).
Rabbi Yochanan explains that the Jerusalem in the list is like Jerusalem but not identical, as houses there can become חלוט (permanently forfeited).
Rav Ashi suggests that there were two cities named Jerusalem, resolving the difficulty.

items.text: Rabbi Yishmael bar Yosei's first teaching
items.text_en: Rabbi Yishmael bar Yosei's first teaching
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael bar Yosei explains that the Sages listed only these cities because the returnees found them and sanctified them, as the original sanctification was only temporary and did not last for the future.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael bar Yosei explains that the Sages listed only these cities because the returnees found them and sanctified them, as the original sanctification was only temporary and did not last for the future.

items.text: Contradiction and resolution from another baraita
items.text_en: Contradiction and resolution from another baraita
items.desc_en: A contradiction is raised from another baraita where Rabbi Yishmael bar Yosei says there were many more walled cities, and the returnees only listed these, not sanctified them. The baraita concludes that the original sanctification was permanent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita where Rabbi Yishmael bar Yosei says the returnees found these cities and sanctified them, but the previous baraita said they did not need to sanctify them.

The Gemara resolves that the baraita should read 'they listed them' (מְנָאוּם) rather than 'they sanctified them' (קִידְּשׁוּם), since the original sanctification was permanent and no new sanctification was needed.
The baraita concludes that any city with a tradition of being walled from Joshua's time retains all the relevant laws, because the original sanctification was permanent.

items.text: Two resolutions: different tannaim or Rabbi Elazar bar Yosei
items.text_en: Two resolutions: different tannaim or Rabbi Elazar bar Yosei
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers two resolutions: either the two baraitot are from different tannaim arguing in the name of Rabbi Yishmael, or one is from Rabbi Elazar bar Yosei, who holds that a city without a wall now but had one before is considered walled.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers the first resolution: the two conflicting baraitot are from different tannaim arguing in the name of Rabbi Yishmael.
The Gemara offers the second resolution: one of the baraitot is from Rabbi Elazar bar Yosei, who holds that a city without a wall now but had one before is considered walled.

items.text: Scriptural support for temporary sanctification and refutation
items.text_en: Scriptural support for temporary sanctification and refutation
items.desc_en: The Gemara provides a scriptural basis for the view that the first sanctification was temporary, citing a verse about Sukkot in Ezra's time. It then refutes this by showing that the verse compares the return to Joshua's conquest, implying permanent sanctification. The discussion concludes with an explanation of why Joshua did not pray for the evil inclination to be removed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural basis of the opinion that the first sanctification was temporary.

The Gemara cites the verse about Sukkot in Ezra's time and draws a comparison to Joshua's conquest, implying that the returnees renewed the counting of Sabbatical and Jubilee years and the sanctification of walled cities.
The Gemara adds another verse that compares the inheritance of the returnees to that of the ancestors, requiring a renewal of all these practices.

sub.text: Gemara's answer for the other opinion
sub.text_en: Gemara's answer for the other opinion
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the other opinion holds that Joshua's generation prayed for the removal of the evil inclination of idolatry, and their merit protected them like a sukkah, so no renewal was needed.

The Gemara notes that the verse uses the variant name 'יֵשׁוּעַ' for Joshua, and questions why Joshua did not pray for the removal of the evil inclination, given that he had the merit of the Land of Israel.

The Gemara resolves that the verse itself indicates that because the ancestors already inherited, the later generation inherits automatically without needing to pray for the removal of the evil inclination.

items.text: Challenge regarding counting Jubilee years and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge regarding counting Jubilee years and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Ezra could count Jubilee years when they had ceased after the exile of the two and a half tribes. It cites a baraita that Jubilee only applies when all inhabitants are on the land and properly settled. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves that they counted Jubilee years only for the purpose of sanctifying Sabbatical years.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Ezra could have counted Sabbatical and Jubilee years, given that Jubilee had already ceased after the exile of the two and a half tribes.
The Gemara cites a baraita that Jubilee applies only when all inhabitants are on the land in their proper tribal order, which ceased after the exile of the two and a half tribes.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves that they counted Jubilee years only for the purpose of sanctifying Sabbatical years.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's counting of Jubilees
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's counting of Jubilees
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's statement that they did not count Sabbatical and Jubilee years, noting that this works for the Rabbis but not for Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that the fiftieth year counts for both the preceding and following cycles. The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah must not follow Rabbi Yehuda.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's counting of Jubilees, noting that it works for the Rabbis but not for Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that the fiftieth year counts for both cycles, making the count redundant.
The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah must not follow Rabbi Yehuda's opinion.

items.text: Contradiction from Jeremiah and resolution
items.text_en: Contradiction from Jeremiah and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from a verse in Jeremiah that implies Sabbatical years were observed, but another verse indicates they were not. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between the sold servant and the one who pierces his ear. The Gemara then notes that the verse is a rebuke, and the people did release them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: if they did not count Sabbatical years, how could Jeremiah command release in the seventh year?
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves the contradiction: the six years apply to the sold servant, the seven to the one who pierces his ear.
The Gemara notes that the verse is a rebuke, and the people did release them, confirming the observance.

items.text: Jeremiah returned them and Josiah ruled over them
items.text_en: Jeremiah returned them and Josiah ruled over them
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that Jeremiah returned the Jewish slaves, and Josiah ruled over them. The Gemara proves this from a verse about the seller not returning, implying that Jeremiah restored them. It further proves Josiah's rule from a verse about his visit to Bethel. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak offers an alternative proof.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan answers that Jeremiah returned the Jewish slaves and Josiah ruled over them, proving the return from the verse 'for the seller shall not return to the sold item' — implying Jeremiah restored them despite the Jubilee being nullified.
The Gemara proves Josiah's rule from the verse about his visit to Bethel, asking about the monument there.
The Gemara explains that Josiah's presence in Betel shows he ruled over the returned slaves.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak offers an alternative proof from the verse 'גַּם יְהוּדָה שָׁת קָצִיר לָךְ בְּשׁוּבִי שְׁבוּת עַמִּי'.

items.text: Mishnah: The unique law of courtyard houses
items.text_en: Mishnah: The unique law of courtyard houses
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that courtyard houses (בתי החצרים) have a special leniency: they combine the advantages of walled cities (redeemable immediately and for twelve months) and fields (redeemable with deduction and return in Jubilee).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that courtyard houses combine the leniencies of walled-city houses and fields.

items.text: Gemara: Derivation from verses
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation from verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that derives the law of courtyard houses from the verse 'על שדה הארץ יחשב', comparing them to ancestral fields. It then limits the comparison: they are not redeemed after two years like fields, but immediately, and they do return in Jubilee.

sub.desc_en: The baraita begins with a derivation from the verse 'על שדה הארץ יחשב', making a verbal analogy between courtyard houses (בתי חצרים) and ancestral fields (שדה אחוזה), establishing that courtyard houses also are redeemed using the גרעון כסף (deduction of value) and return in יובל (Jubilee).
The Gemara raises an objection: perhaps the analogy to ancestral fields is complete, and courtyard houses also cannot be redeemed within less than two years (as with fields)?
The Gemara answers by citing the verse 'גאולה תהיה לו' (a redemption shall be for it), which teaches that the redemption may take place immediately, distinguishing courtyard houses from fields.
The Gemara considers another potential limitation: since their redemption is immediate like houses, perhaps they also do not return in the Jubilee year (like walled-city houses)?
The Gemara rejects the hypothetical by quoting the continuation of the verse 'וביובל יצא' (and in the Jubilee it shall go out), establishing that courtyard houses indeed return in the Jubilee.

items.text: Rav Huna's explanation of the baraita
items.text_en: Rav Huna's explanation of the baraita
items.desc_en: Rav Huna explains that the baraita is needed for a case where one consecrates a courtyard house, another redeems it from the Temple, and the Jubilee arrives in the second year. Without the verse, one might think it is either fully acquired by the buyer (like a walled city) or goes to the priests (like a field), so the verse teaches it returns to the original owner.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the baraita means.
Rav Huna explains that the baraita is needed for a case where one consecrates a courtyard house, another redeems it, and the Jubilee arrives in the second year.

Rav Huna argues that without the verse, one might think the house is either fully acquired by the buyer (like a walled city) or goes to the priests (like a field), so the verse teaches it returns to the original owner.

items.text: Rav Zeira's objection and Abaye's response
items.text_en: Rav Zeira's objection and Abaye's response
items.desc_en: Rav Zeira objects that the same should apply even if the original owner himself redeems it. Abaye responds that this is to prevent the notion that consecrated property goes out without redemption. The Gemara derives this from the law of a Levite, whose consecrated property requires redemption, and applies it to an Israelite.
