sub.desc_en: Rav Zeira objects that the same rule should apply even if the original owner himself redeems it, not only when another redeems it.
Abaye responds that the rule prevents the notion that consecrated property goes out without redemption.
The Gemara derives the principle from the law of a Levite, whose consecrated property requires redemption, and applies it to an Israelite.
A baraita is cited to show that a Levite's sold property goes out for free, but consecrated property does not go out without redemption.

items.text: Dispute with Rabbi Oshaya and support for Rav Huna
items.text_en: Dispute with Rabbi Oshaya and support for Rav Huna
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that this disagrees with Rabbi Oshaya, who holds that all consecrated property returns to the owner in Jubilee without redemption. Rav Papa explains that the verse 'וביובל יצא' is needed for a case where one sells a courtyard house and the Jubilee arrives in the second year. A baraita supports Rav Huna and refutes Rabbi Oshaya.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the previous baraita disagrees with Rabbi Oshaya, who holds that all consecrated property returns to the owner in Jubilee without redemption.
Rabbi Oshaya explains that the verse about a field returning to priests in Jubilee is specific to fields, but other consecrated property remains as is.
The Gemara asks why the verse 'וביובל יצא' (and in the Jubilee it shall go out) is needed according to Rabbi Oshaya.
Rav Papa answers that the verse is needed for a case where one sells a courtyard house and the Jubilee arrives in the second year.

Rav Papa explains that without the verse, one might compare it to a walled city house (which is permanently acquired by the buyer) or to a field (which requires completion of years), so the verse clarifies that it returns in Jubilee.

A baraita is cited that supports Rav Huna and refutes Rabbi Oshaya, stating that if one consecrates a courtyard house and another redeems it, and the Jubilee arrives without redemption, it returns to the original owner in Jubilee.

items.text: Definition of בתי החצרים
items.text_en: Definition of בתי החצרים
items.desc_en: The Mishnah defines 'houses of courtyards' as two courtyards with two houses each, even if walled since Joshua's time. The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from the verse 'which have no wall' that even if they have a wall, they are considered as having none, and specifies the minimum number of houses and courtyards.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah defines 'houses of courtyards' as two courtyards with two houses each, even if walled since Joshua's time.
The baraita derives from the verse 'which have no wall' that even if they have a wall, they are considered as having none, and specifies the minimum number of houses and courtyards.

The Gemara objects that the phrase could mean one house and one courtyard, and explains that if so the verse would have written only 'courtyards', and a courtyard without a house is called an enclosure (קרפף).

items.text: Levitical redemption rules
items.text_en: Levitical redemption rules
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that an Israelite who inherits from a Levite father or a Levite who inherits from an Israelite father does not redeem according to the standard order. Rabbi derives this from the verse 'for the houses of the cities of the Levites are their possession', requiring both a Levite and Levitical cities. The Sages limit this to Levitical cities only.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that an Israelite who inherits from a Levite father does not redeem according to the standard order.
The Mishnah adds that likewise a Levite who inherits from an Israelite father does not redeem according to the standard order.
The Mishnah cites the verse 'for the houses of the cities of the Levites are their possession' and presents Rabbi's position that both a Levite and Levitical cities are required.
The Sages state that these matters are said only regarding Levitical cities, not requiring the seller to be a Levite.

items.text: Gemara on Levitical redemption
items.text_en: Gemara on Levitical redemption
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah's ruling applies to a Levite who inherits from an Israelite, not a full Levite. It derives the requirement for a Levite from the verse 'and if a man redeems from the Levites', and excludes a Levite who is a mamzer or a netin. The Sages maintain that the requirement for a Levite is not stated.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: If the Mishnah's ruling does not apply to a full Levite, then to whom does it apply? It answers: to a Levite's son (i.e., an Israelite who inherits from a Levite father).

The Gemara clarifies the Mishnah's wording: 'He does not redeem according to this order' means that the redemption rule applies only when the seller is both a Levite and the city is a Levitical city, according to Rabbi.
The Gemara derives the requirement for a Levite from the verse 'and if a man redeems from the Levites' (וַאֲשֶׁר יִגְאַל מִן הַלְוִיִּם).

A baraita expounds the verse: one might think a Levite can redeem only from an Israelite (where one's power is strengthened and the other's weakened), but not from another Levite; therefore the verse says 'from the Levites' to include all cases.
The baraita concludes: 'from the Levites' excludes a Levite who is a mamzer (ממזר) or a netin (נתין), i.e., those of impaired lineage.

items.text: Sages' position on Levitical redemption
items.text_en: Sages' position on Levitical redemption
items.desc_en: The Sages explicitly state that the requirement for a Levite is not applied; only the requirement for Levitical cities is relevant.

sub.desc_en: The Sages state that the requirement for a Levite is not applied; only the requirement for Levitical cities is relevant.

items.text: Prohibition against changing land use in Levitical cities
items.text_en: Prohibition against changing land use in Levitical cities
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not convert a field into a suburb, a suburb into a field, a suburb into a city, or a city into a suburb. Rabbi Elazar limits this to Levitical cities; in Israelite cities, one may convert a field into a suburb but not vice versa, to avoid destroying cities. Priests and Levites may sell and redeem forever, as per the verse.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the general prohibition against changing land use categories in Levitical cities.
Rabbi Elazar limits the prohibition to Levitical cities; in Israelite cities, converting a field to a suburb is permitted but not vice versa, to avoid destroying cities.
The Mishnah adds that priests and Levites may sell and redeem forever, citing the verse 'גְּאוּלַּת עוֹלָם תִּהְיֶה לַלְוִיִּם' (a perpetual redemption right shall be for the Levites).

items.text: Source for prohibition in Levitical cities
items.text_en: Source for prohibition in Levitical cities
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the prohibition against changing land use in Levitical cities. Rabbi Elazar cites the verse 'and the field of the suburb of their cities shall not be sold', interpreting 'not be sold' as 'not be changed'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the prohibition against changing land use in Levitical cities.

Rabbi Elazar cites the verse 'וּשְׂדֵה מִגְרַשׁ עָרֵיהֶם לֹא יִמָּכֵר' and interprets 'לֹא יִמָּכֵר' as 'לֹא יְשַׁנֶּה' (not be changed), deriving the prohibition from the fact that the verse cannot mean a total ban on sale, since Levites may sell.

items.text: Derivation of perpetual redemption for Levites
items.text_en: Derivation of perpetual redemption for Levites
items.desc_en: A baraita derives from the verse 'eternal redemption shall be for the Levites' that Levites may redeem their sold property at any time, unlike Israelites who are limited by the Jubilee cycle, the sanctification of the field, or the permanent sale of a walled city.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by citing the verse 'גאולת עולם תהיה ללוים' (eternal redemption shall be for the Levites) and asks why it is necessary, given the verse about selling according to the number of harvest years.

The baraita provides a second derivation: since it is stated that a dedicated field becomes holy to God at the Jubilee, one might think this applies to a Levite's field, so the verse teaches that the Levite may always redeem it.

The baraita provides a third derivation: since it is stated that a house in a walled city becomes permanent property of the buyer, one might think this applies to a Levite's house, so the verse teaches that the Levite may always redeem it.

items.text: Levitical cities and walled city laws
items.text_en: Levitical cities and walled city laws
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Levitical cities can have walled city laws when they are medium-sized towns, not large cities. Rav Kahana resolves that it depends on whether the wall was built before or after settlement. A baraita supports that only a wall built before settlement qualifies. Rav Yosef bar Rav Sala Chasida explains that the case is where the wall was built by gentiles before settlement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Levitical cities can have walled city laws when they are described as medium-sized towns, not large walled cities.
Rav Kahana resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a city walled before settlement and one settled before being walled.
The Gemara objects that a city settled before being walled does not qualify as a walled city, citing a baraita that requires the wall to precede settlement.
The baraita further specifies that the wall must have been built by gentiles, using a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the conquest of Og.
The baraita adds that the wall must have been built by gentiles before the conquest, not after.

sub.text: Rav Yosef bar Rav Sala Chasida
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef bar Rav Sala Chasida
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef bar Rav Sala Chasida explains before Rav Pappa that the case involves walled cities that fell to the Levites by lottery.

items.text: Rav Ashi's explanation of the Mishnah's phrase
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's explanation of the Mishnah's phrase
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains why the Mishnah repeats 'them and their open spaces' — to teach that even if the houses are hidden and sold, they do not become subject to the Jubilee laws.

sub.desc_en: The gemara notes that the Mishnah's repeated phrase 'them and their open spaces' refers to houses that are hidden.
Rav Ashi explains that the repetition is necessary, lest one think that if the hidden houses are sold they become subject to Jubilee; the Mishnah teaches that they do not.

items.text: Baraita on a priest consecrating his own field
items.text_en: Baraita on a priest consecrating his own field
items.desc_en: The baraita derives from a verse that a priest who consecrates his own field cannot keep it; it must be distributed to his fellow priests, analogous to an Israelite's field that goes to priests in the Jubilee.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with a question: from where do we derive that a priest who consecrates his own field cannot keep it, since he might argue that it should remain his as it is already destined for priests?
The baraita presents a logical argument (דין) that if the priest acquires fields of others, surely he should acquire his own, and then cites a verse to refute this.
The baraita resolves by drawing an analogy (היקש) between the priest's consecrated field and an Israelite's ancestral field: both leave the owner's hand and are distributed to the priests.

items.text: Objection to the baraita's logic
items.text_en: Objection to the baraita's logic
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects to the baraita's kal va'chomer argument: in the case of others, the priest merely acquires, but here he takes it for himself, so the analogy fails.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects to the baraita's kal va'chomer (a fortiori) argument: in the case of others, the priest merely acquires (זוכה בעלמא), but here he takes it for himself (קא שקיל ליה), so the analogy fails.

items.text: Rami bar Chama's answer
items.text_en: Rami bar Chama's answer
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama suggests the verse 'And a man's sacred items shall be his' might imply the priest's consecrated field is his, so the baraita is needed to reject that.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama explains that the baraita is necessary because one might think the verse 'וְאִישׁ אֶת קֳדָשָׁיו לוֹ יִהְיוּ' (And a man's sacred items shall be his) implies the priest's consecrated field is his, so the baraita teaches otherwise.

items.text: Rejection of Rami bar Chama's answer
items.text_en: Rejection of Rami bar Chama's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects Rami bar Chama's answer: sacred items are not in his possession, but here the field is in his possession, so the analogy does not hold.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects Rami bar Chama's answer by distinguishing sacred items (קדשיו), which are not in the owner's possession, from the field here, which is in the owner's possession.

items.text: Rav Nachman's answer
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's answer
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman explains that the verse 'for it is an eternal possession for them' might imply the priest's field is his possession, so the baraita teaches that only his 'possession' (inherited field) is his, but not his 'cherem' (consecrated field).

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman answers that the verse 'כי אחזת עולם הוא להם' (for it is an eternal possession for them) might imply the priest's field is his possession, so the baraita teaches that only his 'אחוזתו' (inherited field) is his, but not his 'חרמו' (consecrated field).

items.text: Conclusion of the chapter and tractate
items.text_en: Conclusion of the chapter and tractate
items.desc_en: The daf concludes with the standard formula ending the chapter and the entire tractate of Arakhin.

sub.desc_en: The daf concludes with the standard formula ending the chapter and the entire tractate of Arakhin.
